lessons.plain: Monitoring means watching numbers and records from your systems so you notice trouble before customers do. On AWS, three services split the job. Amazon CloudWatch collects performance numbers, such as CPU use or error counts, and stores application log lines. AWS CloudTrail keeps an audit record of who changed what in your account. Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus is a hosted store for metrics from container platforms such as Kubernetes. Think of a shop: CloudWatch is the till total and the shop diary, CloudTrail is the security camera at the office door, and Prometheus is a specialist meter fitted to one busy machine.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your web server started failing at 10:02, and you suspect someone changed a firewall setting a minute earlier. Which kind of record would show you who made that change: a CPU graph, the application's error log, or a log of every administrative action taken in the account?
lessons.teach:
Amazon CloudWatch is AWS's managed monitoring service. A metric is a time-ordered series of numbers, such as CPU percent. Metrics are grouped under a namespace, a label like AWS/EC2, and narrowed by dimensions, which are name-value pairs such as InstanceId=i-123. Many AWS services publish metrics automatically. EC2 virtual servers send them every five minutes by default, or every minute if you turn on detailed monitoring. CloudWatch Logs stores text. Each source writes to a log stream, and related streams sit together in a log group. On the log group you set retention, which is how long lines are kept. A metric filter scans new incoming lines for a pattern and turns each match into a metric. It does not look back at lines that arrived before you created it.

AWS CloudTrail is an audit log of API calls: who called which action, from where, and when. Management events are actions that create, change or delete resources. They appear in a 90-day event history with no setup. A trail is a configuration that keeps events longer by delivering them to an S3 bucket, and it can also send them to CloudWatch Logs. Data events, such as reading an object in S3, are recorded only if you enable them on a trail.

Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus is a hosted store for metrics in the Prometheus format, which is common on Kubernetes. You create a workspace, an isolated store for your metrics. A collector scrapes metrics from your containers and pushes them into the workspace using remote write, the standard Prometheus method for sending metrics to another store. You query the data with PromQL, Prometheus's query language.

Worked example: an orders API starts returning errors. Step 1: the app writes its lines to the log group /orders/api. Step 2: a metric filter matching "ERROR" publishes a metric called OrdersErrors. Step 3: the graph of OrdersErrors spikes at 10:02. Step 4: CloudTrail shows a security group change at 10:01, made by a named role. The metric told you when, the logs told you what, and CloudTrail told you who.

Common mistake: leaving log group retention at its default, which is never expire, or assuming the 90-day event history includes data events. The first quietly grows your storage bill. The second means the evidence an investigation needs was never recorded.

questions.prompt: A logistics company called Tidewater runs its tracking app in containers on Kubernetes. The app already exposes metrics in the Prometheus format. The team wants those metrics kept in a hosted store instead of running their own Prometheus server. Step 1: they create an Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus workspace named tracking-prod. This is an isolated store for their metrics. Step 2: [missing]. Step 3: an engineer runs a PromQL query against tracking-prod and sees a request-rate line for the past hour. Which choice correctly fills Step 2?
choices: Create a CloudTrail trail that delivers the containers' API events into the tracking-prod workspace
Turn on detailed monitoring so the containers publish metrics every minute instead of every five
Set up a collector that scrapes the containers' metrics and sends them to tracking-prod using remote write
Create a CloudWatch Logs metric filter on the tracking-prod log group that matches the word "request"
questions.why: Data reaches a Managed Service for Prometheus workspace when a collector scrapes the containers and pushes the metrics in with remote write, the standard Prometheus way of sending metrics to another store.

questions.prompt: A media company graphs the CloudWatch metric CPUUtilization under the namespace AWS/EC2. It wants the graph to show only one virtual server, the one whose ID is i-0abc77. What narrows the metric to that single server?
choices: A log stream named i-0abc77 inside a log group
A new namespace called AWS/EC2/i-0abc77
A dimension, the name-value pair InstanceId=i-0abc77
A CloudTrail trail filtered to the instance i-0abc77
questions.why: Dimensions are name-value pairs that narrow a metric within its namespace, so InstanceId=i-0abc77 selects that one server.

questions.prompt: At a ticketing firm, the checkout service wrote 40 lines containing "TIMEOUT" to its CloudWatch Logs log group between 08:00 and 08:45. At 09:00 an engineer creates a metric filter matching "TIMEOUT". Between 09:00 and 09:30, 6 more matching lines arrive. How many matches will the new metric count for the whole 08:00 to 09:30 window?
choices: 40, because only lines from before the filter existed are counted
6, because a metric filter only scans lines that arrive after it is created
46, because the filter scans the entire log group when it is created
0, because metric filters only work on log groups with a set retention
questions.why: A metric filter only examines new incoming lines, so the 40 earlier lines are never counted and only the 6 later ones become metric data.

questions.prompt: A clinic's security team learns that someone may have downloaded patient files from an S3 bucket 30 days ago. The account has never had a CloudTrail trail configured. What will they find when they search CloudTrail?
choices: Each download is in the 90-day event history, because all API calls are recorded automatically
The downloads are shown only in CloudWatch metrics under the namespace AWS/S3
No record of anything, because CloudTrail keeps nothing at all without a trail
No record of the downloads, because reading S3 objects is a data event and is only recorded when enabled on a trail
questions.why: The 90-day event history holds management events with no setup, but data events such as reading S3 objects are captured only if enabled on a trail, so the evidence was never recorded.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how CloudWatch, CloudTrail and Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus divide the monitoring job, and name one limit or setting that catches people out.
lessons.modelAnswer: CloudWatch handles performance. Metrics are numeric time series, organised by namespace and dimensions. CloudWatch Logs holds application text in log groups and streams, and a metric filter can turn matching lines, like ERROR, into a metric you can graph. CloudTrail answers who did what. It records API calls, and management events sit in a free 90-day history. For anything longer, you need a trail that delivers to S3 and optionally to CloudWatch Logs. Data events, such as S3 object reads, have to be switched on explicitly. Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus is a hosted workspace for Prometheus-format metrics, mostly from Kubernetes. Collectors push data in with remote write, and you query it with PromQL. Two things catch people out. Log groups keep data forever unless you set retention, which costs money. And a metric filter only counts lines that arrive after you create it.
rubricPoints: CloudWatch metrics are numeric time series identified by namespace and dimensions.
CloudWatch Logs organises lines into log groups and streams, and retention is set per log group.
A metric filter turns matching log lines into a metric, counting only new lines.
CloudTrail records API calls; 90-day management history is automatic, and a trail is needed for longer storage and data events.
Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus stores Prometheus-format metrics in a workspace, fed by remote write and queried with PromQL.
Names a real limit, such as never-expire default retention, data events being off by default, or five-minute basic EC2 metrics.

suggested.rationale: The core skill is choosing which service and setting answers a given question, such as who changed something, when errors began, or why the evidence is missing, and exam-style scenarios practise that choice best.

lessons.plain: Different kinds of workloads leave different clues when they go wrong. A virtual server you run yourself has a machine you can measure: how busy its processor is, how full its memory and disk are. A serverless function has no machine you can see, so you watch each request instead: how many ran, how long they took, how many failed or were turned away. An AI model service adds its own clues: how long each answer takes, how much text went in and out, and whether you hit a usage cap. It is like checking a car: you read different gauges for a petrol engine, an electric one, and a hired taxi.
lessons.guessPrompt: If your code runs as a serverless function with no server you can log into, what would you watch instead of the server's CPU to tell whether it is struggling?
lessons.teach:
Workload shape means how your code is hosted, and it decides which signals exist by default and which you must add yourself. Amazon CloudWatch is the AWS service that stores metrics, which are numbers recorded over time, and logs, which are text records of events.

Compute means virtual servers you manage, such as Amazon EC2 instances. You own the operating system. CloudWatch gets the metrics visible from outside the machine at no extra setup: CPUUtilization, network and disk traffic, and status checks, which are pass-or-fail tests of the underlying host and of the instance itself. Memory use and free disk space live inside the operating system, so they appear only if you install the CloudWatch agent, a small program that sends operating-system metrics and log files to CloudWatch.

Serverless means code that runs on demand with no server for you to manage, such as AWS Lambda functions. Host CPU is not something you watch. Instead you watch per-request behaviour: Invocations (how many calls), Errors, Duration (run time per call), Throttles (calls refused because the concurrency limit, the cap on simultaneous copies, was reached), ConcurrentExecutions, and for queue or stream triggers, IteratorAge, the age of the oldest record not yet processed. Function logs flow to CloudWatch Logs automatically.

AI workloads, such as a managed model service like Amazon Bedrock or a hosted model endpoint on Amazon SageMaker, add latency per call, throttling against a request or token quota, and token counts, meaning the pieces of text going in and out, which drive both cost and speed. If you host a model on your own GPU instances, GPU utilization and GPU memory are collected by an agent, just like memory on EC2. A model can also reply quickly with a valid but wrong answer, so quality checks sit beside the metrics.

Worked example: users report the app is slow. On EC2, CPUUtilization reads 95 percent, so the server is saturated. On Lambda, there is no host CPU graph to check; Duration is flat but Throttles jumped, so calls are being refused and retried. On Bedrock, invocation latency rose together with output token count, because a prompt change made answers longer.

Common mistake: using one dashboard for every shape, such as hunting for CPU on a function or expecting EC2 memory without the agent. In production the alarm you needed never existed, so customers find the outage before your monitoring does.

questions.prompt:
A ticket-resale company runs an AWS Lambda function that reads purchase records from a stream. Customers say confirmations arrive late. The on-call engineer works through it:

Step 1: This is a serverless workload, so there is no host CPU graph to check. Per-request metrics are what matter.
Step 2: Errors stay at 0 and Duration holds steady at about 120 ms per call, so each call is healthy and quick.
Step 3: ???
Step 4: The function is falling behind the stream, so the engineer adds an alarm on that metric to catch the backlog next time.

Which choice is the missing Step 3?
choices: Check IteratorAge, which climbed from 3 seconds to 35 minutes, so old records are waiting unprocessed
Check Invocations, which are high, and conclude that a high call count means the backlog is cleared
Open the CPUUtilization graph for the function's host and look for a reading near 100 percent
Install the CloudWatch agent on the function so that its memory use appears as a metric
questions.why: For a stream-triggered function, IteratorAge is the age of the oldest unprocessed record, so a rising value shows a growing backlog even while each call stays fast and error-free.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm runs its routing service on Amazon EC2 instances. An engineer wants an alarm when memory use goes above 85 percent, but finds no memory metric in CloudWatch, even though CPUUtilization and status checks are there. What explains this?
choices: Memory use lives inside the operating system, so it appears only after the CloudWatch agent is installed
Memory is folded into CPUUtilization, so the engineer should alarm on CPU above 85 percent
Memory appears only after status checks fail, so the alarm must be built on status checks
Memory is reported only for serverless functions, so the service must move to Lambda first
questions.why: CloudWatch sees EC2 metrics visible from outside the machine by default, while memory is inside the operating system and needs the CloudWatch agent to send it.

questions.prompt: A law office uses Amazon Bedrock, a managed model service, to summarize case files. Over one month the number of calls stayed about the same, but the bill doubled and each reply took longer. Which signal most directly explains both changes?
choices: GPU utilization, because the managed model's graphics processors must be saturated
CPUUtilization, because the model is running out of processor capacity
Throttles, because refused calls are the main driver of cost
Token counts, because more text going in or out raises both cost and response time
questions.why: Token counts measure the text going into and out of the model, and they drive both cost and speed, so longer inputs or outputs explain a higher bill and slower replies with the same number of calls.

questions.prompt: A travel agency's support chatbot calls a hosted model endpoint on Amazon SageMaker. Latency is 300 ms, there are no throttles and no errors, yet customers complain that the bot states the wrong baggage policy. What is missing from this monitoring?
choices: The CloudWatch agent for GPU memory, because low GPU memory produces wrong facts
An alarm on IteratorAge, because old records in a queue make answers inaccurate
An alarm on Throttles, because refused calls cause the model to answer incorrectly
Quality checks on the answers, because a model can reply quickly with a valid but wrong answer
questions.why: Latency, throttling and error metrics only show that calls succeed. A model can return a fast, valid but wrong answer, so quality checks have to sit beside the metrics.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how monitoring changes between an EC2-based app, a Lambda-based app, and an app that calls an AI model service, and name one blind spot or tradeoff each shape brings.
lessons.modelAnswer: What we watch depends on who owns the machine. On EC2 we own the operating system, so we get CPU, network, disk traffic and status checks for free, but memory and disk-space usage need the CloudWatch agent; forget it and we are blind to memory leaks or full disks. With Lambda there is no host to watch, so we track invocations, errors, duration, throttles, concurrency and, for queue or stream triggers, iterator age. The tradeoff is less to manage but no host-level view, so a throttle spike can be the only clue. For an AI model service we add per-call latency, token counts and quota throttling; tokens tie speed and cost together. The blind spot there is quality: a model can answer fast and still be wrong, so metrics alone do not prove it works.
rubricPoints: States that the hosting shape decides which metrics exist by default and which must be added.
Notes EC2 gives CPU and status checks free but memory and disk space need the CloudWatch agent.
Names Lambda's per-request signals such as duration, errors, throttles, concurrency or iterator age.
Names AI signals such as latency, token counts and quota throttling.
Identifies a limit, such as no host view in serverless or answer quality not shown by metrics.

suggested.rationale: Diagnosing a throttling function from its request metrics, with no server to inspect, makes the learner practise the core shift from host signals to per-request signals.

lessons.plain: The CloudWatch agent is a small program you install on a server, or run beside your containers, so it can report what happens inside the machine. Out of the box, AWS watches your virtual servers from the outside. It sees CPU and network traffic, but not how full the memory or disk is. It also cannot read your application's log files. The agent works like a meter reader who goes inside the building. It collects those inside numbers and log lines and sends them to Amazon CloudWatch, AWS's central monitoring service. There you can graph them, search them and raise alarms on them.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your web server on a virtual machine keeps crashing because it runs out of memory. The monitoring console shows CPU and network graphs for it, but no memory graph. Why might the memory number be missing?
lessons.teach:
The CloudWatch agent is software that collects operating-system metrics and log files and pushes them to Amazon CloudWatch. A metric is a number measured over time. Default EC2 (virtual server) metrics come from the hypervisor, the layer that runs the virtual machine. The hypervisor cannot see inside the guest operating system, so memory use, disk-space use and your log files are invisible until something inside reports them.

The agent reads a JSON configuration file. That file lists which metrics to collect, such as mem_used_percent or disk_used_percent, and which log files to tail. Custom metrics land in the CWAgent namespace by default (a namespace is a named folder for metrics). Logs go to log groups in CloudWatch Logs. The agent also needs permission to write data. You grant it through an IAM role, an identity that AWS hands to the instance through an instance profile. That role should carry the CloudWatchAgentServerPolicy managed policy.

Worked example: you want a memory alarm on an EC2 fleet. First, attach a role with that policy to the instances. Second, install the agent package on all of them at once using Systems Manager Run Command (a remote command service) with the AWS-ConfigureAWSPackage document. Third, write the configuration and store it in Systems Manager Parameter Store, a central key-value store, so every instance shares one copy. Fourth, start the agent pointed at that parameter. Finally, check the CWAgent namespace for mem_used_percent, and then build the alarm.

On Amazon ECS (a managed container service), the agent runs as a daemon service, which places one copy on every container host. On Amazon EKS (managed Kubernetes), the Amazon CloudWatch Observability add-on deploys the agent as a DaemonSet, meaning one pod per node, alongside Fluent Bit for logs. Both setups feed Container Insights, CloudWatch's container view.

A common mistake is installing the agent but forgetting the IAM role. The agent runs, but every write is denied, so no data arrives. In a running system, an alarm built on that missing metric sits in INSUFFICIENT_DATA and never warns you before memory runs out.

questions.prompt: A logistics company runs 25 Linux EC2 instances that host a parcel-tracking app. An engineer built an alarm on disk_used_percent, but it has sat in INSUFFICIENT_DATA for two days. She troubleshoots as follows. Step 1: she confirms the CloudWatch agent (the software inside the instance that reports operating-system metrics and log files) is installed and running on the instances. Step 2: she opens the agent's JSON configuration and confirms that disk_used_percent is listed. Step 3: [missing]. Step 4: after her fix, disk_used_percent starts appearing in the CWAgent namespace (the named folder where the agent's custom metrics land), and the alarm leaves INSUFFICIENT_DATA. Which action belongs in Step 3?
choices: Edit the configuration so the agent writes disk_used_percent into the AWS/EC2 namespace, not CWAgent
Turn off the agent and rely on the default EC2 metrics, because the hypervisor already reports disk-space use
Reinstall the agent package with Systems Manager Run Command, because a running agent that sends nothing must be corrupted
Check that the instances have an IAM role, passed to them through an instance profile, that carries the CloudWatchAgentServerPolicy managed policy, and attach it if it is missing
questions.why: An agent that is running and correctly configured but has no IAM role with write permission has every write denied, so the fix is to give the instances the role with CloudWatchAgentServerPolicy.

questions.prompt: A design studio's EC2 render server keeps crashing when it runs out of memory, yet the default EC2 metrics in CloudWatch never showed memory use. Why not?
choices: Default EC2 metrics do include memory, but they are kept in the CWAgent namespace
Memory is reported only after an alarm on it has been created
Default EC2 metrics come from the hypervisor, the layer that runs the virtual machine, and it cannot see memory use inside the guest operating system
Memory metrics are only collected for instances inside Amazon ECS or Amazon EKS clusters
questions.why: The hypervisor sees the virtual machine only from outside, so memory, disk-space use and log files need something inside the guest, such as the CloudWatch agent, to report them.

questions.prompt: A media company runs an Amazon ECS cluster (a managed container service) on 12 container hosts. It wants exactly one copy of the CloudWatch agent running on every host, including any hosts added later. How should the agent be run?
choices: As a DaemonSet created by the Amazon CloudWatch Observability add-on
By storing the configuration in Parameter Store, which starts the agent on each host by itself
As an ECS daemon service, which places one copy of the agent on every container host
As a single ECS task with one replica, which reports for the whole cluster
questions.why: On ECS, a daemon service is what places one copy of the agent on each container host; the Observability add-on and DaemonSets belong to EKS.

questions.prompt: A retail team adds the Amazon CloudWatch Observability add-on to its Amazon EKS cluster (managed Kubernetes), which has 8 worker nodes. What does the add-on set up?
choices: One agent pod for the whole cluster that reads metrics from all 8 nodes over the network
An IAM role with CloudWatchAgentServerPolicy, with no agent, because EKS sends node memory metrics by default
The CloudWatch agent as a DaemonSet, meaning one pod on each of the 8 nodes, plus Fluent Bit for logs, feeding Container Insights
A Systems Manager Run Command job that installs the agent package once on each node
questions.why: The add-on deploys the agent as a DaemonSet, one pod per node, alongside Fluent Bit for logs, and both feed CloudWatch's Container Insights view.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why we need the CloudWatch agent at all, and how you would roll it out across EC2, ECS and EKS. Name one limit or tradeoff.
lessons.modelAnswer: Default EC2 metrics come from the hypervisor, so they show CPU, network and disk I/O, but not memory use, disk-space use or our log files. The CloudWatch agent runs inside the instance and sends those to CloudWatch. Metrics go to the CWAgent namespace and logs go to log groups. On EC2, I would attach a role with CloudWatchAgentServerPolicy and install the agent with Systems Manager Run Command. I would keep one JSON config in Parameter Store so the whole fleet stays consistent. On ECS, I would run it as a daemon service, one per host. On EKS, I would use the CloudWatch Observability add-on, which runs it as a DaemonSet with Fluent Bit. One tradeoff is cost: agent metrics are custom metrics and log ingestion is billed, so we should collect only what we will alarm on or investigate. Another limit is that if the role is missing, data silently never arrives.
rubricPoints: States that default EC2 metrics lack memory, disk-space and log data because they come from outside the guest OS.
Says the agent needs an IAM role such as CloudWatchAgentServerPolicy to write to CloudWatch.
Describes a JSON config, ideally shared through Parameter Store, and installing it through Systems Manager.
Distinguishes deployment: daemon service on ECS, DaemonSet or Observability add-on on EKS.
Names a limit or tradeoff, such as custom-metric and log costs or silent failure without permissions.

suggested.rationale: No mission or planned engine installs the agent, so the most useful practice is reasoning through exam-style cases, such as a missing memory metric or an agent that runs without permission.

lessons.plain: A CloudWatch alarm is a watcher that keeps looking at one number over time, such as a server's CPU use, and changes its mood when that number crosses a line you chose. When it changes, it can do something: send a message, restart a machine, or add capacity. A composite alarm is a watcher of watchers: it looks at several alarms and only speaks up when a combination you describe is true. Think of a smoke detector that rings on its own, versus a building system that calls the fire brigade only when smoke and heat are both detected.
lessons.guessPrompt: If a web server's CPU briefly spikes to 95% for one minute every hour but is otherwise calm, should an alarm wake an engineer every time? What rule would you use instead?
lessons.teach:
A metric alarm in Amazon CloudWatch (the AWS monitoring service) watches one metric, a time series of numbers such as CPUUtilization. You choose a statistic (Average, Maximum, Sum and so on), a period (the time bucket each data point covers, for example 5 minutes), a threshold with a comparison (greater than 80), and how many periods must breach. The 'M out of N' setting means: of the last N evaluation periods, at least M data points must breach. The alarm sits in one of three states: OK, ALARM, or INSUFFICIENT_DATA (not enough data to decide). You also choose how missing data is treated: as breaching, not breaching, ignored, or missing.

Worked example: CPU Average greater than 80, period 5 minutes, 3 out of 3. At 10:00 the value is 85 (one breach), 10:05 is 90 (two), 10:10 is 88 (three of three), so the state moves from OK to ALARM. A single one-minute spike never fills three five-minute buckets, so it stays quiet.

Actions run on a state change. A metric alarm can notify an Amazon SNS topic (a managed publish-subscribe messaging service), take EC2 actions (stop, terminate, reboot or recover a virtual server), trigger an Auto Scaling policy (add or remove servers), invoke a Lambda function (run-on-demand code), or open a Systems Manager OpsItem or incident (an operations ticket).

A composite alarm evaluates a rule expression over other alarms using AND, OR and NOT, for example ALARM(HighCPU) AND ALARM(HighLatency). It reduces noise because you page people once, on the meaningful combination. Composite alarms cannot run EC2 or Auto Scaling actions; leave those on the underlying metric alarms. They also support action suppression, which mutes them while a chosen alarm, such as a maintenance flag, is active.

Common mistake: wiring SNS paging to every child alarm as well as the composite, which defeats its purpose and floods on-call engineers until they start ignoring alerts.

questions.prompt: A ticket-booking company puts a metric alarm on its web tier's server-error count. The settings are statistic Sum, period 1 minute, threshold greater than 10, and 2 out of 4 (of the last 4 evaluation periods, at least 2 data points must breach). The alarm starts in OK. Here is the trace. At 09:00 the Sum is 4, which is not a breach. At 09:01 the Sum is 15, so there is 1 breach among the last four periods. At 09:02 the Sum is 6, so there is still only 1 breach among the last four. At 09:03 the Sum is 12. Missing step: what happens to the alarm state at 09:03, and why?
choices: It moves to ALARM, because 2 of the last 4 data points (15 and 12) now breach.
It stays OK, because all four periods must breach before the state changes.
It stays OK, because the two breaches were not in back-to-back periods.
It moves to INSUFFICIENT_DATA, because the values keep going up and down.
questions.why: M out of N only counts how many of the last N data points breach, not whether they are in a row, so 15 and 12 make 2 breaches out of 4 and the state flips to ALARM.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm builds a composite alarm (an alarm that combines other alarms with AND, OR and NOT): ALARM(HighMemory) AND ALARM(SlowResponses). The firm wants the affected virtual server rebooted automatically when the composite goes into ALARM. They try to add an EC2 reboot action directly to the composite alarm. What should they do instead?
choices: Put the reboot on an underlying metric alarm, since composite alarms cannot run EC2 actions.
Replace the reboot with an Auto Scaling policy on the composite alarm.
Change the composite's missing-data setting to breaching so EC2 actions become allowed.
Put the reboot action on the composite alarm with OR instead of AND.
questions.why: Composite alarms cannot take EC2 or Auto Scaling actions, so those actions belong on the underlying metric alarms.

questions.prompt: A clinic's database team has two metric alarms, HighDiskQueue and HighReadLatency, and a composite alarm ALARM(HighDiskQueue) AND ALARM(HighReadLatency). All three alarms send to the same SNS (managed publish-subscribe messaging) paging topic. On-call engineers say they get three pages for every incident and have begun ignoring them. What is the best fix?
choices: Add a third child alarm so the composite becomes more specific.
Lower the threshold on both child alarms so problems are caught earlier.
Remove the SNS paging from the two child alarms and keep it only on the composite.
Switch the composite's rule from AND to OR so it fires sooner.
questions.why: A composite alarm reduces noise only if people are paged once on the meaningful combination, so paging on every child alarm defeats its purpose.

questions.prompt: An online retailer patches its servers every night, and during patching its composite alarm fires and pages people for no real reason. The team already has an alarm named PatchWindowActive that is in ALARM state only while patching runs. Which composite alarm feature keeps the composite's actions muted during patching?
choices: Adding a Lambda (run-on-demand code) action to the composite alarm
Action suppression, with PatchWindowActive chosen as the suppressor alarm
Treating missing data as ignored on the composite alarm
Setting the composite's period to longer than the patch window
questions.why: Action suppression mutes a composite alarm's actions while a chosen alarm, such as a maintenance flag, is active.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would set up alarms so a slow service pages on-call once, not five times, and name one limit or tradeoff of the approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: I'd create metric alarms for the individual signals, say average CPU above 80 and p99 latency above 2 seconds, each using a 5-minute period and something like 3 out of 3 data points so short spikes don't trip them. I'd decide how missing data is treated so a silent metric doesn't hide a problem. Those child alarms would keep their automatic actions, like an Auto Scaling policy, but no paging. Then a composite alarm with the rule ALARM(HighCPU) AND ALARM(HighLatency) would send the single SNS notification to on-call. The tradeoff: requiring several datapoints and combining alarms delays detection and could miss a problem that shows in only one signal. Also, composite alarms can't stop, reboot or scale servers themselves, so those remediation actions must stay on the metric alarms.
rubricPoints: A metric alarm compares a statistic over a period against a threshold and moves between OK, ALARM and INSUFFICIENT_DATA.
M out of N datapoints and period length control sensitivity to brief spikes.
Actions include SNS notification, EC2 actions, Auto Scaling, Lambda and Systems Manager items.
A composite alarm combines other alarms with AND, OR and NOT to cut alert noise.
Composite alarms cannot take EC2 or Auto Scaling actions, so remediation stays on metric alarms.
Names a tradeoff such as slower detection or missing a single-signal problem.

suggested.rationale: Tuning thresholds, M-of-N datapoints and composite rules against a replayed metric is learned best by building alarms and watching them change state.

lessons.plain: An alarm is a rule that watches one number over time and tells you when that number crosses a line you chose. When an alarm stays quiet during a real problem, or goes off when nothing is wrong, the rule itself is usually wrong, not the system it watches. Think of a smoke detector. It might be mounted in the wrong room. It might be set to react only to thick smoke. It might be wired to a doorbell nobody hears. Troubleshooting means checking each part of the rule in turn: what it watches, how it summarizes, when it decides, and who it tells.
lessons.guessPrompt: A server's CPU jumps to 100% for one minute, then sits at 20% for the next four minutes. An alarm averages CPU over each 5-minute window and fires above 80%. Do you think it fires? Why or why not?
lessons.teach:
An Amazon CloudWatch alarm is a managed monitoring rule. It reads a metric, which is a time series of numbers. A metric is identified by its namespace (the service or app group), its name, and its dimensions (labels such as an instance ID). The alarm sums up the metric over a period (a time window) using a statistic: Average, Maximum, Sum or a percentile. It compares each summarized value, called a datapoint, to a threshold. It goes into the ALARM state when M of the last N datapoints breach the threshold. The other states are OK and INSUFFICIENT_DATA, which means not enough data to decide. A missing-data setting tells the alarm how to treat gaps: as missing, as breaching, as not breaching, or ignored. Actions, such as publishing to a notification topic, run only when the state changes.

Worked example. Take the case from the question: an alarm on CPU, Average, 5-minute period, threshold 80, 1 of 1 datapoints. Minute one reads 100 and minutes two to five read 20. The average is (100+20+20+20+20)/5 = 36. 36 is below 80, so the state stays OK and the spike is hidden. Switching to Maximum gives 100, which breaches the threshold, and the alarm fires.

When an alarm never fires, check these in order. Is it stuck in INSUFFICIENT_DATA? That usually means the namespace, name or dimension does not match, for example the ID of an old instance that was replaced. It can also mean the alarm is in a different Region, or the period is shorter than how often the metric is published. Is the statistic hiding spikes? Is M of N too strict? Are actions disabled? Is the notification subscription unconfirmed?

Common mistake: setting missing data to breaching on a sparse metric, one that only reports when events happen, such as an error count. A quiet night with no traffic then looks like an outage, and the on-call engineer gets paged for nothing. Repeated false pages train people to ignore the alarm, so the real outage gets missed too.

questions.prompt:
A web shop called Pinecart has an alarm on API response time. It uses the Maximum statistic, a 1-minute period, a threshold of 500 ms, and needs 3 of the last 3 datapoints to breach. Over five minutes the datapoints were 620, 410, 650, 700 and 380 ms, yet the alarm never fired.

Step 1: Compare each datapoint to 500. Minutes 1, 3 and 4 breach (620, 650, 700). Minutes 2 and 5 do not (410, 380).

Step 2: ???

Step 3: Because the alarm demands an unbroken run of breaches, short dips hide a real problem. Changing the rule to 2 of the last 3 datapoints would have fired at minute 3, when 620 and 650 breach inside the window 620, 410, 650.

Which statement correctly fills in Step 2?
choices: The five datapoints average 552 ms, which is above 500, so the alarm should have gone to ALARM.
Look at each window of the last 3 datapoints: (620, 410, 650), (410, 650, 700) and (650, 700, 380). Each window has only 2 breaches, never 3, so the alarm stays OK.
The datapoints of 410 and 380 are below the threshold, so the alarm cannot decide and moves to INSUFFICIENT_DATA.
Three of the five datapoints breach, which meets the 3-breach requirement, so the alarm should be in ALARM and something else is blocking it.
questions.why: An M of N alarm checks only the most recent N datapoints, and no window of three here contains three breaches, so the alarm correctly stays OK.

questions.prompt: A logistics company has a custom metric for warehouse scanner queue length. The metric is published once every 5 minutes. An engineer creates an alarm on it with a 1-minute period, and the namespace, name and dimensions all match. The alarm sits in INSUFFICIENT_DATA most of the time. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The alarm period is shorter than how often the metric is published, so most 1-minute windows contain no data.
The statistic should be Sum instead of Average, because Average cannot handle queue lengths.
The threshold is set too high, so no datapoint ever breaches it.
The notification topic subscription has not been confirmed, so the alarm cannot leave INSUFFICIENT_DATA.
questions.why: INSUFFICIENT_DATA means there is not enough data to decide, and a 1-minute period on a metric that reports every 5 minutes leaves most windows empty.

questions.prompt: A ticket-booking site has an alarm on a payment-failure count. The metric only reports a value when a payment fails. Missing data is set to breaching. The on-call engineer is paged almost every night between 2 a.m. and 5 a.m., when hardly anyone is buying tickets, but the payment system is healthy. Which change fixes the false pages without hiding real failures?
choices: Change the region of the alarm so it matches the overnight traffic.
Switch the statistic from Sum to Average so that small counts look smaller.
Set missing data to be treated as not breaching, because no reports on this metric means no failures.
Disable the alarm actions between 2 a.m. and 5 a.m. every night.
questions.why: On a sparse metric, a gap means nothing happened, so treating gaps as not breaching stops quiet nights from looking like outages while real failure counts still trigger the alarm.

questions.prompt: A media company has an alarm on database connection errors that publishes to a notification topic. The confirmed email subscription received one message when the alarm went to ALARM at 09:00. The errors continued until 11:00, and the alarm stayed in ALARM the whole time, but no further emails arrived. The team expected an email every period. What explains this?
choices: The missing-data setting was set to ignored, which blocks repeat notifications.
The statistic was Maximum, which only reports the first breaching datapoint.
The email subscription expired after the first message and must be confirmed again.
Alarm actions run only when the state changes, and the alarm stayed in ALARM, so there was nothing new to trigger.
questions.why: Actions run only on a state change, so an alarm that enters ALARM once and stays there notifies once, not every period.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would work out why a CloudWatch alarm stayed silent during an incident. Name one tradeoff in making it more sensitive.
lessons.modelAnswer: First I check the alarm's state history. If it sat in INSUFFICIENT_DATA, the alarm isn't seeing the metric at all. The cause is usually a wrong namespace, metric name or dimension, such as an old instance ID. It could also be the wrong Region, or a period shorter than the metric's publishing interval. If it stayed OK, the data arrived but never counted as breaching. Then I look at the statistic, because Average can smooth away a short spike that Maximum or a percentile would catch. I also check the threshold and how strict the M-of-N rule is. If it did go to ALARM but nobody heard, the action side is broken: actions disabled or an unconfirmed subscription. The tradeoff is that shorter periods, Maximum, and 1-of-1 catch problems sooner but page people for brief blips. Too many false pages teach the team to ignore alarms.
rubricPoints: Uses the alarm state history to tell no-data problems apart from data that never breached.
Names metric identity mismatches (namespace, dimension, Region) as the cause of INSUFFICIENT_DATA.
Explains that the choice of statistic and period can hide spikes.
Mentions M-of-N datapoints and how missing data is treated as decision settings.
Checks the action path: actions enabled and the notification target working.
States the sensitivity versus false-alarm tradeoff.

suggested.rationale: Changing the statistic, period, M-of-N and missing-data settings against a replayed metric, and watching the alarm state change, is the fastest way to build this troubleshooting skill.

lessons.plain: A CloudWatch alarm watches one number, such as CPU use or free disk space, and changes state when that number crosses a line you set. The alarm can do more than send a message. It can call another AWS service to fix the problem. There are two routes. In the direct route, the alarm itself carries a short list of built-in actions. In the second route, the alarm announces its change of state to Amazon EventBridge, a managed event router. EventBridge then hands the news to almost any service you choose. Think of a smoke detector that can either trip the sprinklers itself or call a dispatcher who sends whichever crew fits.
lessons.guessPrompt: An alarm fires when a server's disk is 90% full, and you want a cleanup script to run automatically. Do you think the alarm should run the script itself, or tell a separate router that decides what runs? What might each choice gain or lose?
lessons.teach:
An alarm action is something a CloudWatch alarm does when it moves into a state. The three states are OK, ALARM, and INSUFFICIENT_DATA, which means not enough data points to judge. Actions run on the transition into a state. They do not keep repeating while the alarm stays there.

The direct route uses actions the alarm supports natively. It can publish to an Amazon SNS topic, which is a managed notification channel. It can stop, terminate, reboot, or recover an EC2 instance (a virtual server). It can run an Auto Scaling policy, which adds or removes servers. It can invoke an AWS Lambda function, which is a small piece of code run on demand. It can also open a Systems Manager OpsItem or an Incident Manager incident, both of which are tracked operational tickets. The direct route is simple, with few moving parts.

The EventBridge route works because every alarm state change is automatically published as an event on the default event bus. An event bus is the stream of events in your account. You write a rule, which is a pattern that matches certain events, and attach targets. Targets include a Systems Manager Automation runbook (a scripted multi-step fix), a Step Functions workflow, or several services at once. Choose this route when the built-in list is not enough or when one alarm should trigger many things.

Here is a worked example. Step 1: an alarm watches disk-used percent on a web server and crosses 90%. Step 2: it moves from OK to ALARM and emits a state-change event. Step 3: an EventBridge rule matches the alarm's name with new state ALARM. Step 4: the rule starts a runbook that compresses old logs. Step 5: disk use drops, and the alarm returns to OK.

A common mistake is a rule that matches the alarm name but not the state. The cleanup then also runs when the alarm returns to OK or goes to INSUFFICIENT_DATA. Another frequent failure is missing permissions. Without permission, the target refuses the call, so the alarm fires and nothing gets fixed.

questions.prompt: A logistics company runs an order-processing database server. A CloudWatch alarm watches free memory. When memory runs low, the alarm should start a Step Functions workflow, which is a managed multi-step process, to restart a worker service and then notify the on-call team. Step 1: free memory falls below 200 MB for three periods in a row. Step 2: the alarm moves from OK to ALARM, and the state change is automatically published as an event on the default event bus. Step 3: (missing). Step 4: the rule's target, the Step Functions workflow, restarts the service and posts a message to an SNS topic. Step 5: memory recovers and the alarm returns to OK, and the workflow does not start again. Which choice correctly fills in Step 3?
choices: An EventBridge rule matches events that carry this alarm's name and a new state of ALARM.
The alarm repeats its action every minute while it stays in ALARM, and a rule counts those repeats before acting.
An EventBridge rule matches events that carry this alarm's name, whatever the new state is.
The alarm's own direct action list is set to start the Step Functions workflow by itself.
questions.why: Matching both the alarm name and the new state ALARM sends the event to the workflow only on the move into ALARM, so the return to OK in Step 5 does not restart the service again.

questions.prompt: A CloudWatch alarm on a reporting server's CPU moves into ALARM at 09:00. It stays in ALARM until 11:30, then returns to OK. Its only action is to publish to an SNS topic when it enters ALARM. How many times does that action run?
choices: Once for every evaluation period between 09:00 and 11:30 while the alarm stays in ALARM
Once, at 09:00, when the alarm moves into ALARM
Never, because alarm actions only run on INSUFFICIENT_DATA
Twice, at 09:00 and again at 11:30 when it returns to OK
questions.why: Alarm actions run on the transition into a state and do not repeat while the alarm stays there, and this action is tied only to entering ALARM.

questions.prompt: A video-streaming startup wants one alarm, which watches the error count on its API servers, to do three things at once: start a Systems Manager Automation runbook, start a Step Functions workflow, and open an Incident Manager incident. Which approach fits best?
choices: Put all three services in the alarm's direct action list
Create three identical alarms on the same metric so that each one can carry one of the three actions directly
Use the EC2 recover action, which automatically runs any follow-up services
Create an EventBridge rule that matches the alarm's change to ALARM, with the three services as targets
questions.why: Runbooks and Step Functions are not on the alarm's built-in action list, and the EventBridge route is the one meant for when one alarm should trigger many things.

questions.prompt: At a hospital booking system, an alarm on a queue backlog correctly moves into ALARM. The EventBridge rule's pattern matches both the alarm's name and the ALARM state. Yet the Systems Manager Automation runbook target never carries out its fix. Which of these is the most likely cause?
choices: Alarm state changes are published only to a custom event bus, not to the default one
EventBridge rules can only send events to SNS topics
The rule lacks permission to call the target, so the target refuses the call
The alarm has to pass through INSUFFICIENT_DATA first before any state-change event is published
questions.why: When permission is missing, the target refuses the call, so the alarm fires and the rule matches but nothing gets fixed.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the two ways a CloudWatch alarm can trigger an automatic fix, when you would pick each, and one limit or tradeoff of each route.
lessons.modelAnswer: An alarm can fix things itself or hand off to EventBridge. Directly, it has a fixed menu of actions. It can notify through SNS, stop, reboot, terminate, or recover an EC2 instance, run an Auto Scaling policy, invoke a Lambda function, or open an OpsItem or incident. That route has fewer moving parts, but you are limited to that menu. Alternatively, every alarm state change lands on the default EventBridge bus as an event. A rule matching that alarm can send it to many targets, such as an Automation runbook or a Step Functions workflow, or to several targets at once. The tradeoff is more pieces to configure. The rule must also filter on the new state, or the fix runs when the alarm clears too. Either way, actions fire once on a transition, not continuously. Each target needs permission to be called, or the alarm fires and nothing happens.
rubricPoints: Names the direct route and at least two built-in alarm actions such as SNS, EC2 actions, Auto Scaling, or Lambda.
Explains that alarm state changes are published to the default EventBridge bus where rules route them to targets.
Gives a reason to choose EventBridge, such as unsupported targets or fanning out to several services.
Notes that actions fire on a state transition rather than repeating.
Mentions a pitfall: rules not filtering on the ALARM state, or missing permissions for the target.

suggested.rationale: Wiring an alarm to an action and watching which state transitions trigger it is best learned by building alarms hands-on, which the planned metric alarm builder would provide.

lessons.plain: A CloudWatch dashboard is a single page of graphs and numbers about your cloud systems, built from pieces called widgets. Think of it as the wall of screens in a control room. Customizable means you choose which charts appear and how they are laid out. Spanning accounts and Regions means one wall can show screens from many separate AWS accounts and many geographic locations at once. Shareable means people can view it, sometimes without logging into AWS. That way an on-call engineer can see the whole estate in one place instead of hopping between consoles.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your company runs the same app in two AWS accounts, each in two geographic Regions. If you want one page of graphs covering all four, what do you think has to be true about where the graphs get their data and who is allowed to read it?
lessons.teach:
A CloudWatch dashboard is a saved page of widgets. A widget is one tile, such as a line graph, a single number, a text note, an alarm status, or a log query result. Behind the page sits a JSON document, a structured text description listing every widget, its position, and the metrics it plots. Because it is plain text, you can build it in the console or deploy it as code through an API call or an infrastructure template. That lets you copy a dashboard between environments.

Dashboards are global, meaning they are not tied to one Region. Each widget carries its own Region setting, so one page can plot a load balancer in Virginia next to one in Ireland.

To cross accounts, you choose one monitoring account, the central account where people look. You then link source accounts, the accounts that produce the data, so they share their metrics, logs, and traces with it. The linking uses CloudWatch cross-account observability, or the older cross-account console sharing, which relies on an IAM role. An IAM role is a set of permissions another account is allowed to assume. Once linked, each widget can also name a source account.

Worked example. Step 1: make the shared-ops account the monitoring account. Step 2: link the prod and staging accounts as sources. Step 3: in shared-ops, add a graph of request errors with prod/us-east-1 and staging/eu-west-1 as two lines. Step 4: add a dashboard variable, a dropdown that swaps a value such as the service name, so one dashboard serves many services.

You can share a dashboard publicly through a link, with named email addresses, or through your single sign-on provider. In every case, viewers get read access through a role, so check what that role can see.

A common mistake is a widget that shows no data because its Region or account is wrong. The metric exists, but the widget is looking in the wrong place. During an incident, that blank tile looks like silence when the system is actually failing.

questions.prompt: A media company runs its video-encoding service in a source account called encode-prod, in Region eu-central-1. Its central monitoring account, watchtower, is already linked to encode-prod. An engineer adds a line graph of encoding failures to a dashboard in watchtower, but the tile stays blank. They work through it. Step 1: they open CloudWatch in encode-prod and confirm the encoding-failure metric exists in eu-central-1 and is receiving data. Step 2: they recall that dashboards are global, so the dashboard itself is not in the wrong Region. Step 3: (missing). Step 4: the tile refreshes and the failure line appears. Which action is the missing Step 3?
choices: Share the dashboard through a public link so the encoding-failure metric becomes visible to the widget
Recreate the whole dashboard inside eu-central-1, because a dashboard can only plot metrics from the Region it was created in
Make encode-prod the monitoring account so that its own metrics can be plotted on the watchtower dashboard
Edit that widget so its Region setting is eu-central-1 and its account setting is encode-prod
questions.why: Each widget carries its own Region and account setting, so a blank tile for a metric that exists means the widget is looking in the wrong place and must be pointed at eu-central-1 in encode-prod.

questions.prompt: A team has built a CloudWatch dashboard by hand in its test account and now wants an identical one in its production account without clicking through the console again. What property of dashboards makes this straightforward?
choices: Dashboards are global, so the test dashboard automatically appears in every account the company owns
Sharing the dashboard with named email addresses creates an editable copy in each recipient's account
Widgets copy themselves to any account that a monitoring account has linked as a source
The dashboard is described by a plain-text JSON document that can be deployed as code through an API call or template
questions.why: Because a dashboard is defined by a JSON document listing its widgets and metrics, that text can be deployed into another environment as code.

questions.prompt: An online grocery company runs 25 small services, each publishing the same latency and error metrics under its own service name. The operations lead wants one dashboard rather than 25 near-identical copies. What should they add?
choices: A separate monitoring account for each service, each linked to the dashboard
An alarm-status widget per service, placed side by side on one very long page
A dashboard variable: a dropdown that swaps the service name so the same widgets show any service
A text widget listing all 25 service names so viewers know which graph to read
questions.why: A dashboard variable is a dropdown that swaps a value such as the service name, letting one dashboard serve many services.

questions.prompt: A clinic's IT team wants to share a CloudWatch dashboard of appointment-system health with an outside contractor through a public link. Before sending the link, what should they check?
choices: Whether the dashboard has been moved into the contractor's home Region
Whether the contractor's account has been linked as a source account
What the role that viewers receive for read access is allowed to see
Whether every widget has been converted into a text note first
questions.why: In every sharing method, including a public link, viewers get read access through a role, so that role's permissions determine what they can see.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would give the on-call team one dashboard covering three accounts and two Regions, and name one risk or tradeoff of sharing it.
lessons.modelAnswer: A CloudWatch dashboard is a global page of widgets, and each widget states which Region and account its data comes from, so one page can mix locations. First I would pick a central monitoring account. Then I would link our other accounts to it as source accounts so their metrics and logs flow in. After that, I would build the dashboard in the monitoring account. Each graph would plot the same metric from each account and Region side by side, and a variable dropdown would switch between services. I would keep the dashboard's JSON definition in source control so we can redeploy it. For people without AWS logins, I can share it by link, by named emails, or through single sign-on. The tradeoff is exposure. Viewers read through a role, so a public link could reveal operational data. I would use the email or single sign-on options and scope the permissions. I would also check that every widget's Region and account are correct, because a blank tile can hide a real outage.
rubricPoints: Dashboards are global and each widget sets its own Region.
Cross-account viewing needs a monitoring account linked to source accounts.
Dashboards are defined as JSON so they can be deployed and reused as code.
Variables let one dashboard be customized across services or resources.
Sharing can be public, by named email, or via single sign-on, and each grants read access that must be scoped.
A wrong Region or account on a widget shows no data and can hide an outage.

suggested.rationale: The skill is mostly choosing the right setup, such as a monitoring account versus per-account dashboards, or which sharing mode fits, so reasoning through exam-style scenarios teaches it best.

lessons.plain: Amazon SNS (Simple Notification Service) is a managed publish-and-subscribe messaging service. It is a broadcast list for machines. Something publishes one message to a named channel called a topic, and SNS delivers a copy to everyone subscribed: an email inbox, a phone, a queue, or a small function. Many AWS services can publish to a topic by themselves. A monitoring alarm, a storage bucket or a backup job can each say "this just happened." Think of a fire alarm wired to a building's paging system. The alarm only has to shout once, and the paging system decides who hears it.
lessons.guessPrompt: You set up an alarm to email you when a server's CPU stays high. You add your email address to the notification channel, and the CPU really does spike. No email arrives. What simple step do you think you might have skipped?
lessons.teach:
A topic is a named SNS channel that receives messages. A publisher is anything that sends a message to the topic. A subscription connects the topic to one endpoint, which is where copies get delivered. Common endpoint types are email, SMS, an HTTPS URL, an Amazon SQS queue (a managed message queue) and an AWS Lambda function (code that runs on demand). This works because publishers never need to know who is listening. You add or remove responders on the topic without touching the alarm.

A CloudWatch alarm watches a metric and is always in one of three states: OK, ALARM, or INSUFFICIENT_DATA (too little data to judge). For each state change you can attach an action that publishes to a topic.

Worked example. You create a topic named ops-alerts. You add an email subscription, and SNS sends a confirmation link to that address. Until someone clicks it, the subscription stays pending and receives nothing. You build an alarm with the rule "CPU above 80 percent for 3 consecutive 5-minute periods" and attach the action "on ALARM, notify ops-alerts." You also add "on OK, notify ops-alerts" so the team hears when it recovers. When CPU stays at 95 percent for 15 minutes, the alarm moves to ALARM. It publishes once, and every confirmed subscriber gets a copy.

Other services publish the same way, but the topic must allow them to. A topic access policy is a permission document attached to the topic. It must name the service that is allowed to publish, such as S3 for bucket events or EventBridge for event rules. Without that permission, the publish is silently refused.

Common mistake: encrypting the topic with the AWS-managed SNS key. That key's policy cannot be edited, so you cannot grant other services the right to use it, and their publishes fail. Use a customer managed key and grant the publishing service permission to use it in the key policy.

The consequence for a running system is an alarm that shows ALARM in the console while nobody is ever paged.

questions.prompt: A veterinary clinic wants its intake code to run whenever a new X-ray file lands in its storage bucket. Here is the setup, with one step missing. Step 1: create an SNS topic named xray-intake and encrypt it with a customer managed key, which is an encryption key the clinic controls. The key policy, which is the permission document on the key, grants S3 permission to use the key. Step 2: add a subscription from xray-intake to a Lambda function, which is code that runs on demand. Step 3: [missing]. Step 4: set the bucket's event notification to publish to xray-intake when a new object is created. Step 5: upload a test file and confirm that the Lambda function runs. What belongs in Step 3?
choices: Switch the topic to the AWS-managed SNS key, because that key already trusts every AWS service.
Add an email subscription to the topic so that S3 knows who is listening before it publishes.
Attach a topic access policy to xray-intake that names S3 as a service allowed to publish to it.
Create a CloudWatch alarm on the bucket and attach an action that publishes to xray-intake when the alarm reaches the OK state.
questions.why: A service such as S3 can only publish to a topic whose access policy names it as an allowed publisher; without that policy, the publish is silently refused even when the key permissions are correct.

questions.prompt: A logistics company has a CloudWatch alarm on queue backlog. The alarm already publishes to an SNS topic named dispatch-alerts, which has two confirmed email subscribers. The team now wants a Lambda function to post the same alerts into their chat tool. What is the simplest correct change?
choices: Create a second alarm that watches the same metric and points it at the Lambda function.
Delete the email subscriptions, because a topic can deliver to only one type of endpoint.
Add a subscription from dispatch-alerts to the Lambda function, and leave the alarm unchanged.
Edit the alarm so that it publishes directly to the Lambda function as well as to the topic.
questions.why: Publishers do not need to know who is listening, so you add a new responder as a subscription on the topic without touching the alarm.

questions.prompt: A media company's alarm watches a metric that a monitoring agent reports. The agent crashes, and for the next hour no data points arrive. The team wants to be notified when this happens. Which alarm state should they attach an SNS publish action to?
choices: PENDING, which is the state an alarm enters while it waits for confirmation.
INSUFFICIENT_DATA, which is the state an alarm enters when there is too little data to judge.
ALARM, because missing data always counts as a breach of the threshold.
OK, because an alarm with no data has nothing to complain about.
questions.why: INSUFFICIENT_DATA is the alarm state for too little data to judge, and you can attach a publish action to that state change just as you can to OK or ALARM.

questions.prompt: At a retail firm, an EventBridge rule should publish order-failure events to an SNS topic named order-issues. The topic access policy correctly names EventBridge as an allowed publisher. The topic is encrypted with the AWS-managed SNS key. Yet no messages ever arrive at the topic. What is the most likely cause, and what is the fix?
choices: The topic access policy must also name each subscriber. Add every endpoint to the policy.
The key policy of the AWS-managed SNS key cannot be edited to let EventBridge use it. Re-encrypt the topic with a customer managed key whose key policy grants EventBridge permission.
The topic needs an OK action configured. Add an OK action to the topic.
EventBridge can publish only through a CloudWatch alarm. Create an alarm in between the rule and the topic.
questions.why: The AWS-managed SNS key's policy cannot be changed to grant other services use of the key, so their publishes fail until the topic uses a customer managed key that grants the publishing service permission.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how a CloudWatch alarm or another AWS service ends up notifying people through SNS. Include at least one way this chain can silently break.
lessons.modelAnswer: SNS is a publish-and-subscribe service. We create a topic and subscribe endpoints to it, such as email, SMS, an SQS queue or a Lambda function. A CloudWatch alarm has three states: OK, ALARM and INSUFFICIENT_DATA. We attach an action to a state change that publishes to the topic, and SNS then fans a copy out to every confirmed subscriber. The benefit is decoupling: we can change who gets paged without editing the alarm. The tradeoff is that the chain has several links that can each fail quietly. An email subscription does nothing until its confirmation link is clicked. A service like S3 or EventBridge needs the topic's access policy to allow it to publish. If the topic is encrypted, it needs a customer managed key whose policy lets that service use the key, because the AWS-managed key cannot be shared that way. Any of these failures leaves the alarm firing with no one notified.
rubricPoints: Defines a topic, publisher and subscription, and names example endpoint types.
States that alarm actions publish to a topic on a state change such as ALARM or OK.
Notes that email subscriptions must be confirmed before they receive messages.
Explains that other services need the topic access policy to permit them to publish.
Mentions that encrypted topics need a customer managed key that grants the publishing service access.
Names the consequence: an alarm fires but nobody is notified.

suggested.rationale: Wiring an alarm's state-change actions to a notification topic, and then seeing why a notification never arrives, is best learned by building it in the planned metric alarm builder.

lessons.plain: When a system runs on AWS, it constantly produces numbers about itself, such as how busy a server is or how long requests take. It also keeps a record of who changed what. Analyzing those numbers tells you something is wrong. Automating remediation means a fix runs by itself as soon as the problem appears, so nobody has to wake up and click buttons. Think of a smoke detector wired to a sprinkler. The detector notices smoke, and the sprinkler responds without waiting for a person. In AWS, a monitoring service is the detector, and small functions or management scripts are the sprinkler.
lessons.guessPrompt: A web server's average response time over five minutes looks fine, yet some customers say pages sometimes take ten seconds. Why might the average hide their pain, and what number would show it better?
lessons.teach:
Amazon CloudWatch is AWS's monitoring service. It collects metrics, which are numbers measured over time, such as EC2 CPUUtilization or a load balancer's TargetResponseTime. It shows each metric through a statistic over a period. A statistic is a summary such as Average, Maximum, Sum or a percentile. A period is the time bucket being summarized, for example 1 minute. A percentile like p99 is the value that 99% of data points fall below, so it shows the slow tail that an average smooths away.

Automating remediation means joining detection to action. A CloudWatch alarm watches a metric against a threshold and changes state when the metric crosses it. That state change can trigger one of two kinds of fix. The first is AWS Lambda, a serverless function service that runs your code on demand, which suits custom logic. The second is AWS Systems Manager (SSM), a fleet management service whose Run Command and Automation features run commands or step-by-step runbooks on instances. AWS CloudTrail is the audit log of API calls: who did what, when and from where. It explains changes that metrics only hint at, and its events can trigger fixes too.

Here is a worked example. Checkout latency is reported as slow. You view TargetResponseTime at p99 with a 1-minute period and see spikes to 8 seconds, while the Average stays at 300 ms. CPUUtilization on one instance is pinned at 100%. CloudTrail shows that someone changed that instance's configuration an hour earlier. You create an alarm on p99 above 2 seconds for 3 periods in a row. Its action invokes an SSM Automation runbook that restarts the application service and records the result. Next time, the fix runs within minutes.

A common mistake is alarming on Average with a long period. Short spikes vanish, the alarm never fires, and users suffer while the dashboards look green. Another risk is an automated fix with no limit. It can restart a server endlessly and hide the real cause, so log every action and alert a human if the fix repeats.

questions.prompt: A ticketing company runs its booking API behind a load balancer. Customers report occasional booking timeouts. Step 1: You view TargetResponseTime with a 1-minute period. The p95 jumps to 6 seconds for a few minutes at a time, while the Average stays near 250 ms. Step 2: CloudTrail, the audit log of API calls, shows that a teammate changed a database setting 30 minutes before the first spike. Step 3: (missing) You create a CloudWatch alarm. Step 4: The alarm's action invokes a Lambda function that rolls back the setting and logs what it did. If the function runs more than twice in an hour, it notifies the on-call engineer. Which alarm best fills Step 3?
choices: Alarm on p95 TargetResponseTime above 1.5 seconds for 3 consecutive 1-minute periods
Alarm on Average TargetResponseTime above 6 seconds for 3 consecutive 1-minute periods
Alarm on p95 TargetResponseTime above 1.5 seconds over a single 1-hour period
Alarm on Average TargetResponseTime above 1 second over a single 1-hour period
questions.why: A high percentile over short periods captures the brief slow tail, and requiring 3 periods in a row avoids firing on a single blip, while Average or a long period smooths the spikes away.

questions.prompt: A video streaming service checks its request latency over a 1-minute period. The p99 is 4 seconds and the Average is 200 ms. What does the p99 value tell you?
choices: Almost every request in that minute took about 4 seconds
99% of requests finished in under 4 s, so the slowest 1% took longer
The 99 slowest requests averaged exactly 4 seconds between them
4 seconds was the quickest response recorded during that minute
questions.why: A percentile such as p99 is the value that 99% of data points fall below, so it exposes the slow tail that the 200 ms Average hides.

questions.prompt: A logistics company's warehouse servers keep running out of disk space. A CloudWatch alarm already fires when disk use crosses 90%. The team wants the alarm to automatically run the same cleanup command on every affected instance in the fleet. Which service fits this fix best?
choices: A CloudWatch dashboard, so engineers can watch disk use rise across the fleet
CloudTrail, because it records every API call that led to the disks filling up
Systems Manager Run Command, to run the cleanup on the instances
A longer alarm period, so the alarm fires less often and the noise goes away
questions.why: Systems Manager is the fleet management service whose Run Command feature runs commands on instances, which is exactly what this fix needs.

questions.prompt: An online retailer has an alarm that invokes a Lambda function to reboot an instance whenever its CPU stays high. By morning, the function has rebooted the instance 40 times, and nobody knows why the CPU keeps climbing. What safeguard was missing?
choices: Deleting the alarm and relying on CloudTrail afterwards to show when reboots happened
Making the Lambda function reboot faster so that users notice less downtime overall
Logging every automated action and alerting a human when the fix keeps repeating
Changing the alarm to Average CPU over a 6-hour period so it fires much less often
questions.why: An automated fix with no limit can repeat endlessly and hide the real cause, so each action should be logged and a person alerted when the fix repeats.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would go from 'the app feels slow' to a fix that runs without a human, using CloudWatch, CloudTrail, and either Lambda or Systems Manager. Name one limit or tradeoff of automating the fix.
lessons.modelAnswer: First I look at CloudWatch metrics with the right statistic. For latency I use p99 over a short period, because an average hides the slow tail users actually feel. Then I check related metrics like CPU to find the bottleneck. I check CloudTrail to see whether someone changed something recently, since it records every API call with who and when. Once I know the pattern, I set an alarm that fires when the metric crosses a threshold for a few periods in a row. Its action triggers the fix. I use Systems Manager when the fix is a command or runbook on instances, like restarting a service, and Lambda when I need custom logic. The tradeoff is that automation can mask a root cause or loop forever. So I log each run, limit repeats, and still notify a human to find the underlying problem.
rubricPoints: Picks a statistic and period that reveal the problem, such as p99 rather than Average for latency.
Uses CloudTrail to find who or what changed, since metrics show symptoms but not causes.
Describes an alarm crossing a threshold over several periods as the trigger.
Matches the action to the tool: Systems Manager for instance commands or runbooks, Lambda for custom code.
Names a limit, such as masking root causes, remediation loops or the need to notify a human.

suggested.rationale: This objective is about choosing the right metric, statistic and remediation tool for a given symptom, which exam-style scenarios practise better than any single existing mission.

lessons.plain: Automated remediation means a problem gets fixed by software instead of a person typing commands at 3 a.m. The classic kind follows a fixed recipe: when this alarm fires, run that script. Newer AWS tooling adds AI helpers. The AWS DevOps Agent works like a tireless junior on-call engineer: it looks at your metrics, logs and recent changes, guesses the root cause and proposes a fix. Kiro is an AI-assisted coding environment that helps you write the scripts and alarms that do the fixing. Think of a car: the fixed recipe is the airbag, the agent is the mechanic diagnosing a strange noise.
lessons.guessPrompt: An AI tool investigates an outage and says a deploy at 09:00 caused it, recommending a rollback. Should it roll back production on its own immediately, or should something else happen first? Why?
lessons.teach:
Automated remediation is any fix applied by software in response to a detected problem. It comes in two styles.

Deterministic remediation follows a fixed, pre-written path. A metric alarm (a rule that watches a number and changes state when it crosses a threshold) triggers a routed event, which starts a runbook (a scripted sequence of steps, for example in AWS Systems Manager Automation). The same input always produces the same action, which makes it predictable and safe for known problems.

AI-assisted remediation handles problems nobody wrote a recipe for. The AWS DevOps Agent, an AI agent (software that reasons over data and takes steps toward a goal), investigates an incident by correlating telemetry (metrics, logs, traces), recent deployments and code changes, then reports a likely root cause and recommends mitigations. Kiro is an AI-assisted development environment: you describe what you want in plain language or a written spec, and it drafts code such as runbooks, infrastructure templates or small functions for you to review.

Worked example. Step 1: latency on an API alarms after a 09:00 deploy. Step 2: the DevOps Agent pulls the alarm, error logs and deploy history, and reports that errors began with the new version. Step 3: it recommends rolling back; an engineer checks the evidence and approves. Step 4: afterwards, the engineer uses Kiro to draft a runbook and alarm that roll back automatically if error rate spikes within ten minutes of a deploy. The unknown problem became a known one with a deterministic fix.

Common mistake: giving an AI agent broad permissions to change production and trusting its conclusion without checking. Agents can be confidently wrong. Use least-privilege permissions, human approval for risky actions, and review generated code like any teammate's. In a running system, an unchecked wrong fix can turn a slowdown into a full outage, while a well-reviewed runbook fixes the same fault in seconds every time.

questions.prompt: A ticketing company runs a fleet of worker servers that process a payment queue. Step 1: at 02:10, a memory alarm on the fleet fires, 30 minutes after a configuration change raised the batch size from 50 to 500 messages. Step 2: the AWS DevOps Agent pulls the memory metrics, the out-of-memory errors in the worker logs and the change history. It reports that the crashes began right after the batch-size change. Step 3: it recommends reverting the batch size to 50. The on-call engineer checks the memory graph against the change record and approves the revert. Step 4: (missing). Which step 4 best completes this incident so that the same fault is handled faster next time?
choices: Do nothing further, because the DevOps Agent will investigate this fault again whenever it recurs.
Give the DevOps Agent full administrator permissions on production so it can apply fixes like this one without waiting for a human.
Ask Kiro to write a runbook and deploy it straight to production, because AI-generated code does not need a teammate's review.
Use Kiro to draft a runbook and an alarm that revert the batch size automatically if memory passes 85% soon after a config change, and review the draft before it goes live.
questions.why: Once the cause is known, a reviewed runbook plus alarm gives a predictable, deterministic fix for it, so it no longer needs a fresh AI investigation.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm sets up a rule that watches free disk space on its database server. When free space drops below 10%, a routed event starts a Systems Manager Automation runbook that deletes old temporary files. What kind of remediation is this?
choices: AI-assisted remediation, because the runbook works out the likely root cause from logs and traces
Deterministic remediation, because an AI agent picks the best runbook for each incident
Deterministic remediation, because a fixed, pre-written path runs the same action every time the threshold is crossed
AI-assisted remediation, because software starts the fix without a human
