questions.why: An alarm triggering a fixed runbook gives the same output for the same input, which is what makes remediation deterministic.

questions.prompt: A streaming service sees intermittent timeouts on its search API. No runbook covers it, and nobody yet knows whether recent code changes, a deployment or something else is the cause. Which tool fits the first step of finding the likely root cause?
choices: An existing Systems Manager Automation runbook, because runbooks handle any problem automatically
The AWS DevOps Agent, because it correlates telemetry, deployments and code changes to report a likely root cause and suggest mitigations
A new metric alarm, because alarms explain why a threshold was crossed
Kiro, because it drafts code from a plain-language description
questions.why: The problem is unknown and has no recipe, so it needs an investigation that correlates evidence, and that is the DevOps Agent's role.

questions.prompt: A retailer let an AI agent apply changes to production with broad permissions and no approval step. During a checkout slowdown, the agent confidently concluded that the database was at fault and restarted it, which caused a full outage. The real cause was a bad cache setting. Which practice would most directly have prevented this?
choices: Replacing all runbooks with AI-assisted remediation so every fix is reasoned out fresh
Least-privilege permissions for the agent, plus human approval before risky actions such as restarting a database
Adding more telemetry so the agent's conclusions are always correct
Letting Kiro rewrite the agent's code after each incident
questions.why: Agents can be confidently wrong, so limiting their permissions and requiring a human to approve risky actions stops an unchecked wrong fix from turning a slowdown into an outage.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how the AWS DevOps Agent and Kiro fit alongside alarm-triggered runbooks for fixing problems automatically, and name one limit or risk of relying on the AI tools.
lessons.modelAnswer: We have two layers. For problems we already understand, like a disk filling or a bad deploy, we use deterministic remediation: an alarm fires, an event starts a Systems Manager runbook, and the same fix runs every time. For problems we have not seen, the AWS DevOps Agent acts like an on-call investigator: it correlates metrics, logs and recent deployments and tells us the likely root cause and a suggested mitigation. Kiro is the AI coding assistant we use to draft the runbooks, alarms and templates that turn that lesson into an automatic fix next time. The limit is that AI output can be wrong, so we don't let an agent make risky production changes unchecked. We give it least-privilege permissions, require human approval for actions like rollbacks, and review any code Kiro writes before it ships.
rubricPoints: Defines automated remediation as software applying a fix after a problem is detected.
Distinguishes fixed alarm-to-runbook remediation from AI-assisted investigation.
Describes the DevOps Agent as correlating telemetry and changes to propose a root cause and mitigation.
Describes Kiro as an AI coding assistant that drafts runbooks, alarms or infrastructure code for review.
Names a risk such as wrong conclusions or excessive permissions and a guardrail like human approval or least privilege.
Notes that lessons from AI-assisted incidents should become deterministic runbooks.

suggested.rationale: No mission or planned engine exercises these AI tools directly, so reasoning through an exam-style incident about when to trust an agent versus a deterministic runbook teaches the judgement the exam tests.

lessons.plain: Amazon EventBridge is a managed event router. Things that happen in your cloud account, like a server stopping, a file landing in storage, or a scheduled time arriving, are written up as small messages called events. EventBridge reads each event, checks it against rules you write, and forwards matching events to the services that should react, such as a notification topic, a function, or a queue. Think of a mailroom clerk who reads every envelope's label and drops it in the right pigeonhole. When something goes wrong, the work is figuring out whether the envelope never arrived, was misread, or could not be delivered.
lessons.guessPrompt: You set up a rule that should send you a message whenever a virtual server stops. A server stops, and nothing arrives. Before reading on, name two different places along the path where the event could have been lost.
lessons.teach:
An event is a small JSON document describing a change. It always carries fields such as source (who emitted it, for example aws.ec2), detail-type (what kind of change), and detail (the specifics). An event bus is the channel events arrive on. Every account has a default bus for AWS service events, and you can create custom buses for your own applications. A rule sits on one bus and holds an event pattern, which is a template the event must match. A rule can also run on a schedule instead. Each rule sends matches to targets, the services that receive the event, such as an SNS notification topic, a Lambda function, an SQS queue, or a Systems Manager runbook.

Matching is strict. Values are case-sensitive, fields must sit at the same nesting level as in the real event, and listing several values in an array means any one of them can match. Enriching means reshaping or adding to the event before delivery. An input transformer pulls chosen fields out and builds a friendlier message. EventBridge Pipes can also call a function to add data before passing the event on.

Worked example: when an instance stops, EC2 emits an event on the default bus with source aws.ec2, detail-type "EC2 Instance State-change Notification", and a detail containing the instance-id and "state": "stopped". Your pattern lists that source and detail-type and puts state under detail. EventBridge compares all three fields, and they match. The input transformer extracts instance-id into the line "Instance i-0abc stopped", which is delivered to the SNS topic.

Debugging follows the same path. If the rule's MatchedEvents metric stays at zero, the pattern or the bus is wrong. Check for a capitalized "Stopped", state placed at the top level instead of under detail, a rule in the wrong Region, or a rule on a custom bus while the event went to the default bus. If matches rise but FailedInvocations also rises, delivery failed. Usually the target's resource policy or the rule's role does not allow EventBridge to call it. Attach a dead-letter queue, which holds events that failed delivery after retries, so failed events are kept rather than lost. A common mistake is copying a pattern from memory instead of from a real sample event. Without that check, alerts and automatic fixes silently never run.

questions.prompt: A bakery chain's inventory app publishes its own events to a custom bus named stock-bus. A real sample event copied from the bus looks like this: source "com.crumb.inventory", detail-type "Stock Level Changed", and detail {"store": "store-12", "level": "LOW"}. The team wants a message in an SQS queue (a managed message queue) whenever a store's level is LOW or EMPTY. Step 1: create the rule on stock-bus, not on the default bus, because that is where the app sends its events. Step 2: in the event pattern, list source "com.crumb.inventory" and detail-type "Stock Level Changed", copied exactly from the sample. Step 3: ??? Step 4: add an input transformer that pulls out store and builds the line "store-12 needs restock", then deliver it to the SQS queue target. Which choice completes Step 3?
choices: Add "level": ["LOW", "EMPTY"] at the top level of the pattern, next to source and detail-type
Add "level": ["LOW", "EMPTY"] inside a detail block of the pattern
Add "level": "LOW" inside a detail block of the pattern
Add "level": ["low", "empty"] inside a detail block of the pattern
questions.why: In the real event, level sits under detail and its values are uppercase, so the pattern must nest it under detail with matching case, and an array of two values lets either LOW or EMPTY match.

questions.prompt: A logistics company has a rule on its default bus that sends Amazon RDS database events to a Lambda function (a small piece of code that runs on demand). In CloudWatch, the rule's MatchedEvents metric climbs every time a database event occurs, but FailedInvocations climbs by the same amount and the function never runs. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The event pattern uses the wrong capitalization for one of its values
The rule is attached to a custom bus instead of the default bus
EventBridge is not allowed to call the function, because the function's resource policy or the rule's role lacks permission
The rule was created in a different Region from the database
questions.why: Rising matches show the pattern and bus are correct, so rising FailedInvocations points to a delivery problem, usually missing permission for EventBridge to call the target.

questions.prompt: A hospital's operations team wants to be alerted when AWS reports a change to one of its Amazon RDS databases. They create a custom bus named ops-bus and put a rule on it. They copied the pattern from a real sample event and confirmed the rule is in the same Region as the database, yet the rule's MatchedEvents metric stays at zero. What should they change?
choices: Attach a dead-letter queue to the rule so the missing events are kept
Add an input transformer so the event is reshaped before matching
Grant the target a resource policy that allows EventBridge to call it
Create the rule on the default bus, because AWS service events arrive there
questions.why: AWS service events arrive on the default bus, so a rule on a custom bus never sees them and its MatchedEvents stays at zero.

questions.prompt: A retail company's rule sends matching events to a Systems Manager runbook (an automated set of fix-up steps). Occasionally delivery fails even after EventBridge retries, and those events disappear. The team wants failed events kept so they can inspect them later instead of losing them. What should they attach to the rule?
choices: A schedule so the rule runs at fixed times instead of on events
An EventBridge Pipe that calls a function to add data before delivery
A dead-letter queue that holds events whose delivery failed after retries
An input transformer that extracts only the fields the runbook needs
questions.why: A dead-letter queue stores events that could not be delivered after retries, so they are kept for inspection rather than silently lost.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how an event travels from an AWS service to a target through EventBridge, and how you would tell a pattern problem apart from a delivery problem. Include one limit or tradeoff of strict pattern matching.
lessons.modelAnswer: A service like EC2 puts an event, a JSON document with source, detail-type, and detail, onto the default event bus in its Region. Each rule on that bus compares the event with its pattern. Matching is exact and case-sensitive, and fields must be nested the way the real event nests them. When an event matches, EventBridge can reshape it with an input transformer and then delivers it to the rule's targets, such as an SNS topic or a Lambda function. To debug, I look at the rule's metrics. If MatchedEvents is zero, the pattern, Region, or bus is wrong, and I test the pattern against a real sample event. If events match but FailedInvocations climbs, the target is refusing delivery, often because a permission is missing, and a dead-letter queue keeps those events for inspection. The tradeoff is that strict matching prevents noisy false triggers, but a single wrong letter means the rule silently never fires.
rubricPoints: Defines an event, an event bus, a rule with its pattern, and a target.
States that matching is exact, case-sensitive, and depends on correct nesting under detail.
Mentions enrichment or reshaping, such as an input transformer, before delivery.
Separates pattern failures (zero MatchedEvents, wrong bus or Region) from delivery failures (FailedInvocations, missing permissions).
Mentions a dead-letter queue or retries for failed deliveries.
Names a tradeoff, such as strictness avoiding noise but causing silent misses.

suggested.rationale: Routing events through rules and tracing why one never reached its target is best learned by building and breaking patterns in a messaging and events lab.

lessons.plain: A Systems Manager Automation runbook is a written-down fix that a machine can follow. Instead of an engineer logging in at 3 a.m. to stop a server, take a snapshot of its disk, and start it again, the runbook lists those steps in order, and AWS Systems Manager (a managed operations service) carries them out. AWS ships many ready-made, predefined runbooks for common chores, and you can write custom ones for your own procedures. It is like a pilot's checklist: anyone, or any alarm, can trigger it, and the same steps happen the same way every time.
lessons.guessPrompt: If a runbook is going to restart 200 servers for you, what two safety limits would you want to set before pressing go?
lessons.teach:
An Automation runbook is a document that Systems Manager executes as an ordered list of steps. Predefined runbooks are owned by AWS and are named with an AWS- or AWSSupport- prefix, for example AWS-RestartEC2Instance. Custom runbooks are documents you write in YAML or JSON. A runbook declares parameters (inputs such as an instance ID) and mainSteps. Each step uses an action, meaning a built-in step type: aws:executeAwsApi calls any AWS API, aws:runCommand runs a shell script on a managed instance, aws:waitForAwsResourceProperty pauses until a resource reaches a state, aws:branch picks the next step based on a value, and aws:approve waits for a human to approve.

It works because each step reports success or failure, so the runbook can stop, retry, or branch instead of blindly continuing. The runbook acts through an assume role, an IAM role (a set of permissions) that Systems Manager borrows while it runs.

Worked example: a custom runbook takes InstanceId. Step 1, aws:executeAwsApi calls CreateSnapshot on the instance's volume. Step 2, aws:waitForAwsResourceProperty waits until the snapshot is completed. Step 3, aws:executeAwsApi calls RebootInstances. Step 4 checks the instance status is ok. If step 2 times out, execution stops and the reboot never happens, so you never reboot without a backup.

You can run a runbook manually, on a schedule, from an EventBridge rule reacting to an alarm, or as an AWS Config remediation. For many resources, rate control lets you target by tag and set concurrency (how many run at once) and an error threshold (how many failures before it halts).

Common mistake: the assume role lacks permission for an API a step calls, or the caller lacks iam:PassRole to hand that role over. The execution then fails at that step, so the fix you counted on silently does not happen when the alarm fires.

questions.prompt: A media company writes a custom runbook that takes InstanceId and NewType so it can resize a web server automatically. Step 1: aws:executeAwsApi calls StopInstances on the instance. Step 2: MISSING. Step 3: aws:executeAwsApi calls ModifyInstanceAttribute to set the new instance type, which only succeeds on a stopped instance. Step 4: aws:executeAwsApi calls StartInstances. Which step 2 makes sure step 3 never runs against an instance that is still shutting down?
choices: aws:runCommand, running a shutdown script on the instance's operating system
aws:branch, jumping to step 4 if the instance is still running
aws:waitForAwsResourceProperty, pausing until the instance state is stopped
aws:approve, so an engineer confirms the stop before the resize continues
questions.why: aws:waitForAwsResourceProperty pauses the runbook until the resource reaches the named state, so the resize runs only after the instance has actually stopped, and the runbook stops if that state never arrives.

questions.prompt: An operations engineer sees a runbook in the Systems Manager console named AWSSupport-TroubleshootRDP. Who owns this runbook, and why?
choices: The engineer's own account, because the name contains no AWS- prefix
AWS, because runbooks named with the AWSSupport- prefix are predefined
The engineer's own account, because every runbook in the console is a custom document
Whoever created the most recent execution, because running a runbook copies it
questions.why: Predefined runbooks are owned by AWS and carry an AWS- or AWSSupport- prefix, while custom runbooks are ones you write yourself.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm runs a patching runbook across 300 instances tagged Role=worker, using rate control with a concurrency of 15 and an error threshold of 4. During the run, the fourth instance fails. What does the error threshold do here?
choices: It halts the execution once the number of failures reaches the threshold
It retries each failed instance 4 times before moving on to the next one
It limits the run to 4 instances at once, overriding the concurrency setting
It skips the 4 failed instances and finishes the other 296 as normal
questions.why: Concurrency sets how many targets run at once, and the error threshold sets how many failures are allowed before the whole execution stops.

questions.prompt: A retailer wires an EventBridge rule so that a high-disk alarm starts a custom runbook whose first step uses aws:executeAwsApi to call ModifyVolume and grow the disk. The alarm fires, the runbook starts, but the execution fails at that first step and the disk stays full. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The runbook's assume role does not have permission to call ModifyVolume
The runbook needed an aws:approve step before any API call could run
aws:executeAwsApi can only call read-only APIs, not ones that change resources
Custom runbooks cannot be started from an EventBridge rule, only manually
questions.why: The runbook acts through its assume role, so if that IAM role lacks permission for an API a step calls, the execution fails at that step and the expected fix never happens.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what a Systems Manager Automation runbook is, when you would use a predefined one versus writing a custom one, and one limit or risk you must manage when running it.
lessons.modelAnswer: A runbook is a document that Systems Manager runs as ordered steps, like calling an AWS API, running a script on an instance, waiting for a resource state, branching, or pausing for approval. Each step succeeds or fails, so the run stops instead of pushing on after a problem. I use a predefined AWS runbook, such as one that restarts an instance, when it already does the chore, because it is tested and maintained for me. I write a custom runbook when our procedure is specific, like snapshot, wait, reboot, then health check. Runbooks can be started by hand, on a schedule, by an EventBridge rule from an alarm, or by Config remediation. The risks: it acts through an assume role, so missing permissions make it fail mid-run, and running across many targets needs concurrency and error-threshold limits so a bad fix does not spread to the whole fleet.
rubricPoints: Defines a runbook as a document of ordered steps executed by Systems Manager.
Distinguishes AWS-owned predefined runbooks from custom ones you write.
Names at least one step action and how parameters feed the steps.
Mentions a way to trigger it, such as manually, EventBridge from an alarm, or Config remediation.
Names the assume role permission dependency or rate-control limits as a risk.

suggested.rationale: A runbook is a step workflow with waits, branches and failure stops, which the planned workflow state machine engine lets the learner build and trace.

lessons.plain: Optimizing compute means making sure each virtual server is the right size for its work: not so small that it runs slow, not so large that you pay for idle power. You watch performance numbers over time, such as how busy the processor is or how much memory is in use, then resize or change the server type. Labels called tags let you group servers by team or environment so you can review and fix them in batches. It is like checking a delivery fleet: you look at which vans run overloaded and which drive half-empty, then swap sizes to match the loads.
lessons.guessPrompt: A server's processor has averaged 6% busy and never gone above 15% for two weeks, while its memory sits near 90%. Would you move it to a smaller server with less of everything, and why or why not?
lessons.teach:
Compute optimization is matching a server's size and family to its measured workload, then fixing it when it drifts. On AWS a virtual server is an EC2 instance; its instance type sets how much CPU, memory and network it gets, and its family (general purpose, compute optimized, memory optimized, burstable) sets the ratio between them.

The evidence is performance metrics: numbers recorded every few minutes, such as CPUUtilization (how busy the processor is) and network throughput, collected by Amazon CloudWatch, the monitoring service. Memory and disk-space use are not visible from outside the instance, so they only appear if the CloudWatch agent, a small program on the server, publishes them. AWS Compute Optimizer is a recommendation service that reads about two weeks or more of these metrics and labels each instance over-provisioned (paying for unused capacity), under-provisioned (starved and likely slow) or optimized, with suggested replacement types. Resource tags are key-value labels like env=prod or team=dispatch; you filter recommendations, costs and automation by them so a team can act on its own servers.

Worked example: users report a slow API every afternoon. Step one, CloudWatch shows CPUUtilization flat at about 20% from 14:00. Step two, the instance is a burstable t3 type, which earns CPU credits while idle and spends them to run above a baseline; CPUCreditBalance shows zero at 14:00, so the server is being held to its baseline. Step three, Compute Optimizer flags it under-provisioned. Step four, filter by tag team=api to find sibling instances with the same pattern, then move them to a larger or non-burstable type, or enable unlimited bursting and accept the extra charge.

The common mistake is downsizing on CPU alone. Without the agent publishing memory, a low-CPU server that is memory-bound looks idle, and shrinking it causes swapping or out-of-memory crashes in production. Resizing also requires stopping the instance, so schedule it in a maintenance window or behind a load balancer.

questions.prompt: A freight company runs an invoicing server on a memory-optimized EC2 instance (a virtual server whose family gives it a lot of memory relative to CPU), tagged team=billing. AWS Compute Optimizer (a service that reads about two weeks or more of performance metrics and labels instances as over-provisioned, under-provisioned or optimized) labels it over-provisioned. A new engineer works through the case before acting. Step one: Amazon CloudWatch (the monitoring service) shows CPUUtilization averaging 9% over the last three weeks. Step two: [missing]. Step three: memory use sits at about 88% most of the day, so a much smaller type would push the server into swapping or out-of-memory crashes. Step four: the engineer keeps the memory-heavy family, and if any change is made, schedules it in a maintenance window because resizing requires stopping the instance. What is step two?
choices: Downsize to the smallest type in the family right away, since 9% CPU proves the server is mostly idle
Check CPUCreditBalance to see whether the server is being held down to a baseline CPU level
Confirm the CloudWatch agent is installed and publishing memory metrics, then review those memory figures
Filter Compute Optimizer by the tag team=billing and apply every suggested replacement type at once
questions.why: Memory use is not visible from outside the instance, so the engineer must check the agent's memory metrics before trusting a low-CPU reading as proof the server is idle.

questions.prompt: A media startup wants a CloudWatch alarm for when one of its EC2 instances runs low on memory. With no extra software installed on the instances, which of these metrics will NOT appear in CloudWatch until the CloudWatch agent (a small program running on the server) is set up to publish it?
choices: Network throughput, which shows how much data moves in and out
CPUCreditBalance, which shows how much burst credit a burstable instance has saved up
Memory use, which shows how much of the server's RAM is taken
CPUUtilization, which shows how busy the processor is
questions.why: CloudWatch can measure CPU, network and burst credits from outside the instance, but memory use can only be seen from inside, so it needs the agent to publish it.

questions.prompt: A retail company has hundreds of EC2 instances shared by many teams. The warehouse team wants to review Compute Optimizer recommendations for their own servers only, without touching anyone else's. Every instance carries resource tags (key-value labels attached to resources). What is the most direct way for the team to do this?
choices: Read the CPUUtilization graph of every instance in the account and pick out the busy ones
Install the CloudWatch agent on every instance so that memory figures are included in the review
Filter the recommendations by a tag such as team=warehouse so only that team's instances are listed
Ask Compute Optimizer for recommendations only on instances it has labeled under-provisioned
questions.why: Tags like team=warehouse let you filter recommendations, costs and automation so a team can act on its own servers.

questions.prompt: A clinic's booking system runs on a single EC2 instance with no load balancer in front of it. Compute Optimizer labels the instance under-provisioned, and an engineer decides to change it to a larger instance type at 11:00 on a busy weekday. What is the most likely effect on the running system?
choices: Nothing noticeable, because the new instance type takes effect while the server keeps running
Memory metrics stop reaching CloudWatch, because the CloudWatch agent is removed whenever the type changes
The booking system goes offline while the resize happens, because changing the instance type requires stopping the instance
The instance switches to unlimited bursting automatically, so the only effect is an extra charge
questions.why: Resizing requires stopping the instance, so a lone server with no load balancer goes down, which is why resizes belong in a maintenance window or behind a load balancer.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would decide whether to resize a group of EC2 instances, which metrics and tags you would use, and one limit of relying on the recommendations.
lessons.modelAnswer: First I'd scope the work with tags, say team=dispatch and env=prod, so I'm only reviewing our servers. Then I'd look at at least two weeks of CloudWatch metrics: CPUUtilization, network, and for burstable types CPUCreditBalance, because a zero balance means the server is pinned to its baseline and will feel slow. I'd make sure the CloudWatch agent is publishing memory, since memory isn't visible from outside the instance. Compute Optimizer then tells me which instances are over-provisioned, under-provisioned or optimized and suggests types. The limit: recommendations are only as good as the metrics behind them. Without memory data, a memory-bound server looks idle and downsizing it can crash it, and a short window misses monthly peaks. Resizing also needs a stop, so I'd do it in a maintenance window or behind a load balancer.
rubricPoints: Uses tags to scope which instances are reviewed or acted on.
Names concrete metrics such as CPUUtilization and CPUCreditBalance over a meaningful time window.
Notes memory needs the CloudWatch agent to be visible.
Describes Compute Optimizer's over-provisioned, under-provisioned and optimized findings.
Names a limit, such as missing memory data, short history, or resizing needing a stop.

suggested.rationale: Rightsizing is mostly reasoning from metrics, credit balances and tags to a resize decision, which an exam-style scenario exercises better than any current mission.

lessons.plain: Amazon EBS (Elastic Block Store) is network-attached disk for a virtual server in AWS. You pick a volume type, and each type promises a certain number of small reads and writes per second (IOPS), a certain amount of data per second (throughput), and a price. Think of it like renting a delivery van: some vans carry many small parcels quickly, some carry huge loads slowly, and some only go fast while their fuel reserve lasts. This objective is about reading the disk's own gauges to see when it has hit its limit, then choosing the cheapest volume type that still keeps up with the work.
lessons.guessPrompt: A database disk ran fast every morning for an hour, then suddenly became slow every afternoon, even though traffic stayed the same. What do you think the disk might have run out of?
lessons.teach:
An EBS volume is block storage that AWS attaches to an EC2 instance over the network. Each volume type sets limits on IOPS (input/output operations per second, the count of reads and writes) and throughput (megabytes moved per second). When work exceeds either limit, requests wait in line and latency (time per request) rises.

The main types: gp3, general-purpose SSD with a fixed baseline (3,000 IOPS, 125 MiB/s) and extra IOPS or throughput bought separately from size. gp2, older SSD whose IOPS scale with size (3 per GiB) and can burst to 3,000 by spending credits. io1/io2, provisioned-IOPS SSD, costly but steady and high, for demanding databases. st1, throughput-optimized hard disk for large sequential reads such as logs. sc1, cold hard disk, cheapest, for rarely read data. The hard-disk types cannot be boot volumes and do badly on small random IO.

CloudWatch, the AWS monitoring service, publishes per-volume metrics: VolumeReadOps and VolumeWriteOps (operation counts), VolumeReadBytes and VolumeWriteBytes, VolumeTotalReadTime and VolumeTotalWriteTime (seconds spent), VolumeQueueLength (requests waiting), VolumeIdleTime, and BurstBalance (percent of burst credits left, for gp2, st1, sc1).

Worked example: a 100 GiB gp2 database volume. Baseline is 100 × 3 = 300 IOPS. Morning load needs 1,500 IOPS, so it bursts. BurstBalance falls from 100 to 0 by noon. Then VolumeWriteOps Sum over 60 seconds flattens near 18,000, which is 18,000 ÷ 60 = 300 IOPS. VolumeQueueLength climbs, and average latency (VolumeTotalWriteTime ÷ VolumeWriteOps) jumps. Fix: change the type to gp3 using Elastic Volumes, which modifies the volume while attached. gp3 gives 3,000 IOPS with no credits, and usually costs less per GiB than gp2.

Common mistake: reading the Sum of ops as IOPS without dividing by the period in seconds, so you misjudge how close you are to the limit. Another is paying for io2 when gp3 with extra IOPS would do. Also remember the instance itself has an EBS bandwidth ceiling; a fast volume on a small instance can still stall. Left unfixed, a starved volume makes the whole application slow while CPU looks idle.

questions.prompt: A ticketing company runs its search index on a 250 GiB gp2 volume. Its baseline is 250 × 3 = 750 IOPS. During a sale, BurstBalance falls to 0. The CloudWatch graph for VolumeReadOps, shown as a Sum over a 300-second period, then flattens near 225,000. MISSING STEP: turn that Sum into IOPS. The engineer then compares the result with the baseline and sees that the volume is pinned at its limit. VolumeQueueLength is rising, so she plans to change the volume to gp3 using Elastic Volumes. Which choice correctly completes the missing step?
choices: 225,000 ÷ 60 = 3,750 IOPS, which is above the 3,000 burst ceiling
225,000 is already the IOPS figure, so the volume is far above its 750 IOPS baseline
The volume is still bursting at 3,000 IOPS, because Sum values ignore credits
225,000 ÷ 300 = 750 IOPS, which equals the baseline
questions.why: IOPS is the Sum of operations divided by the period length in seconds, and 225,000 ÷ 300 = 750 IOPS, which matches the 250 GiB gp2 baseline now that the burst credits are gone.

questions.prompt: A payroll app's EBS volume reports a VolumeTotalWriteTime of 12 seconds and a VolumeWriteOps of 24,000 for the same 60-second period. What was the average time per write?
choices: 400 writes per second
12 seconds per write
2,000 milliseconds per write
0.5 milliseconds per write
questions.why: Average latency is the total write time divided by the number of writes. That is 12 s ÷ 24,000 = 0.0005 s, or 0.5 ms.

questions.prompt: A clinic's reporting database needs a steady 6,000 IOPS with no bursting. A colleague proposes moving it to io2. The goal is the lowest cost that still meets this need. What is the better choice?
choices: gp2 sized large enough to burst to 6,000 IOPS
st1, because it is built for throughput
gp3 with extra IOPS bought on top of its 3,000 baseline
sc1, because it is the cheapest type
questions.why: gp3 lets you buy extra IOPS separately from size, with no credits involved, so it can meet a steady 6,000 IOPS without the higher cost of io2. gp2 bursts only to 3,000 IOPS, and the hard-disk types handle small random IO poorly.

questions.prompt: A team moves a busy volume to gp3 and buys 10,000 IOPS. The volume's CloudWatch metrics show it running well below that figure. Even so, VolumeQueueLength stays high, the app is slow, and the instance is a small type with CPU mostly idle. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The instance's own EBS bandwidth ceiling is limiting the traffic
The volume should be changed to st1 to handle random IO better
The gp3 volume has used up its BurstBalance credits
CloudWatch is double-counting operations, so the queue is not real
questions.why: Every instance has its own ceiling on EBS bandwidth, so a fast volume attached to a small instance can still stall. gp3 has no burst credits to run out of, and st1 performs badly on small random IO.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would tell from CloudWatch that an EBS volume is the bottleneck, and how you would pick a replacement volume type, naming one tradeoff between cost and performance.
lessons.modelAnswer: First I check whether the disk is at its ceiling. I turn VolumeReadOps plus VolumeWriteOps into IOPS by dividing the Sum by the period's seconds, and compare that to what the type allows. If it is flat at the limit while VolumeQueueLength grows and latency (total time divided by ops) rises, the volume is the bottleneck. On gp2, st1 or sc1 I look at BurstBalance; if it hits zero, the slowdown is credit exhaustion. For most workloads I move to gp3, because it gives a steady 3,000 IOPS baseline and lets me buy more IOPS or throughput without buying more size, often cheaper than gp2. I only pay for io2 when the database needs very high, consistent IOPS. The tradeoff: hard-disk types like st1 and sc1 are much cheaper per GiB but are poor at small random IO and cannot boot, and I must also check the instance's own EBS bandwidth limit.
rubricPoints: Converts operation counts into IOPS by dividing the sum by the period length.
Uses rising queue length and latency alongside flat IOPS to confirm the volume is saturated.
Identifies BurstBalance reaching zero as credit exhaustion on gp2, st1 or sc1.
Recommends gp3 as the usual choice because performance is bought independently of size.
Names a cost versus performance tradeoff such as io2 expense or HDD weakness on random IO.
Mentions that the instance's EBS bandwidth limit can be the real ceiling.

suggested.rationale: Choosing a volume type is best learned by reasoning through exam-style scenarios that pair a metric pattern with a cost constraint, and no current mission or planned engine simulates EBS volumes.

lessons.plain: Amazon S3 is AWS's object storage: you put whole files (called objects) into containers called buckets and read them back over the internet. When moving data in and out feels slow or expensive, four tools help. Multipart upload splits one big file into pieces sent side by side. Transfer Acceleration lets distant users hand data to a nearby AWS entry point instead of crossing the public internet the whole way. DataSync is a managed mover for copying large amounts of existing data from your own servers. Lifecycle policies are automatic housekeeping rules. Think of moving house: split boxes across helpers, use the motorway, hire movers, and clear out old junk on schedule.
lessons.guessPrompt: You need to upload a single 4 GB video file to cloud storage, and the connection keeps dropping halfway through. Without any special tools you start over each time. What would you change about how the file is sent so that a dropped connection costs you less?
lessons.teach:
Multipart upload means splitting one object into parts, uploading each part independently, often in parallel, then telling S3 to join them. Each part except the last is between 5 MB and 5 GB, with up to 10,000 parts. A single upload request tops out at 5 GB, so bigger objects must use multipart, and AWS suggests it from around 100 MB. It is faster because parts travel at the same time, and more reliable because a failed part is retried alone.

S3 Transfer Acceleration is a bucket setting that routes uploads and downloads through the nearest AWS edge location (a point of presence close to users), then across AWS's private backbone network to the bucket's Region. It helps when users are far from the bucket, and it costs an extra per-gigabyte fee. AWS DataSync is a managed transfer service: you install an agent (a small virtual machine) next to your file servers, and it copies data from shares (NFS or SMB) into S3, EFS or FSx on a schedule, with verification and bandwidth limits. It suits migrations and recurring bulk copies, not users uploading files from an app.

S3 Lifecycle policies are rules on a bucket that act on objects by age or prefix: transition them to cheaper storage classes, expire (delete) them, or abort incomplete multipart uploads.

Worked example: a user in Sydney uploads a 2 GB file to a bucket in Virginia. Step one, the client splits it into 200 parts of 10 MB. Step two, with acceleration on, parts go to a Sydney edge location rather than across the open internet. Step three, three parts fail and only those three are retried. Step four, the client sends a complete request and S3 assembles the object.

Common mistake: forgetting that abandoned multipart uploads leave parts you are still billed for, invisible in normal listings. In a running system storage costs creep up silently; a lifecycle rule that aborts incomplete uploads after a few days prevents it.

questions.prompt:
A logistics company runs a nightly job that uploads a 6 GB database export to an S3 bucket (S3 is AWS's object storage service). Fill in the missing step.

Step 1: The file is larger than 5 GB, which is the most a single upload request can carry, so the job uses multipart upload. Multipart upload means sending the object in separate parts and then asking S3 to join them.
Step 2: The job splits the file into 60 parts of 100 MB each and sends several parts at the same time.
Step 3: The server crashes after 40 parts arrive. The job never sends the final complete request, so S3 never assembles an object.
Step 4: ???
Step 5: The storage bill no longer includes the 40 orphaned parts, and nobody had to find or delete them by hand.

Which choice is the missing Step 4?
choices: An administrator spots the 40 parts in the bucket's normal object listing and deletes them manually.
A lifecycle rule on the bucket aborts multipart uploads that are still incomplete after 3 days, which removes the stored parts.
A lifecycle rule moves objects older than 3 days to a cheaper storage class, which lowers the cost of the parts.
S3 notices the failed job and deletes the uploaded parts on its own as soon as the server crashes.
questions.why: Abandoned parts stay billed and do not show up in normal listings, so a lifecycle rule (an automatic bucket rule that acts on objects by age or prefix) that aborts incomplete multipart uploads is what cleans them up.

questions.prompt: A media team tries to upload an 8 GB video to S3 using one single upload request, and the upload fails. What is the most likely reason?
choices: S3 Transfer Acceleration must be turned on before any object larger than 5 GB can be stored.
A lifecycle policy has to exist on the bucket before it will accept large objects.
One upload request can carry at most 5 GB, so an 8 GB object must be sent with multipart upload.
Objects larger than 5 GB have to be copied into S3 by an AWS DataSync agent.
questions.why: A single upload request tops out at 5 GB. Larger objects must be split into parts with multipart upload, which allows up to 10,000 parts.

questions.prompt: A hospital keeps 40 TB of imaging files on on-premises file shares that use the NFS protocol. Every night it wants new files copied into S3, with the copies checked for correctness and a limit on how much network bandwidth the copy uses. Which approach fits best?
choices: Turn on S3 Transfer Acceleration so the files travel through the nearest edge location.
Add a lifecycle rule that transitions the files from the shares into S3 each night.
Have staff upload the files through a web app that uses multipart upload.
Install an AWS DataSync agent next to the file servers and schedule a recurring copy task into S3.
questions.why: DataSync is a managed transfer service. Its agent, a small virtual machine placed next to the file servers, copies data from NFS or SMB shares into S3 on a schedule, with verification and bandwidth limits.

questions.prompt: A developer configures a client to upload a 900 MB file with multipart upload, using 3 MB parts (300 parts in total). Why will this setup be rejected?
choices: Every part except the last must be at least 5 MB, so 3 MB parts are too small.
Parts must be uploaded one at a time, and 300 parts cannot be sent in parallel.
Multipart upload can only be used for objects larger than 5 GB.
300 parts is more than the maximum number of parts allowed in one multipart upload.
questions.why: Each part except the last must be between 5 MB and 5 GB, so 3 MB parts break that rule. 300 parts is well under the 10,000-part limit, and multipart upload is allowed for objects smaller than 5 GB too.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate asks which of multipart upload, Transfer Acceleration, DataSync and Lifecycle policies to use for slow S3 transfers. Explain in your own words what each one solves, and name at least one limit or tradeoff.
lessons.modelAnswer: They solve different problems. Multipart upload splits a large object into parts uploaded in parallel and retried individually, so big files go faster and survive dropped connections; anything over 5 GB has to use it. The catch is that abandoned uploads leave billable parts behind. Transfer Acceleration helps when the users are far from the bucket's Region: traffic enters the nearest AWS edge location and rides AWS's backbone. It adds a per-gigabyte charge and does little if the users are already close. DataSync is for moving existing data from our own file servers into S3 or other AWS storage, using an agent with scheduling and verification. It is not for app users uploading files. Lifecycle policies don't speed transfers. They move or delete objects by age, and they should abort incomplete multipart uploads so stray parts don't keep costing us.
rubricPoints: Multipart upload sends parts in parallel, retries failed parts alone, and is required above 5 GB.
Transfer Acceleration routes through nearby edge locations and the AWS backbone, for distant clients, at extra cost.
DataSync is an agent-based managed service for bulk or scheduled copies from on-premises file shares.
Lifecycle policies transition or expire objects by rule and can abort incomplete multipart uploads.
At least one tradeoff is named, such as acceleration cost or hidden charges for leftover parts.

suggested.rationale: No mission or planned engine exercises S3 transfers, and the exam tests this as choosing the right tool for a described situation, so reasoning through scenarios teaches it best.

lessons.plain: Shared storage is a disk that many servers can use at the same time, like a shared network drive in an office where everyone opens the same folders. On AWS, Amazon EFS (Elastic File System) is a managed shared file system for Linux servers that grows and shrinks on its own. Amazon FSx is a family of managed file systems built on well-known products, for needs EFS does not cover, such as Windows file shares or very fast scientific computing. EFS lifecycle policies move files nobody has opened recently onto cheaper storage, the way you might box up old papers and put them in the basement.
lessons.guessPrompt: A team stores 1 TB of shared files, but most of them have not been opened in months. If you could automatically move untouched files to a cheaper shelf, what new cost or delay might you pay when someone finally opens one?
lessons.teach:
A shared file system lets many machines read and write the same files at once over the network. Amazon EFS is a managed file system that speaks NFS (Network File System, the standard Linux file-sharing protocol). It is elastic, meaning capacity grows as you write. By default it keeps copies across several Availability Zones (separate data centers in a Region). A cheaper One Zone option keeps data in one zone only.

Amazon FSx offers managed versions of other file systems. FSx for Windows File Server speaks SMB (the Windows sharing protocol) and joins Active Directory, the Windows identity service. FSx for Lustre is built for high-performance computing and can link to an S3 bucket. FSx for NetApp ONTAP and FSx for OpenZFS suit teams moving existing enterprise storage. Choose the protocol and workload first: Linux sharing means EFS, Windows sharing means FSx for Windows, and heavy compute means Lustre.

EFS has storage classes, which are price tiers. Standard is fast but costs the most. Infrequent Access (IA) and Archive store data cheaply but charge a fee each time data is read. A lifecycle policy moves files after a set number of days without access. A second rule can move a file back to Standard the first time it is read.

Worked example. A 1 TB file system holds 800 GB that has not been read in 60 days. You set a policy to move files to IA after 30 days. Overnight, about 800 GB moves, and the storage bill for that data drops sharply. Next month a user opens one old report. You pay a small read fee, and the return-on-access rule moves that file back to Standard.

A common mistake is setting a very short lifecycle period on data that is read often, such as nightly batch inputs. Read fees can then cancel out the savings. On performance, watch CloudWatch metrics. If BurstCreditBalance falls toward zero on bursting throughput, or PercentIOLimit stays near 100, the file system will slow down. Switching to Elastic or Provisioned throughput removes the dependence on burst credits.

questions.prompt: A research lab runs an Amazon EFS file system (managed Linux file sharing over NFS) holding 500 GB. 400 GB are old experiment logs that nobody has read in 120 days. 100 GB are input files that a processing job reads every night. Step 1: The team sets a lifecycle policy that moves files to Infrequent Access (IA) after 45 days without access, plus the rule that returns a file to Standard the first time it is read. Step 2: The nightly input files are read every day, so they never reach 45 days idle and stay in Standard. Step 3: ??? Step 4: Weeks later a scientist opens one old log. The lab pays a small read fee, and that log moves back to Standard. What is Step 3?
choices: The 400 GB of idle logs move to IA, and the storage cost for that data drops
Nothing moves until someone reads the logs and triggers the policy
The 400 GB of logs are deleted, because they passed the 45-day limit
All 500 GB move to IA, because the policy applies to the whole file system
questions.why: A lifecycle policy moves only files that have gone the set number of days without access, so just the idle logs shift to the cheaper IA class, while the daily-read inputs stay in Standard.

questions.prompt: An accounting firm is moving a Windows application to AWS. Several Windows servers must share the same folders using SMB (the Windows file-sharing protocol), and access must be controlled through the firm's Active Directory (the Windows identity service). Which managed shared storage fits best?
choices: Amazon EFS with the Standard storage class
Amazon FSx for Windows File Server
Amazon FSx for Lustre linked to an S3 bucket
Amazon EFS One Zone to keep costs low
questions.why: FSx for Windows File Server speaks SMB and joins Active Directory, while EFS speaks NFS for Linux and Lustre is for high-performance computing.

questions.prompt: A web team's EFS file system uses bursting throughput. Pages that load shared images have become slow. In CloudWatch, BurstCreditBalance has dropped close to zero over the past week. What change removes this dependence on burst credits?
choices: Shorten the lifecycle policy so more files move to IA
Switch the file system to Elastic or Provisioned throughput
Add a rule that returns files to Standard on first read
Move the file system to the EFS One Zone option
questions.why: Elastic and Provisioned throughput modes do not rely on burst credits, so a draining BurstCreditBalance no longer slows the file system.

questions.prompt: A logistics company sets an EFS lifecycle policy to move files to Infrequent Access after 1 day without access. Its shipment files are read by a job every two days. After a month, the storage bill is barely lower than before. What is the most likely reason?
choices: The policy only works on file systems larger than 1 TB
Each read of a file in IA charges a fee, cancelling the savings
Files in IA cannot be read until they are moved back by hand
IA keeps data in only one Availability Zone, which costs extra
questions.why: IA is cheap to store but charges a fee on every read, so a period shorter than the gap between reads keeps pushing frequently used files into IA, and the read fees eat the savings.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would choose between EFS and an FSx option for a new workload, and how an EFS lifecycle policy saves money, including one situation where it could cost more instead.
lessons.modelAnswer: First I ask which protocol and workload we have. If Linux servers need a shared folder, EFS fits. It is managed NFS that grows automatically and is spread across Availability Zones by default. If Windows machines need an SMB share joined to Active Directory, I pick FSx for Windows File Server. For high-performance compute reading big datasets, often from S3, I pick FSx for Lustre. ONTAP or OpenZFS suit teams moving existing enterprise storage. On EFS, a lifecycle policy moves files that have not been read for a set number of days into Infrequent Access or Archive. Those tiers cost far less to store but charge a fee per read. A return-on-access rule brings a file back to Standard when someone opens it. The tradeoff is that if we set the period too short on data that is reread often, read fees can exceed the savings. I would also watch BurstCreditBalance and PercentIOLimit for slowdowns.
rubricPoints: Matches the protocol to the service: NFS on Linux to EFS, SMB on Windows to FSx for Windows.
Names FSx for Lustre for high-performance compute and mentions the other FSx options.
Explains that lifecycle policies move files by days since last access into cheaper tiers.
States that IA and Archive charge per read, so frequently reread data can cost more.
Mentions moving files back to Standard on first access.
Notes a performance signal such as falling burst credits or PercentIOLimit near 100.

suggested.rationale: No current mission or planned engine exercises file-system choice directly, so reasoning through exam-style scenarios about protocol, access patterns and lifecycle cost teaches this best.

lessons.plain: A managed database runs on a server you never log into, so you watch it from the outside. Amazon RDS (a managed relational database service) gives you three windows. CloudWatch metrics are dials such as CPU, free disk space and open connections, and alarms sound when a dial crosses a line. Performance Insights is a closer look: it shows how busy the database is and which queries are waiting, and on what. Proactive recommendations are advice that AWS raises for you, such as 'storage is nearly full'. Think of a car: the dashboard gauges, a mechanic's diagnostic readout, and a service reminder.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your database server shows only 20% CPU, yet users say every page is slow. What else could the database be spending its time on besides the CPU?
lessons.teach:
Amazon CloudWatch is AWS's metrics and alarm service. RDS sends it instance metrics every minute, including CPUUtilization, FreeStorageSpace (disk left), FreeableMemory, DatabaseConnections, ReadLatency and WriteLatency (seconds per disk operation), and ReplicaLag (how far a read copy trails the primary). A CloudWatch alarm watches one metric and changes state when the value breaches a threshold for a set number of periods. On that state change it can notify people through Amazon SNS, a publish-and-subscribe messaging service.

Performance Insights is an RDS feature that samples active database sessions and reports DB load. A session is one connection doing work. DB load is measured in average active sessions (AAS), the number of sessions running or waiting at a given moment. It is split by wait event, meaning what the session is waiting on: CPU, disk I/O, locks and so on. It also lists top SQL, the statements that create the most load. Compare DB load with the instance's vCPU count, which is its number of virtual processors. If load stays above that line, work is queuing. Performance Insights also publishes DBLoad to CloudWatch, so you can set an alarm on it.

Proactive recommendations are findings that AWS generates from your configuration and metrics. Examples are storage that is nearly full, an outdated engine version, or a risky parameter. Amazon DevOps Guru for RDS goes further and flags unusual patterns in load.

Worked example: an instance has 2 vCPUs. Users report slowness. CPUUtilization is 25%, so CPU is not the cause. Performance Insights shows DB load at 6 AAS, three times the vCPU line, and most of it is an I/O wait event. Top SQL points to one report query that is scanning a whole table. You add an index, and load falls to 1 AAS. You then create an alarm on DBLoad above 2 for 3 consecutive minutes, sending to SNS.

A common mistake is to alarm only on CPU. Lock waits and I/O waits can make a database slow while CPU stays low. A team that does this goes unwarned until customers complain.

questions.prompt:
A ticketing company runs an RDS database on an instance with 8 vCPUs (virtual processors). At peak hours, users say booking pages hang. The steps so far:

Step 1: CPUUtilization (the CloudWatch metric for processor use) is 20%, so the processor is not busy.
Step 2: Performance Insights shows DB load at 20 average active sessions (AAS), meaning about 20 sessions are running or waiting at any moment. Most of that load is a lock wait event.
Step 3: ???
Step 4: Top SQL points to one update statement that holds locks on the bookings table for a long time. The team shortens that transaction, and DB load drops to 5 AAS.
Step 5: They create a CloudWatch alarm on DBLoad above 8 for 5 consecutive minutes, notifying the on-call team through Amazon SNS (a publish-and-subscribe messaging service).

Which statement correctly fills in Step 3?
choices: Because CPU is only 20%, the database has spare capacity and the slowness must come from the users' network, not RDS.
20 AAS is well above the 8-vCPU line, so work is queuing, and sessions are mostly waiting on locks, not on CPU.
20 AAS is below 100%, so no work is queuing and the lock waits can be ignored.
20 AAS means 20% CPU is in use, so the team should add more vCPUs to bring load down.
questions.why: When DB load stays above the vCPU count, work is queuing, and the wait event shows the cause, here locks, even while CPU stays low.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm's RDS instance has 4 vCPUs. Performance Insights reports a steady DB load of 3 average active sessions (AAS) during business hours. What does this tell you?
choices: On average, about 3 sessions are running or waiting, which is below the 4-vCPU line, so work is not queuing.
Exactly 3 users are connected to the database, so DatabaseConnections will also read 3.
The instance is overloaded because any DB load above 1 AAS means sessions are queuing.
Three-quarters of the database's storage is in use.
questions.why: AAS counts sessions running or waiting at a moment, and load below the vCPU count means the processors can keep up without a queue.

questions.prompt: A retail company has a read replica, which is a read-only copy of its RDS primary database. Store managers sometimes see stock counts that are several minutes out of date when they read from the replica. The ops team wants to be emailed through Amazon SNS before this becomes noticeable. Which CloudWatch alarm fits best?
choices: An alarm on CPUUtilization of the primary above 80%.
An alarm on ReplicaLag above a chosen threshold for several consecutive periods.
An alarm on WriteLatency of the primary above a set number of seconds.
An alarm on FreeableMemory of the replica below a set amount.
questions.why: ReplicaLag measures how far the read copy trails the primary, so alarming on it directly catches stale replica data.

questions.prompt: A media startup alarms only on CPUUtilization above 75% for its RDS database. One evening, a batch job makes many sessions wait on disk I/O. CPU stays near 15%, yet the app slows badly. What is the most likely result, and what would have warned them?
choices: A proactive recommendation automatically pages the team, so the CPU alarm is all they need.
No alarm fires and they hear about it from customers; an alarm on Performance Insights' DBLoad metric would have caught the rising load.
The CPU alarm fires anyway, because I/O waits always raise CPUUtilization above 75%.
No alarm fires, but this is expected, because a database cannot be slow while CPU is low.
questions.why: I/O and lock waits can slow a database while CPU stays low, so a CPU-only alarm stays silent, whereas an alarm on DBLoad rises with sessions that are waiting.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would tell whether a slow RDS database is short on CPU or stuck waiting on something else, and what alarms you would set. Name one limit of relying on CloudWatch CPU metrics alone.
lessons.modelAnswer: I start in Performance Insights. It measures DB load as average active sessions, which is how many sessions are working or waiting at once, and splits that load by wait event. If load sits above the instance's vCPU count and is mostly CPU, we are short on compute. If it is mostly I/O or lock waits, a bigger CPU will not help. The top SQL list then tells me which statement to fix, often by adding an index. For alarms I watch FreeStorageSpace, DatabaseConnections, read and write latency, and DBLoad, which Performance Insights sends to CloudWatch. Each alarm notifies through SNS. I also review RDS proactive recommendations, such as storage running low, before they become outages. The limit is that CPUUtilization can look healthy while queries queue behind locks or slow disk, so a CPU-only alarm can stay silent during a real slowdown.
rubricPoints: Defines DB load as average active sessions and compares it to the vCPU count.
Uses wait events to tell CPU pressure apart from I/O or lock waits.
Uses top SQL to find the statement causing the load.
Names useful CloudWatch alarm metrics, including DBLoad and FreeStorageSpace, with SNS notification.
Mentions acting on proactive recommendations before problems hit.
States that CPU alone can miss slowdowns caused by waiting.

suggested.rationale: The skill on the exam is reasoning from a symptom to the right signal: reading DB load against vCPUs and wait events, and then choosing which alarm would catch the problem. An exam-style situation to work through practises that best.

lessons.plain: Amazon RDS Proxy is a managed connection pooler: a middleman that sits between your application and a managed relational database (Amazon RDS or Aurora). Opening a database connection is slow and each one uses database memory, so a database only allows so many. When hundreds of short-lived app instances each open their own connection, the database runs out and starts refusing them. The proxy keeps a small set of connections already open and lends them out briefly. Think of a taxi rank: instead of every traveller buying a car, a few cabs shuttle everyone, and the road never jams.
lessons.guessPrompt: A database accepts at most 100 open connections. During a traffic spike, 500 short-lived functions each try to open their own connection to it. What do you expect to happen, and what kind of component could you put between the functions and the database to help?
lessons.teach:
Amazon RDS Proxy is a fully managed connection pool for RDS and Aurora databases. A connection pool is a set of database connections that are opened once and reused, instead of opened and closed for every request. Your application points at the proxy's endpoint (its network address) rather than the database's, and the proxy multiplexes: many client connections share a few real database connections, each borrowed only while a query or transaction runs, then returned.

Why it works: most requests hold a connection idle far longer than they use it. Handshakes and authentication also cost database CPU and memory. The proxy pays that cost once. It reads database credentials from AWS Secrets Manager (a managed secret store) and can let clients authenticate with IAM, the AWS identity system. During a failover, when a standby database takes over, the proxy holds client connections and reroutes them, so apps see a shorter interruption.

Worked example. The database allows 100 connections. A burst launches 500 AWS Lambda functions (short-lived serverless code), each opening a connection. Step 1, without a proxy: connections 101 to 500 fail with a too-many-connections error; in CloudWatch the RDS DatabaseConnections metric sits flat at its ceiling while app errors climb. Step 2, add a proxy capped at, say, 50 percent of the database's maximum: 50 real connections. Step 3: each function runs a 20 millisecond query, borrows a pooled connection, returns it. Step 4: 500 clients share 50 connections and the database stays healthy.

Common mistake: expecting the proxy to fix slow queries or a CPU-bound database. It only fixes connection pressure. A related trap is pinning: if a session changes state the proxy cannot safely share, such as a temporary table or a session variable, that client is pinned to one database connection for its lifetime, and multiplexing is lost. In a running system, heavy pinning quietly turns the proxy back into one-connection-per-client, and the original exhaustion returns under load.

questions.prompt: A ticket-booking company runs its booking API on 300 containers (small packaged copies of the app running side by side). Its RDS MySQL database allows at most 150 connections. Step 1: during a concert sale, the CloudWatch DatabaseConnections metric stays flat at 150 and the API returns too-many-connections errors. Step 2: the team creates an RDS Proxy capped at 40 percent of the database's maximum, giving 60 real connections, with the database credentials stored in AWS Secrets Manager. Step 3: [missing]. Step 4: each request borrows a pooled connection for its 15 millisecond transaction and then returns it, so 300 containers share 60 real connections and the errors stop. What is Step 3?
choices: Have each container set a session variable at login so the proxy can tell the clients apart
Raise the database's connection limit to 300 so every container gets its own dedicated connection
Move the database to a larger instance class, because the flat metric shows the database is short of CPU
Change the app's database address from the database endpoint to the proxy's endpoint, so connections go through the pool
questions.why: The proxy only pools connections that actually reach it, so the app must point at the proxy's endpoint instead of the database's.

questions.prompt: An analytics firm puts RDS Proxy in front of its Aurora database. In plain terms, what does it mean that the proxy multiplexes connections?
choices: It copies every query to several databases at once and returns the fastest answer
It splits one large query into smaller parts that run in parallel on the database
It opens one new database connection per client and closes it after each request to save memory
Many client connections share a few real database connections, each borrowed only while a query or transaction runs and then returned
questions.why: Multiplexing means many clients take turns using a small set of pooled database connections, holding one only while work is running.

questions.prompt: A logistics company's reporting page is slow. In CloudWatch, the RDS database shows CPU near 100 percent from a few heavy queries, while DatabaseConnections sits at only 30 out of an allowed 400. A colleague proposes adding RDS Proxy. What is the best assessment?
choices: Good idea, because the proxy will lower CPU by spreading the queries across more connections
Poor fit, because the proxy only relieves connection pressure and does not fix slow queries or a CPU-bound database
Good idea, but only if clients also switch to IAM authentication
Good idea, because the proxy caches query results and will make the heavy queries finish faster
questions.why: Connections are far below the limit and the bottleneck is CPU from slow queries, which a connection pool does not address.

questions.prompt: A retail company added RDS Proxy and its too-many-connections errors stopped. Months later, after a code change, every request now creates a temporary table at the start of its session, and under peak load the database's connection limit is reached again. What is the most likely cause?
choices: Temporary tables force a failover, and the proxy opens extra connections to the standby database
The proxy can no longer read the credentials from Secrets Manager, so it opens a fresh connection for every query
The temporary tables pin each client to one database connection, so multiplexing is lost and the proxy behaves like one connection per client
The proxy's cap of real connections is reset to zero whenever a temporary table is created
questions.why: Session state such as a temporary table cannot be safely shared, so the proxy pins that client to its own connection, and heavy pinning brings the original exhaustion back.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate, in your own words, why adding RDS Proxy can stop a database from refusing connections during a Lambda traffic spike, and name one situation where the proxy will not help or loses its benefit.
lessons.modelAnswer: Every function that opens its own database connection costs the database memory and a handshake, and the database has a hard connection limit. In a spike, hundreds of short-lived functions hit that limit and get refused, even though each one only needs the database for a few milliseconds. RDS Proxy is a managed connection pool in front of the database: it keeps a capped number of real connections open and lends one to each client only for the duration of its query or transaction, so many clients share a few connections. It also gets credentials from Secrets Manager and smooths failovers. The limit: it fixes connection pressure, not slow queries or a database that is out of CPU. And if clients set session state like temporary tables or session variables, the proxy pins them to one connection, sharing stops, and exhaustion can come back.
rubricPoints: States that RDS Proxy is a managed connection pool sitting between the app and the database.
Explains that many short-lived clients exhaust the database's connection limit.
Explains multiplexing: clients borrow a pooled connection only while a query or transaction runs.
Names that the proxy does not fix slow queries or a CPU-bound database.
Mentions pinning from session state as a way the benefit is lost.

suggested.rationale: Choosing RDS Proxy is best learned by reasoning through exam-style scenarios that separate connection exhaustion from other database slowness, and no current mission or planned engine exercises connection pooling directly.

lessons.plain: An EC2 instance is a rented virtual server. Making it fast is not only about picking a bigger one. The server also needs a wide enough pipe to its disks and to the network, and it needs to sit in the right place relative to its neighbours. Think of a delivery depot. A bigger depot does not help if the road to the warehouse is a single lane, or if the depots that trade with each other all day are in different towns. Placement groups are how you tell AWS where to put your servers: packed close together for speed, or spread apart so one failure cannot take out all of them.
lessons.guessPrompt: You run ten servers that pass huge amounts of data to each other every second. Would you ask the cloud provider to put them in the same rack or in different buildings, and what would you be giving up?
lessons.teach:
Three things limit an EC2 instance beyond its CPU and memory: its storage path, its network path, and where it physically sits.

Storage path. Amazon EBS (Elastic Block Store) is network-attached disk. An EBS-optimized instance has bandwidth reserved for disk traffic, so disk I/O does not compete with application traffic. Most current instance types are EBS-optimized by default. Each instance type also has a maximum EBS throughput. Instance store is disk that is physically attached to the host. It is very fast, but its data is lost when the instance stops or is terminated.

Network path. Enhanced networking uses the ENA (Elastic Network Adapter) to give higher bandwidth, more packets per second, and lower latency. EFA (Elastic Fabric Adapter) goes further and supports tightly coupled high-performance computing (HPC) and machine-learning jobs. Network bandwidth also grows with instance size.

Placement groups control where instances land. A cluster group packs instances close together inside one Availability Zone (AZ), which gives the lowest latency between them. A spread group puts each instance on separate hardware, with at most seven running instances per AZ per group. That suits a few critical servers. A partition group splits instances into partitions that share no racks, which suits large distributed systems such as Kafka or HDFS that know their own topology.

Worked example: a team's HPC job is slow. First, CloudWatch shows that the EBS throughput metrics are flat at the instance's limit. You move to a larger instance type with a higher EBS limit. Second, traffic between nodes is high-latency. You confirm ENA is enabled and relaunch the nodes into a cluster placement group. Third, you launch all nodes in one request using a single instance type, so AWS can find enough capacity on nearby hardware.

Common mistake: adding instances to a cluster group later, or mixing instance types, and then hitting an insufficient-capacity error. If that happens, stop and restart every instance in the group to retry. The cluster tradeoff also matters for a running system: because everything is in one AZ, a single AZ outage takes out the whole group.

questions.prompt:
A logistics company runs a 24-broker Kafka cluster in a single Availability Zone (AZ). An AZ is one isolated data-centre location within an AWS Region. Kafka is a distributed message system that keeps copies, called replicas, of each piece of data on several brokers. The team is planning how to rebuild the cluster.

Step 1: They notice that if two replicas of the same data sit on one rack, a single rack failure loses both copies.
Step 2: ______
Step 3: They configure Kafka with the rack layout so it places each piece of data's replicas in different groups of racks.

Which action belongs in Step 2?
choices: Move the Kafka data onto instance store disks, because physically attached disk is faster than network-attached EBS.
Launch the brokers into a partition placement group, which splits them into partitions that share no racks.
Launch the brokers into a cluster placement group so they sit as close together as possible and replicate with the lowest latency.
Launch the brokers into a spread placement group so every one of the 24 brokers runs on its own separate hardware in that AZ.
questions.why: A partition placement group divides instances into groups that share no racks, which suits large distributed systems like Kafka that can be told their own topology, while a spread group allows at most seven running instances per AZ.

questions.prompt: A media firm runs video rendering on an EC2 instance and writes temporary frame files to the instance store, which is disk physically attached to the host. To save money, an engineer stops the instance every night and starts it again each morning. What happens to the frame files?
choices: They are kept, but only if the instance is EBS-optimized.
They are lost only when the instance is terminated, not when it is stopped.
They are kept, because stopping an instance only pauses it.
They are lost, because instance store data does not survive a stop.
questions.why: Instance store is very fast, but its data is lost when the instance stops or is terminated, so it suits only scratch data you can recreate.

questions.prompt: An insurance company runs its claims database on an older EC2 instance type that is not EBS-optimized. EBS (Elastic Block Store) is network-attached disk. During busy hours, when the application sends a lot of network traffic, disk reads and writes slow sharply. Which change most directly targets this problem?
choices: Move to an EBS-optimized instance type, which reserves bandwidth just for disk traffic.
Put the database instance into a cluster placement group.
Attach an Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA) to the instance.
Put the database instance into a spread placement group.
questions.why: On an instance that is not EBS-optimized, disk I/O competes with application traffic for the same bandwidth, and EBS optimization reserves separate bandwidth for disk traffic.

questions.prompt: A research lab runs six instances of one type in a cluster placement group, which packs instances close together in one AZ. Months later it tries to add four instances of a different type to the same group and gets an insufficient-capacity error. Based on the guidance for this situation, what should the team do to retry?
choices: Keep retrying the four new instances one at a time until capacity appears.
Turn on Enhanced Networking (ENA) on the six existing instances.
Stop and restart every instance in the group so AWS can try to find nearby capacity for all of them together.
Convert the group to a spread placement group so AWS can use more hardware.
questions.why: Adding instances to a cluster group later or mixing types often causes insufficient-capacity errors, and stopping and restarting every instance in the group lets AWS retry placing them all together on nearby hardware.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would pick between cluster, spread, and partition placement groups, and what you sacrifice with each. Also say why a bigger instance alone might not fix slow disk or network performance.
lessons.modelAnswer: A placement group tells AWS where to put instances. Cluster packs them close in one Availability Zone for the lowest latency and highest throughput between them, which is great for HPC. The cost is that one AZ failure hits everything, and you can get capacity errors if you add instances later or mix types. Spread puts each instance on separate hardware, so one hardware failure hurts only one instance. It is capped at seven running instances per AZ, so it fits a handful of critical servers. Partition groups racks into isolated partitions for big distributed systems like Kafka, trading some locality for fault isolation. A bigger instance is not always enough, because disk and network have their own limits. The instance needs EBS-optimized bandwidth and a high enough EBS throughput cap, plus enhanced networking through ENA or EFA. Check the throughput metrics first to see which path is actually saturated.
rubricPoints: Cluster gives the lowest latency inside one AZ but shares that AZ's failure risk and can hit capacity errors.
Spread isolates each instance on separate hardware and is limited to seven running instances per AZ.
Partition isolates groups of racks for large distributed, topology-aware systems.
EBS-optimized bandwidth and per-type EBS throughput limits cap disk performance.
Enhanced networking with ENA, or EFA for HPC, raises network throughput and lowers latency.
Metrics should identify which path is saturated before you resize anything.

suggested.rationale: No mission or planned engine simulates EC2 placement or bandwidth limits, so reasoning through exam-style scenarios about which bottleneck and which placement group applies teaches this best.

lessons.plain: Scaling a compute environment means automatically adding servers when demand rises and removing them when it falls, so you pay for what you need and users still get fast answers. On AWS, the main tool is EC2 Auto Scaling, which manages a fleet of virtual servers as one group. Think of a supermarket that opens more checkout lanes when the queues get long and closes them when the store is quiet. A manager sets rules ahead of time, such as never fewer than two lanes and never more than ten, and staff follow those rules without being asked each time.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your web fleet has 4 servers averaging 80% CPU, and you want the average to sit near 50%. Roughly how many servers should the fleet grow to?
lessons.teach:
An Auto Scaling group (ASG) is a managed fleet of identical virtual servers (EC2 instances) that AWS keeps at a chosen size. It builds each new instance from a launch template, a saved recipe listing the machine image, instance type, network and security settings. Three numbers bound the group. Minimum is the floor, maximum is the ceiling, and desired capacity is how many instances the group runs right now. A scaling policy is the rule that changes desired capacity.

There are several kinds of policy. Target tracking keeps a metric, such as average CPU, near a target value, much like a thermostat. Step scaling adds or removes a set number of instances when an alarm crosses a threshold, with bigger steps for bigger breaches. Scheduled scaling changes capacity at known times, such as 08:00 on weekdays. Predictive scaling forecasts load from past patterns and adds capacity before the load arrives. Instance warmup is the time a new instance needs before its metrics count. A cooldown is a pause after a simple scaling action so the group does not react twice to the same spike.
