The ASG also runs health checks and replaces any instance that fails them. With an EC2 health check, a failure means the server itself is broken. With a load balancer health check, a failure means the application is not answering.

Here is a worked example. Target tracking aims for 50% CPU, with min 2 and max 8. Four instances average 80%. Total load is 4 × 80 = 320 percentage points. 320 ÷ 50 = 6.4, which rounds up to 7 instances. Seven is below the max of 8, so desired capacity becomes 7. If the max were 5, the group would stop at 5 and stay overloaded.

A common mistake is setting the maximum too low, or setting warmup shorter than real boot time. A low max means the group hits its ceiling during a surge and requests fail. A warmup that is too short means the group counts half-booted servers and overshoots or flaps up and down. Spreading the group across several Availability Zones (separate data centres) also lets it replace capacity lost in one of them.

questions.prompt: A ticket-booking company runs its checkout service in an Auto Scaling group with a target tracking policy aiming for 40% average CPU. The group has a minimum of 3 and a maximum of 10. Right now 6 instances average 75% CPU during a concert sale. Step 1: total load is 6 × 75 = 450 percentage points. Step 2: 450 ÷ 40 = 11.25, which rounds up to 12 instances needed. Step 3 is missing. Which choice correctly completes Step 3?
choices: Desired capacity becomes 10, because 12 is above the maximum. The group stops at the ceiling and stays overloaded.
Desired capacity stays at 6 until a cooldown ends, because target tracking waits before making any change.
Desired capacity becomes 12, because target tracking sets the group to whatever number the calculation produces.
Desired capacity becomes 11, because the policy rounds 11.25 down to the nearest whole instance.
questions.why: The maximum is the ceiling the group can never exceed, so the 12 instances the load calls for are capped at 10, and the group remains above its 40% target.

questions.prompt: A payroll firm knows its internal reporting app gets heavy use every weekday from 09:00 to 11:00, and almost none outside those hours. Which scaling policy fits a load that arrives at the same known times each day?
choices: Scheduled scaling, which changes capacity at set clock times
Step scaling, which adds a set number of instances when an alarm crosses a threshold
An EC2 health check, which replaces broken servers
A cooldown, which pauses the group after a scaling action
questions.why: Scheduled scaling is the policy for load that arrives at known times, so it can raise capacity before 09:00 and lower it after 11:00.

questions.prompt: A team's new instances take about 5 minutes to finish booting and loading their application. Someone has set the instance warmup to 1 minute. What is the most likely effect on the Auto Scaling group?
choices: The group can never grow past its minimum size.
The group ignores CPU and scales only on a schedule.
Every new instance fails its health check and is replaced.
The group counts half-booted servers too early, then overshoots or flaps up and down.
questions.why: Warmup is the time before a new instance's metrics count. If it is shorter than the real boot time, the group reads misleading numbers from servers that are not ready and reacts wrongly.

questions.prompt: An online bookshop's web application sometimes freezes and stops answering requests, but the virtual server underneath stays powered on and reachable. The Auto Scaling group never replaces these frozen instances. What change would let the group detect and replace them?
choices: Add a longer cooldown so the group reacts more slowly
Switch from target tracking to predictive scaling
Raise the group's maximum so more instances are available
Use load balancer health checks, which treat an application that is not answering as a failure
questions.why: An EC2 health check only fails when the server itself is broken, while a load balancer health check fails when the application stops answering, so the group then replaces the frozen instances.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how an Auto Scaling group decides how many instances to run, and name one limit or tradeoff of relying on it during a sudden traffic surge.
lessons.modelAnswer: An Auto Scaling group is a fleet of identical instances built from a launch template. We give it a minimum, a maximum and a desired capacity. A scaling policy moves the desired number. Target tracking keeps a metric like CPU near a goal. Step scaling reacts to alarm thresholds. Scheduled scaling handles known busy times, and predictive scaling adds capacity ahead of forecast load. The group also replaces instances that fail health checks. For example, with a 50% CPU target, 4 instances at 80% become 7, as long as the max allows it. Scaling is not instant, though. New instances need time to boot and warm up, so a sudden spike can overload the fleet before help arrives. The maximum also caps growth on purpose to control cost. If the max is too low or the warmup is wrong, we either run out of capacity or flap up and down. For predictable peaks, scheduled or predictive scaling plus a sensible minimum works better.
rubricPoints: Defines the group's minimum, maximum and desired capacity and the launch template.
Names at least two policy types, such as target tracking, step, scheduled or predictive, and says what each does.
Shows how target tracking computes a new size, capped by the maximum.
Notes that new instances take time to boot and warm up, so scaling lags sudden spikes.
Names a tradeoff, such as the cost-control role of the maximum or the flapping caused by a bad warmup or cooldown.
Mentions that the group replaces unhealthy instances using EC2 or load balancer health checks.

suggested.rationale: Choosing scaling policies, capacity limits and warmup values, then watching a simulated fleet respond, is best learned in the planned autoscaling engine.

lessons.plain: Caching means keeping a ready copy of an answer close to whoever asks, so the slow, expensive source does not have to work it out again every time. Think of a busy café that pre-pours the most popular drink: most customers get served instantly and the barista only makes the unusual orders. In AWS, Amazon CloudFront keeps copies of web content at locations near users around the world, and Amazon ElastiCache keeps frequently read data in fast memory next to your application. Both let a system absorb far more traffic without growing its servers or database at the same rate.
lessons.guessPrompt: A product page is read 10,000 times a minute but its price changes only once an hour. If you keep a copy of the page for 60 seconds, roughly how many times a minute does the database still have to build it, and what could go wrong for a customer?
lessons.teach:
A cache is a fast store holding copies of answers. A cache hit means the copy was found; a cache miss means the request goes to the origin, the real source such as a web server or database. TTL (time to live) is how long a copy stays valid. Hit ratio is the share of requests served from cache; the higher it is, the less load reaches the origin.

Amazon CloudFront is a content delivery network (CDN): a managed service that keeps copies at edge locations, servers spread close to users. Its cache key is the set of request parts (path, chosen headers, query strings, cookies) that decide whether two requests count as the same item. Invalidation forces copies to be removed before their TTL ends.

Amazon ElastiCache is a managed in-memory data store running Redis/Valkey or Memcached. A common pattern is cache-aside (lazy loading): the application checks the cache first, and on a miss reads the database and writes the result into the cache with a TTL. Write-through instead updates the cache every time the database is written, keeping it fresh at the cost of extra writes.

Worked example: a page is requested 10,000 times a minute with a 60-second TTL. First request: miss, origin builds it, CloudFront stores it. The next 9,999 requests that minute are hits. When the TTL expires, one miss refreshes it. The origin now does about one build a minute instead of 10,000, so it does not need to scale out.

Common mistake: putting every header, cookie or query string into the CloudFront cache key. Each user then looks like a different request, the hit ratio collapses, and the origin takes the full load during a surge. The opposite mistake, a TTL far too long, serves stale prices. A further risk is a cache stampede: when a popular item expires, many simultaneous misses hit the database at once, so stagger TTLs or let one request refresh while others wait.

questions.prompt: A ticket-booking company puts Amazon ElastiCache (a managed in-memory data store) in front of its venue database using cache-aside (lazy loading). The venue-details lookup for one popular stadium is requested 3,000 times a minute. Trace: Step 1, the first request checks the cache and finds nothing, a cache miss. Step 2, the application reads the venue details from the database. Step 3: ??? Step 4, for the next several minutes, every request for that stadium checks the cache, finds the copy, and is a cache hit, so the database is not queried again for it until the copy expires. Which action is Step 3?
choices: The application invalidates the stadium entry so the following request reads fresh data
The application writes the venue details into the cache with a 300-second TTL
The application returns the venue details to the user without storing a copy anywhere
The application writes the venue details back into the database so the next read is faster
questions.why: In cache-aside, after a miss the application stores the database result in the cache with a TTL, which is what lets the following requests become hits until the copy expires.

questions.prompt: A news website serves its home page through Amazon CloudFront, a content delivery network. To be safe, an engineer adds every cookie, including each visitor's unique session cookie, to the CloudFront cache key. During a breaking-news surge, what is the most likely result?
choices: Each visitor looks like a different request, the hit ratio collapses, and the origin takes nearly the full load
CloudFront ignores cookies during a surge, so the cache key change has no effect on load
Every visitor shares one cached copy, so the hit ratio rises and the origin is barely touched
Copies are removed from edge locations immediately, as if an invalidation had been issued
questions.why: The cache key decides which requests count as the same item, so a unique cookie in the key makes almost every request a miss and sends the load to the origin.

questions.prompt: A mapping service serves a city overview image through Amazon CloudFront. The image is requested 6,000 times a minute from a single edge location, and its TTL (time to live) is 300 seconds. Ignoring any invalidations, about how many times per hour does the origin have to build the image?
choices: 12 times, once each time the TTL expires
360,000 times, once for every request
Once, because the copy never needs refreshing
60 times, once every minute
questions.why: A 300-second TTL expires 12 times in an hour, and each expiry causes one miss that refreshes the copy while the other requests are hits.

questions.prompt: A gaming company caches its global leaderboard in Amazon ElastiCache. Every time the leaderboard entry expires, hundreds of game servers miss at the same moment and all query the database at once, spiking its CPU. What is this problem called, and what is a suitable fix?
choices: A stale-data problem; invalidate the leaderboard entry every few seconds
A cache stampede; let one request refresh the entry while the others wait, or stagger TTLs
A low hit ratio; add more headers and query strings to the cache key
A cache stampede; set the TTL to zero so the entry never sits in the cache
questions.why: Many simultaneous misses on one expired popular item is a cache stampede, and having a single request refresh it (or staggering expiries) stops the database being hit all at once.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how CloudFront and ElastiCache each help a system handle more traffic, and name one tradeoff you accept when you add a cache.
lessons.modelAnswer: Both put a fast copy in front of a slow source so most requests never reach it. CloudFront is a CDN: it stores responses at edge locations near users, so repeated requests for the same path are served there and the web origin barely notices a surge. ElastiCache is an in-memory store beside the application; with cache-aside the app checks it first and only queries the database on a miss, then saves the result with a TTL. The key measure is hit ratio, and for CloudFront that depends on a tight cache key, because including cookies or every header makes each request unique. The tradeoff is freshness: a copy can be out of date until its TTL expires or we invalidate it, so we pick TTLs per data type. We also have to guard against a stampede when a hot item expires and many misses hit the database together.
rubricPoints: Defines a cache hit and miss and explains that hits keep load off the origin or database.
Describes CloudFront as a CDN caching content at edge locations near users.
Describes ElastiCache as an in-memory store, typically used with cache-aside and a TTL.
Explains that hit ratio drives scalability and that an overly broad cache key ruins it.
Names a tradeoff such as stale data versus TTL length, or stampede risk on expiry.

suggested.rationale: This incident has the learner diagnose a slow API caused by cache behaviour, which makes hit ratio, expiry and stampede load on the origin concrete.

lessons.plain: Scaling a managed database means giving it more room to work when traffic grows, without rebuilding it. With Amazon RDS, a managed relational (SQL) database, you can move to a bigger server, let the disk grow by itself, or add read-only copies that share the reading load. With Amazon DynamoDB, a managed key-value table, you choose how much reading and writing per second the table can handle, or let AWS adjust it automatically. Think of a busy restaurant. You can hire a faster chef, which is a bigger server. You can add waiters who only serve and never cook, which are read copies. Or you can pay per meal and let the kitchen grow on its own, which is on-demand mode.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your RDS database is slow because the application writes a huge number of new orders every second. A colleague suggests adding two read-only copies of the database. Do you think that will speed up the writes? Why or why not?
lessons.teach:
Scaling a managed database means changing how much work it can handle without rebuilding it. Amazon RDS (a managed relational database service) and Amazon DynamoDB (a managed NoSQL table service) scale in different ways.

RDS gives you three levers. Vertical scaling means changing the DB instance class, which is the CPU and memory size. It restarts the database, so expect a short outage. Multi-AZ deployments shorten it, because the standby copy is resized first and then becomes the primary. Storage autoscaling grows the disk automatically when free space runs low, up to a maximum you set. Read replicas are asynchronous copies that answer reads only. Asynchronous means they receive changes slightly after the primary does, so they can lag behind it. Your application must send its read queries to the replica's endpoint (its connection address). Aurora, the AWS cloud-built relational engine, can add and remove replicas automatically with Aurora Auto Scaling.

DynamoDB measures throughput in capacity units. One read capacity unit (RCU) covers one strongly consistent read per second of an item up to 4 KB. One write capacity unit (WCU) covers one write per second of an item up to 1 KB. In provisioned mode you set the RCUs and WCUs yourself, and auto scaling adjusts them to keep usage near a target utilization percentage. In on-demand mode you pay per request and AWS absorbs spikes, which suits unpredictable traffic. Requests that go beyond the available capacity are throttled: they are rejected with an error, and the client must retry them.

Worked example. A table has 100 WCU provisioned and an auto scaling target of 70%. Traffic rises to 90 one-KB writes per second. Utilization is now 90%, which is above the 70% target. After a few minutes, auto scaling raises capacity to about 90 ÷ 0.70 ≈ 129 WCU. Until that happens, some writes are throttled, because auto scaling reacts over minutes, not instantly.

Common mistake: adding RDS read replicas to fix slow writes. Replicas take only reads. Every write still lands on the primary, so the fix is a larger instance class. A similar DynamoDB trap is a global secondary index (an extra index with its own capacity) left under-provisioned. When the index throttles, writes to the main table are throttled too, and users see failed saves.

questions.prompt: A ticketing company stores seat holds in a DynamoDB table in provisioned mode. The table has 200 RCU, and auto scaling has a target utilization of 50%. During a concert on-sale, the app makes 160 strongly consistent reads per second, each of an item smaller than 4 KB. Step 1: Each read uses 1 RCU, so demand is 160 RCU. Step 2: Utilization is 160 ÷ 200 = 80%, which is above the 50% target. Step 3 (missing): auto scaling works out the new capacity. Step 4: Until the new capacity takes effect a few minutes later, any reads beyond what is available are throttled and must be retried. What is Step 3?
choices: Capacity stays at 200 RCU, because demand of 160 RCU is still below the 200 RCU provisioned
Capacity rises to about 160 × 1.5 = 240 RCU, adding half of current demand as headroom
Capacity rises to about 160 ÷ 0.50 = 320 RCU, so that 160 RCU of demand is 50% of the new total
Capacity drops to about 160 × 0.50 = 80 RCU, matching the 50% target applied to current demand
questions.why: Auto scaling sizes capacity so that current usage sits at the target utilization, so it divides demand by the target: 160 ÷ 0.50 = 320 RCU.

questions.prompt: A clinic's booking system runs on Amazon RDS. To cut load on the primary database, the team adds a read replica. A week later, the primary's CPU is just as high and the replica is almost idle. The application code was not changed. What is the most likely cause?
choices: Read replicas only take load after storage autoscaling has grown the primary's disk to its maximum
The replica must first be promoted to a Multi-AZ standby before it can answer any read queries
The replica is asynchronous, so it refuses read queries until it has fully caught up with the primary
The application still sends its read queries to the primary's endpoint, not to the replica's endpoint
questions.why: A read replica has its own endpoint, and it only answers reads that the application actually sends to that endpoint.

questions.prompt: A delivery company's DynamoDB orders table has plenty of provisioned WCU. The table also has a global secondary index on customer ID, and that index has very little write capacity. During a lunchtime rush, drivers report that saving orders often fails. What is the best explanation?
choices: Read replicas of the table are lagging behind, so DynamoDB blocks new writes until they catch up
The under-provisioned index is throttling, and that causes writes to the main table to be throttled too
The main table has switched itself to on-demand mode, and that change rejects writes while it is in progress
Strongly consistent reads on the main table use up the WCU the table needs for its writes
questions.why: A global secondary index has its own capacity, and when it throttles, writes to the base table are throttled as well, so users see failed saves.

questions.prompt: A start-up is launching a new DynamoDB table for a mobile game. Traffic is hard to predict: it may be near zero for hours and then spike sharply when an influencer mentions the game. The team wants to avoid throttled requests during sudden spikes and does not want to plan capacity numbers. Which choice fits best?
choices: On-demand mode, where they pay per request and AWS absorbs the spikes without capacity planning
Add a global secondary index, because the extra index adds its own capacity to the main table
Provisioned mode with auto scaling set to a 70% target, because it raises capacity instantly at every spike
Provisioned mode with a low fixed RCU and WCU, relying on clients to retry throttled requests
questions.why: On-demand mode charges per request and absorbs unpredictable spikes, while provisioned auto scaling reacts over minutes and can throttle requests during a sudden jump.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would scale an RDS database and a DynamoDB table when traffic grows. Say which lever helps reads, which helps writes, and name one limit or tradeoff of each approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: For RDS, I look at what is growing first. If it is reads, I add read replicas and point read queries at their endpoints. The tradeoff is that replicas are asynchronous, so they can serve slightly stale data. Replicas never help writes. For write or CPU pressure, I change to a larger instance class. That restarts the database, so there is a brief outage, which Multi-AZ shortens by resizing the standby and failing over to it. Storage autoscaling handles a filling disk, up to the maximum I set. For DynamoDB, I choose between provisioned capacity with auto scaling, which is cheaper for steady traffic, and on-demand, which is better for unpredictable spikes but costs more per request. Auto scaling reacts over minutes, so sudden bursts can still be throttled. I also make sure every global secondary index has enough capacity, because a throttled index throttles writes to the main table.
rubricPoints: Read replicas scale reads only, are asynchronous, and can lag behind the primary.
Write or CPU pressure on RDS needs a larger instance class, which causes a brief restart.
Storage autoscaling grows the RDS disk up to a set maximum.
DynamoDB capacity is set in RCUs and WCUs, with provisioned plus auto scaling or on-demand as the choice.
DynamoDB auto scaling is not instant, so bursts can be throttled.
Under-provisioned global secondary indexes can throttle writes to the main table.

suggested.rationale: Working through stale positions caused by replica lag makes the learner feel the main tradeoff of scaling reads with asynchronous read replicas.

lessons.plain: A load balancer is a front door that spreads incoming requests across several servers. A health check is how that front door keeps asking each server, every few seconds, "are you able to serve?" If a server keeps failing to answer properly, the load balancer stops sending it customers until it recovers. Think of a restaurant host who glances at each waiter before seating a table: a waiter who is clearly swamped or missing gets skipped. The host does not fix the waiter. It just routes around the problem so diners keep being served.
lessons.guessPrompt: A load balancer checks each server every 30 seconds and marks it unhealthy after 2 failed checks in a row. Roughly how long after a server crashes will the load balancer stop sending it traffic?
lessons.teach:
Elastic Load Balancing (ELB) is AWS's managed load balancer service. It forwards requests to targets, which are the servers, containers or IP addresses that do the work. Targets are grouped into a target group. A health check is a repeated test request the load balancer sends to each target in a target group. Only targets that pass receive traffic.

You configure several settings. The protocol and port say how to connect, and the path says which URL to request, for example /health. The interval is the time between checks. The timeout is how long to wait for a reply. The unhealthy threshold is how many failures in a row mark a target unhealthy. The healthy threshold is how many successes in a row bring it back. The success codes are the HTTP status codes that count as passing, by default 200.

The design works because one slow reply does not remove a target, while a streak of failures does. It trades detection speed for stability.

Here is a worked example. The interval is 30 seconds, the unhealthy threshold is 2 and the healthy threshold is 5. A target crashes. It fails the first check, then fails the second about 30 seconds later, and it is marked unhealthy. That takes about one minute. After it restarts it needs 5 passes, which takes about 150 seconds, before it gets traffic again.

A common mistake is a health check that can never pass. One cause is a path that redirects to a login page and returns 302. Another is a path that returns 404. A third is a security group, the instance's firewall rules, that does not allow traffic from the load balancer on the health check port. The application works when you test it yourself, yet every target shows unhealthy.

One consequence for a running system: when every target is unhealthy, Application and Network Load Balancers fail open and send traffic to all targets anyway, so users see errors instead of nothing. Separately, if an Auto Scaling group uses ELB health checks, it replaces instances that fail them. A badly chosen check can therefore cause a loop where healthy instances are endlessly terminated and relaunched.

questions.prompt: A ticketing company's Network Load Balancer checks each target in its target group (the set of servers that share its traffic) every 10 seconds. The unhealthy threshold is 3 and the healthy threshold is 6. A target's process hangs. Step 1: it fails one check, then a second about 10 seconds later, then a third about 10 seconds after that. Step 2: with 3 failures in a row, it is marked unhealthy, roughly 3 x 10 = 30 seconds after the hang, and stops receiving traffic. Step 3: an engineer restarts the process, and it begins passing checks. Step 4 (missing): about how long after the restart does the target start receiving traffic again?
choices: About 10 seconds, because a single passing check returns it to service
About 16 seconds, because the two thresholds are added to the interval
About 30 seconds, because 3 passing checks at 10-second intervals are needed
About 60 seconds, because 6 passing checks in a row at 10-second intervals are needed
questions.why: Recovery depends on the healthy threshold, so 6 consecutive passes multiplied by the 10-second interval gives about 60 seconds.

questions.prompt: On an Elastic Load Balancing target group, which health check setting decides how many failed checks in a row it takes to mark a target unhealthy?
choices: The unhealthy threshold
The interval
The success codes
The timeout
questions.why: The unhealthy threshold is the count of consecutive failures that marks a target unhealthy. The timeout and interval control timing, and the success codes define what counts as a pass.

questions.prompt: A clinic runs its booking site behind an Application Load Balancer. A bad deployment makes every target fail its health check at once. What do users most likely experience?
choices: They are automatically sent to a backup site in another AWS Region
They see errors, because the load balancer fails open and sends traffic to all targets anyway
They are held in a queue until at least one target passes again
They get no response at all, because the load balancer stops forwarding requests
questions.why: When every target is unhealthy, Application and Network Load Balancers fail open. They keep sending traffic to all targets, so users reach broken servers and see errors.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm's Auto Scaling group uses ELB health checks. The instances serve pages correctly when an engineer tests them directly. However, the instances' security group, which holds their firewall rules, does not allow traffic from the load balancer on the health check port. What is the most likely result?
choices: Only the oldest instance is marked unhealthy and replaced once
The instances fail every check and are repeatedly terminated and relaunched
The targets stay healthy, because the application itself is working
The load balancer switches the health check to another open port
questions.why: The health checks can never reach the instances, so every check fails. The Auto Scaling group then keeps replacing working instances in an endless loop.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how ELB health checks decide whether a target gets traffic, and name the tradeoff in choosing the interval and thresholds, plus one reason every target might show unhealthy even though the app works.
lessons.modelAnswer:
The load balancer sends a test request to each target in the target group on a set protocol, port and path, every interval. If the reply arrives within the timeout with a success code like 200, that counts as a pass. A run of failures equal to the unhealthy threshold takes the target out of rotation. A run of passes equal to the healthy threshold puts it back.

The tradeoff is speed against stability. A short interval and low thresholds detect failures fast but can flap targets on a brief hiccup. Longer settings are calmer but leave users hitting a dead server longer.

If every target is unhealthy while the app works, check whether the security group allows the load balancer on the health check port. Also check that the path returns 200, not a redirect or a 404.
rubricPoints: Health checks are repeated test requests to each target, and only passing targets receive traffic.
Interval, timeout and thresholds together determine how quickly a target is removed or restored.
Faster detection risks flapping and slower settings prolong exposure to failed targets.
A blocked security group or a wrong path or status code can make all targets fail.
Auto Scaling using ELB health checks will replace failing instances, and when all targets are unhealthy the load balancer fails open.

suggested.rationale: No listed mission or engine exercises load balancer health checks directly, so reasoning through exam-style scenarios builds the most useful skill: timing out detection, spotting a blocked port or bad path, and predicting replacement loops.

lessons.plain: A Route 53 health check is a small robot that keeps knocking on your website or service from several places around the world and asks, "Are you still answering properly?" Route 53 is Amazon's managed DNS service, the internet's phone book that turns a name like shop.example.com into an address. When the robot reports that a server has stopped answering, the phone book can stop handing out that server's address and give out a backup address instead. Think of a receptionist who stops forwarding calls to a colleague once they have failed to pick up three times in a row, and sends the calls to the standby colleague.
lessons.guessPrompt: Suppose a health check probes your site every 30 seconds and needs 3 failures in a row before it marks the site unhealthy. Your server crashes. Roughly how long before Route 53 notices, and why might some users keep reaching the dead server for even longer?
lessons.teach: A Route 53 health check is a monitor that Route 53 runs against a resource and marks healthy or unhealthy. Route 53 is AWS's managed DNS service, and DNS (the Domain Name System) translates names into IP addresses. There are three kinds of health check. An endpoint check probes an IP address or domain name over HTTP, HTTPS or TCP. A calculated check combines other checks, for example healthy if at least 2 of 3 children are healthy. A CloudWatch alarm check follows the state of a CloudWatch alarm, which is a rule that watches a metric. Endpoint checks are run by health checkers spread across several AWS Regions. You set a request interval of 30 or 10 seconds and a failure threshold, which is the number of consecutive failed probes before the status flips. String matching optionally requires a given text in the start of the response body. The check pays off when you attach it to DNS records using failover routing. With failover routing, a primary record has a health check and a secondary record serves as the backup. When the primary is unhealthy, Route 53 answers queries with the secondary. Worked example: interval 30 seconds, threshold 3, record TTL 60 seconds. TTL (time to live) is how long resolvers and clients may cache a DNS answer. The server dies at time 0. Probes fail at about 30, 60 and 90 seconds, so the check turns unhealthy near 90 seconds and Route 53 starts returning the secondary. A client that cached the old answer just before the switch keeps using it for up to 60 more seconds, so worst-case failover is about 2.5 minutes. A common mistake is pointing an endpoint check at a private IP, or blocking the health checkers in a security group or firewall. A security group is a virtual firewall attached to a resource. The checkers come from the public internet, so the check reports unhealthy even though the server is fine. Traffic then fails over for no reason, or never fails back. For private resources, publish a metric and use a CloudWatch alarm check instead.

questions.prompt: A ticket-sales company uses Route 53 failover routing. Route 53 is AWS's managed DNS service, which answers queries that turn names into IP addresses. The primary record has an endpoint health check (a monitor that probes the server over HTTP) with a request interval of 10 seconds and a failure threshold of 4. The failure threshold is the number of consecutive failed probes before the status flips. The record's TTL (time to live, how long resolvers and clients may cache the DNS answer) is 20 seconds. The primary server crashes at time 0. Step 1: Probes fail at about 10, 20, 30 and 40 seconds. Step 2: ???. Step 3: A client that cached the old answer just before the switch keeps using it for up to 20 more seconds. Step 4: Worst-case failover for that client is therefore about 60 seconds. Which choice correctly fills Step 2?
choices: The check turns unhealthy near 10 seconds, after the first failed probe, and Route 53 starts returning the secondary record.
The check turns unhealthy near 80 seconds, because each failure must be confirmed by a second probe, and then the secondary is returned.
The check turns unhealthy near 40 seconds, after the fourth consecutive failure, and Route 53 starts returning the secondary record.
The check turns unhealthy near 40 seconds, but Route 53 waits one more TTL period before it returns the secondary record.
questions.why: The status flips only after 4 consecutive failed probes at 10-second intervals, so near 40 seconds, and Route 53 then immediately answers with the secondary while cached answers expire within the 20-second TTL.

questions.prompt: An online bookshop has three separate Route 53 health checks, one for each of its three web servers. The team wants a single status that reports healthy only when at least 2 of the 3 servers are healthy, so it can attach that one status to its primary DNS record. Which kind of Route 53 health check does this?
choices: An endpoint health check with string matching that looks for the text of all three servers.
A calculated health check, which combines the results of other health checks into one status.
An endpoint health check with a failure threshold of 2, pointed at the first web server.
A CloudWatch alarm health check, which follows the state of an alarm watching a metric.
questions.why: A calculated check combines child checks with a rule such as healthy if at least 2 of 3 children are healthy, which is exactly what the bookshop needs.

questions.prompt: A payroll firm runs an internal reporting server that has only a private IP address and cannot be reached from the public internet. The firm still wants a Route 53 health check on it to drive failover routing. What is the approach the course recommends?
choices: Create a calculated health check whose only child is an endpoint check pointed at the private IP address.
Create an endpoint health check against the private IP address and enable string matching on the response body.
Create an endpoint health check against the private IP address and shorten the request interval to 10 seconds.
Have the server publish a metric, create a CloudWatch alarm on it, and use a CloudWatch alarm health check.
questions.why: Endpoint health checkers probe from the public internet and cannot reach a private IP, so for private resources you publish a metric and base the health check on a CloudWatch alarm instead.

questions.prompt: A logistics company adds an HTTPS endpoint health check to the public IP of its primary web server, which is attached to a failover record. The server is working fine and customers who reach it get normal pages, yet the health check reports unhealthy and DNS traffic has moved to the secondary. The server's logs show no requests at all from the Route 53 health checkers. What is the most likely cause and its effect?
choices: The server's security group (a virtual firewall attached to the resource) blocks the health checkers, so traffic failed over for no reason.
The check should be a calculated check, because an endpoint check cannot be attached to a record that uses failover routing.
The failure threshold is set too high, so the check flipped to unhealthy after a single slow response from the server.
The record's TTL is too long, so the health checkers keep reading an old cached answer and the status never updates.
questions.why: Health checkers come from the public internet, so if a security group or firewall blocks them the check reports unhealthy even though the server is fine, causing an unnecessary failover that may never fail back.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how a Route 53 health check plus failover routing moves users to a backup site, and name one limit on how fast that really happens or one reason a healthy server might be marked unhealthy.
lessons.modelAnswer: Route 53 runs health checkers from several AWS Regions that probe our primary endpoint over HTTP, HTTPS or TCP on a fixed interval, either 30 or 10 seconds. If the number of consecutive failures reaches the failure threshold, the check goes unhealthy. Our primary DNS record uses failover routing and is tied to that check, so Route 53 stops returning the primary and answers with the secondary record instead. The limit is time: detection takes roughly the interval times the threshold, and clients that cached the old answer keep using it until the TTL expires. Lowering the interval, threshold or TTL speeds failover but costs more and risks flapping. Also, the checkers come from the internet, so if our security group blocks them, or we point the check at a private IP, a perfectly healthy server gets marked unhealthy. For private resources we should use a CloudWatch alarm-based check.
rubricPoints: Health checkers in multiple Regions probe the endpoint on a set interval.
The status flips only after the failure threshold of consecutive failures is reached.
Failover routing returns the secondary record when the primary's health check is unhealthy.
Detection time is about interval times threshold, and DNS TTL caching adds further delay.
Firewalls or security groups blocking the checkers, or private IPs, cause false unhealthy results.
Private resources can be monitored through a CloudWatch alarm-based health check.

suggested.rationale: Choosing interval, threshold and TTL to meet a failover target, and diagnosing a falsely unhealthy check, are best practised by reasoning through exam-style scenarios, since no current mission or planned engine simulates DNS health checks directly.

lessons.plain: A Multi-AZ deployment keeps copies of your system in two or more separate data center locations in the same region, so that if one location loses power or network, another copy carries on. Think of a shop with two branches on different streets, each with its own power supply. If one branch floods, customers are sent to the other, and the stock records are already identical because every sale is written to both branches at the same moment. You pay for the second branch even on quiet days. In return, a single building failure no longer closes the business.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your database keeps a live copy in a second, separate data center, and every change is written to both copies at once. If someone accidentally deletes a whole table, does the second copy save you? Why or why not?
lessons.teach:
A Multi-AZ deployment runs copies of a workload in two or more Availability Zones, so losing one zone does not take the service down. An AWS Region is a geographic area. An Availability Zone (AZ) is one or more separate data centers inside that Region, with its own power, cooling and network, linked to the other AZs by fast connections. Because AZs fail independently, spreading copies across them removes a single point of failure, meaning one component whose loss stops everything.

For a managed database such as Amazon RDS, Multi-AZ means the service keeps a standby. A standby is a second database instance in a different AZ that receives every write through synchronous replication. Synchronous replication means a write is not confirmed to your application until both copies have it, so almost no data is lost on failover. Failover is the automatic switch from a failed primary to the standby. Your application connects through an endpoint, which is a DNS name the service points at whichever copy is currently primary.

Worked example: the primary's AZ loses power at 10:00. The service detects that the primary is unreachable and promotes the standby. It then updates the endpoint's DNS record to the standby's address, usually within one to two minutes. Applications that reconnect by name reach the new primary, and every committed write is there. The recovery point is effectively zero, and the recovery time is the failover duration.

For virtual servers you run yourself, such as EC2 instances, the same idea means placing instances in at least two AZs behind a load balancer. The load balancer sends traffic only to instances that are healthy.

A common mistake is treating the classic RDS standby as a read replica or a backup. That standby serves no traffic. Because replication is synchronous, an accidental table deletion reaches it instantly. Multi-AZ protects against infrastructure failure, not bad data, so you still need backups. Hardcoding an IP address, or caching DNS indefinitely, also breaks recovery: after failover the application keeps calling the dead primary.

questions.prompt: A ticketing company runs its orders database on Amazon RDS with Multi-AZ turned on: a primary in one Availability Zone and a standby in another. At 09:12 an engineer accidentally runs a command that deletes the bookings table. The team reasons about recovery like this. Step 1: The delete is committed on the primary. Step 2: Because replication to the standby is synchronous, the delete is also applied on the standby before it is confirmed. Step 3: [missing]. Step 4: So the team must restore the table from a backup taken before 09:12. Which statement best fills Step 3?
choices: The standby can be queried as a read replica to copy the table back to the primary.
The endpoint's DNS record will automatically point to an older copy that still has the table.
Failing over to the standby would not help, because the standby no longer has the table either.
Forcing a failover will bring the table back, because the standby keeps its own separate copy of the old data.
questions.why: Synchronous replication copies the bad delete to the standby at once, so failover only protects against infrastructure failure, not bad data, and a backup is the only way back.

questions.prompt: A payroll team's managed database uses synchronous replication to a standby in a second Availability Zone. What does synchronous replication mean for each write the application makes?
choices: The write is stored only on the standby, and the primary reads it from there when needed.
The write is not confirmed to the application until both the primary and the standby have it.
The write is sent to the standby on a schedule, such as every five minutes, after the application is told it succeeded.
The write is copied to the standby only when the primary fails, so the standby stays idle until then.
questions.why: Synchronous replication waits until both copies hold the write before confirming it, which is why almost no committed data is lost on failover.

questions.prompt: A small online bookshop runs its web servers on three EC2 instances, all in the same Availability Zone, behind a load balancer. Its database already uses RDS Multi-AZ. The owner wants the website to stay up if one Availability Zone goes down. What change addresses the remaining single point of failure?
choices: Turn on Multi-AZ for the database a second time so it has two standbys.
Spread the web server instances across at least two Availability Zones behind the load balancer.
Add two more EC2 instances in the same Availability Zone so there is more spare capacity.
Replace the load balancer with a fixed IP address that customers connect to directly.
questions.why: With every instance in one zone, losing that zone stops the site; placing instances in two or more zones lets the load balancer send traffic to the healthy ones that remain.

questions.prompt: A delivery company's app connects to its RDS Multi-AZ database using the IP address 10.0.4.22, which an engineer copied from the console and saved in the config file. The primary's Availability Zone suffers a network outage and the service fails over successfully, yet the app keeps showing database errors. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The app is still calling the old primary's IP address instead of the endpoint name, which now points to the new primary.
The standby had been serving read traffic and is now overloaded after promotion.
Multi-AZ only protects against deleted data, not against an Availability Zone outage.
Failover always loses the last hour of writes, so the app's queries find missing records.
questions.why: After failover the service updates the endpoint's DNS name to the new primary, so an app with a hardcoded IP keeps calling the dead primary until it connects by name.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what turning on Multi-AZ for a database actually buys you during an outage, and name one thing it does not protect against.
lessons.modelAnswer: Multi-AZ keeps a standby copy of the database in a different Availability Zone, which is a physically separate data center with its own power and network in the same region. Every write is copied to the standby synchronously, so the write is confirmed only when both copies hold it. If the primary's zone fails, the service promotes the standby and repoints the DNS endpoint at it, usually within a minute or two. Committed data is not lost, so the recovery point is near zero and the recovery time is roughly the failover time. That only works if our app connects by the endpoint name and does not cache DNS. The limit is that Multi-AZ protects against infrastructure failure, not bad data. A mistaken delete or corruption is replicated to the standby immediately, so we still need backups or point-in-time restore. It also costs roughly double, and the classic standby does not serve reads.
rubricPoints: Defines an Availability Zone as an isolated data center location within a Region.
States that the standby receives writes synchronously, so committed data survives failover.
Describes failover as promoting the standby and repointing the DNS endpoint automatically.
Notes the application must connect by endpoint name, not by IP address or long-cached DNS.
Names a limit: no protection from accidental deletes or corruption, so backups are still required.
Mentions a tradeoff such as extra cost or the classic standby not serving read traffic.

suggested.rationale: Multi-AZ is mostly a judgement skill, so reasoning through exam-style outage scenarios builds it best: choosing between a standby, a read replica and a backup, and predicting what survives each failure.

lessons.plain: AWS Backup is a managed backup service: one place where you write down what to protect, how often, how long to keep the copies, and where to store them. It then makes those copies on schedule across many kinds of resources, including servers, disks, databases, object storage buckets and key-value tables. Think of a building manager who photocopies every important file in every office each night, using one master checklist, and files the copies in a locked cabinet. Nobody has to remember to do it office by office. You still have to check that the copies can actually be used.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your team says no more than 4 hours of data may ever be lost. If a tool copies your database once a day at midnight, could that promise be broken, and roughly how much data could you lose in the worst case?
lessons.teach:
AWS Backup is a managed service that schedules and stores backups for many resource types from one central policy. It covers EC2 instances, which are virtual servers; EBS volumes, which are their attached disks; RDS DB instances, which are managed relational databases; S3 buckets, which are object storage; and DynamoDB tables, which are managed key-value tables.

The policy is a backup plan. A plan contains one or more backup rules. Each rule sets a schedule (how often to back up) and a backup window (the time span in which a job may start). It also sets a lifecycle, meaning when copies move to cheaper cold storage and when they expire, plus optional copies to another Region or account. Each saved copy is a recovery point. Recovery points live in a backup vault, a storage container with its own access policy and encryption key. Vault Lock can stop anyone, including administrators, from deleting recovery points early. A resource assignment says which resources the plan covers, often by matching a tag. AWS Backup acts through an IAM role, which is a set of permissions the service assumes.

This works because every resource that carries the tag follows one written rule, so coverage does not depend on someone remembering a script. The schedule sets your RPO (recovery point objective), the most data you can afford to lose.

Worked example: the RPO is 4 hours, and you must survive losing a whole Region. You create a rule that runs every 4 hours and keeps copies for 35 days. You add a copy action to a vault in a second Region. You assign the plan to the tag backup=critical. You tag the RDS instance and the DynamoDB table. S3 buckets must also have versioning turned on before they can be backed up.

A common mistake is creating a new database without the tag. The plan silently skips it, and the gap only appears when someone needs a restore. To prevent this, monitor job status and run test restores, because a backup you have never restored is a hope, not a recovery plan.

questions.prompt: A delivery company has an RPO of 1 hour for its order data, which lives in a DynamoDB table and in an S3 bucket of shipping labels. Auditors also require that no one, not even an administrator, can delete a saved copy early. The engineer's work so far: Step 1, create an AWS Backup plan with a rule that runs every 1 hour and keeps recovery points for 14 days. Step 2, send the recovery points to a backup vault with Vault Lock turned on. Step 3, create a resource assignment that matches the tag backup=hourly. Step 4, add the tag backup=hourly to the DynamoDB table and to the S3 bucket. Step 5 is missing. Which step must be done before the S3 bucket can actually be backed up?
choices: Turn on versioning for the S3 bucket
Add a copy action to a vault in a second Region so the bucket qualifies for backup
Widen the backup window to 12 hours so the S3 job has more time to start
Change the lifecycle so recovery points move to cold storage after 1 day
questions.why: AWS Backup can only back up an S3 bucket that has versioning turned on, so without it the tagged bucket still produces no recovery points.

questions.prompt: In an AWS Backup rule, which setting most directly determines your RPO (recovery point objective), the most data you could lose?
choices: The schedule, meaning how often a backup is taken
The backup vault, meaning where the recovery points are stored
The lifecycle, meaning when copies move to cold storage and expire
The backup window, the time span in which a job may start
questions.why: The schedule sets how far apart recovery points are, so it sets the maximum amount of data lost between the last copy and a failure.

questions.prompt: A hospital's backup plan assigns resources by the tag backup=daily. Last month a team launched a new EC2 instance for a lab system. Today the instance's disk fails, and the team finds there are no recovery points for it at all, though every other system has them. What is the most likely cause, and what practice would have caught it sooner?
choices: The vault's encryption key expired; rotating keys yearly would have caught it
The lifecycle moved its copies to cold storage; checking cold storage would find them
The instance was never tagged, so the plan skipped it; monitoring job status and running test restores would have caught it
The backup window was too short; a longer window would have caught it
questions.why: A plan that selects by tag silently ignores untagged resources, and checking job status plus test restores reveals that gap before a real restore is needed.

questions.prompt: A bank's compliance rule says that once a backup of its RDS database is saved, nobody, including administrators, may delete it before its 90-day retention ends. Which AWS Backup feature meets this requirement?
choices: The IAM role that AWS Backup assumes to take the backups
A resource assignment that matches the database by its tag
Vault Lock on the backup vault holding the recovery points
A lifecycle rule that moves copies to cold storage after 30 days
questions.why: Vault Lock prevents anyone, administrators included, from deleting recovery points before their retention period ends.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how AWS Backup would protect our databases, disks and buckets automatically, and name one limit or tradeoff we must watch for.
lessons.modelAnswer: AWS Backup is a central, managed way to back things up. We write one backup plan, and its rules say how often to back up, during which window, how long to keep each copy, and whether to copy it to another Region or account. The copies, called recovery points, sit in a backup vault. Vault Lock can stop anyone from deleting them early. The plan picks resources by tag, so any EC2 instance, EBS volume, RDS database, versioned S3 bucket or DynamoDB table tagged correctly is covered. The schedule decides our RPO: back up every 4 hours and we can lose up to 4 hours of data. The tradeoff is that more frequent backups, longer retention and cross-Region copies cost more. The big limit is that an untagged resource is silently skipped. A successful backup also proves nothing until we test a restore.
rubricPoints: A backup plan holds rules for schedule, window, retention or lifecycle, and optional cross-Region or cross-account copies.
Recovery points are stored in a backup vault, which Vault Lock can protect from early deletion.
Resources are assigned to the plan, commonly by tag, across EC2, EBS, RDS, S3 and DynamoDB.
Backup frequency sets the achievable RPO.
Untagged resources are skipped silently, so coverage and job status must be monitored.
Restores must be tested, and frequency, retention and copies all add cost.

suggested.rationale: A disaster-recovery planner would have the learner choose backup frequency, retention and cross-Region copies to meet a given RPO, then check coverage and the restore, which is the core skill here.

lessons.plain: Restoring a database means rebuilding it from saved copies after something goes wrong, such as a bad deploy, a deleted table or corrupted data. Point-in-time restore lets you choose an exact moment, like 14:31 yesterday, and get the data as it was then. Two numbers judge the result. The recovery point objective (RPO) is how much recent data you can afford to lose. The recovery time objective (RTO) is how long you can afford to be down. It works like a video recorder for your data: you rewind to just before the mistake. Rewinding takes time, and keeping more recordings costs more.
lessons.guessPrompt: Someone accidentally deletes an important table at 14:32. Your only backup is a nightly copy taken at 02:00. If you restore that copy, roughly how many hours of data changes do you lose, and what kind of backup would shrink that gap to minutes?
lessons.teach:
A database restore rebuilds data from a backup. A snapshot is a full copy taken at one moment. Point-in-time restore (PITR) combines a snapshot with the transaction log, which is the running record of every change made since. Replaying that log up to a chosen second rebuilds the data as it stood at that second.

In Amazon RDS, the managed relational database service, automated backups provide PITR. You can pick any second inside the retention window, which you can set from 1 to 35 days, up to the latest restorable time, usually only a few minutes ago. Manual snapshots never expire on their own, but they capture only the moment they were taken. Amazon DynamoDB, the managed key-value database, offers a similar PITR feature with up to 35 days of history.

The key behaviour is this: a restore creates a new database. It never overwrites the old one. You must then point the application at the new endpoint, which is the network address clients connect to, or swap names.

Worked example. The requirement is RPO 15 minutes and RTO 2 hours. A bad script drops the orders table at 14:32. First, note the time of the damage. Second, restore to 14:31 as a new instance. Third, attach the correct security groups and parameter group, because a restored instance can come up with defaults. Fourth, check that the orders table is back. Fifth, repoint the application. About one minute of data is lost, which meets the RPO. Restore time grows with database size and with how much log must be replayed, so test it to confirm it fits inside 2 hours.

A common mistake is to rely on nightly snapshots alone. That gives an RPO of up to 24 hours. Another is to restore successfully and then forget to repoint the application, so the system keeps writing to the damaged database.

Cost trades against these targets. Longer retention, extra manual snapshots and copies kept in another Region all add storage charges. Tighter RTO and RPO generally cost more.

questions.prompt:
A ticketing company runs its booking database on Amazon RDS, the managed relational database service. The business requires an RPO (the most data, measured in time, it can afford to lose) of 10 minutes and an RTO (the longest it can afford to be down) of 3 hours. Today the only protection is a manual snapshot, a full copy taken at one moment, created every night at 02:00. An engineer checks whether this meets the targets.

Step 1: Picture the worst case. Damage strikes at 01:55, just before the next nightly snapshot.
Step 2: ???
Step 3: Conclude that snapshots alone cannot meet the target. Turn on automated backups with a retention window, for example 7 days. This gives point-in-time restore (PITR), which replays the transaction log, the running record of every change, so the data can be rebuilt to within minutes of the damage.
Step 4: Rehearse a PITR restore of the real-sized database to confirm it finishes well inside 3 hours.

Which statement correctly fills Step 2?
choices: Manual snapshots expire after 35 days, so the older nightly copies may be gone by the time they are needed.
The 02:00 snapshot also holds the transaction log, so only about 5 minutes would be lost and the RPO is met.
The restore from the 02:00 snapshot would overwrite the live database, so the company would break its RTO while the copy runs.
Restoring the previous night's 02:00 snapshot would lose almost 24 hours of bookings, far beyond the 10-minute RPO.
questions.why: A snapshot captures only the moment it was taken, so damage just before the next one loses nearly a full day of changes, which breaks a 10-minute RPO.

questions.prompt: An engineer runs a point-in-time restore of an Amazon RDS database to 08:15 this morning. What does the restore produce?
choices: The original database is rolled back in place to 08:15 and keeps its existing endpoint.
A manual snapshot dated 08:15 that must then be copied to another Region before anyone can use it.
A read-only view of the original database as it looked at 08:15, served from the same endpoint.
A new database instance with its own endpoint, while the original database is left untouched.
questions.why: A restore always creates a new database and never overwrites the old one, so the application must be pointed at the new endpoint (network address) or the names must be swapped.

questions.prompt: An accounting firm's Amazon RDS database has automated backups with the maximum 35-day retention window. An audit finds that records were silently corrupted 40 days ago. The team also has a manual snapshot taken 45 days ago. What restore options do they have?
choices: Nothing can be restored, because every RDS backup expires after 35 days at most.
Restoring the 45-day-old manual snapshot, accepting that it holds the data only as it stood when that snapshot was taken.
Raising the retention window to 60 days now, then running a point-in-time restore to 40 days ago.
Point-in-time restore to the second just before the corruption, because automated backups keep a full 35 days plus a grace period.
questions.why: PITR can only reach back as far as the retention window, which is at most 35 days, but manual snapshots never expire on their own, so the older snapshot is still usable at its own moment in time.

questions.prompt: A logistics team restores its Amazon RDS database to a point just before a faulty data import. They confirm the data looks right, then switch the application to the new endpoint. The application immediately starts timing out when it tries to connect. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The restored instance came up with default settings, such as the default security group (the network access rules), so the application's traffic is not allowed in.
Point-in-time restore keeps the new instance offline until the original database is deleted.
The transaction log was not replayed, so the new instance has no tables for the application to connect to.
The restore overwrote the original database, and the application's connections were dropped during the overwrite.
questions.why: A restored instance can start with default security groups and parameter group, so the correct ones must be attached before the application can connect.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would recover an RDS database from an accidental data deletion using point-in-time restore. Show how the restore meets an RPO and an RTO, and name one limit or cost tradeoff.
lessons.modelAnswer:
Automated backups combine daily snapshots with the transaction log. That means I can restore to any second within the retention window, up to a few minutes ago. If someone deletes data at 14:32, I restore to 14:31. Our loss is about a minute, which is well inside a 15-minute RPO.

The restore builds a brand-new instance and leaves the damaged one alone. So I attach the right security groups and parameter group, check the data, and then repoint the application to the new endpoint.

The RTO is the whole sequence, not just the restore button. Restore time grows with database size and log replay, so we should rehearse it and time it.

There are limits. We cannot go back further than retention allows, at most 35 days. For anything older we need manual snapshots. Longer retention and cross-Region copies also add storage cost, so we size them to what the business actually needs.
rubricPoints: PITR replays the transaction log on top of a snapshot to reach a chosen second inside the retention window.
Restore creates a new database, so the application must be repointed and settings reattached.
RPO is met by how close to the failure you can restore; snapshot-only backups mean a large RPO.
RTO covers the full restore, verification and cutover, and grows with database size, so it should be tested.
Longer retention, extra snapshots and cross-Region copies raise cost, so they are sized to the requirements.

suggested.rationale: A disaster-recovery planner would let the learner choose backup settings against stated RTO, RPO and cost targets, and then walk through the restore and cutover to check that the targets are met.

lessons.plain: Versioning means a storage service keeps older copies of a file instead of throwing them away when the file is changed or deleted. It works like the undo history in a document editor. If someone overwrites a report with a bad copy or deletes it by accident, you can go back to an earlier copy. On AWS, Amazon S3, an object storage service that keeps files in containers called buckets, can keep every version of every object. Amazon FSx, a managed shared file system service, can keep scheduled point-in-time copies so users can bring back yesterday's file themselves.
lessons.guessPrompt: Suppose a bucket keeps every version of every file, and someone deletes report.csv. Do you think the old data is really gone? If it is not, what do you think the service did instead of erasing it?
lessons.teach:
S3 versioning is a bucket setting. When it is on, every upload to an existing key (the object's name) is kept as a new version with its own version ID, and the older copies stay in the bucket. A bucket can be in one of three states: unversioned, enabled, or suspended. Once you enable versioning, you can only suspend it after that. You can never set the bucket back to unversioned. Suspending stops new versions from being created, but every version that already exists is kept.

A plain delete, meaning a delete that does not name a version ID, erases nothing. S3 adds a delete marker, which is a placeholder that becomes the current version. Because the marker is current, a normal read of that key returns 'not found'. Only a delete that names a specific version ID removes that version for good.

Here is a worked example. You upload config.json and it becomes v1. You upload it again and it becomes v2, while v1 stays as a noncurrent version, meaning an older copy that is no longer the current one. Someone then deletes config.json without naming a version, so a delete marker becomes current. To recover the file, you delete the delete marker itself, and v2 becomes current again. If v2 was the bad copy, you can instead copy v1 back over the top, which creates a new current version holding v1's content.

FSx for Windows File Server, a managed Windows shared drive, gets its versioning from shadow copies. These are scheduled point-in-time snapshots of the file system, and users can restore from them through the Previous Versions option in Windows. Shadow copies live inside the same file system and use up its storage, and the oldest ones are removed when the space set aside for them fills. FSx for NetApp ONTAP and FSx for OpenZFS offer a similar feature called snapshots.

A common mistake is to treat versioning as a backup. Shadow copies disappear if the file system is lost. S3 versions sit in the same bucket, so a delete that names a version ID can remove them unless you add protections such as MFA Delete, which requires a one-time code before a version can be permanently deleted. The consequence for a running system is cost. Every version is billed, so a key that is rewritten often can quietly multiply your storage bill. The usual fix is a lifecycle rule that expires noncurrent versions after a set number of days.

questions.prompt: A design agency turned on versioning for its S3 bucket "agency-assets" in March. By June the file logo.png has 12 versions, and the team wants to stop creating new ones. Step 1: they review their options. A versioned bucket can never go back to unversioned, so the only change available is to suspend versioning. Step 2: they suspend versioning on the bucket. Step 3: ??? Step 4: to reduce the cost of the versions already stored, they add a lifecycle rule that expires noncurrent versions after 30 days. What belongs in Step 3, the effect of suspending on the 12 existing versions?
choices: The 12 versions are merged into one unversioned object with no version ID.
A delete marker is placed on each older version, so the older versions no longer cost anything.
Suspending deletes the 11 older versions and keeps only the current one.
All 12 versions are kept and are still billed. Suspending only stops new versions from being created.
questions.why: Suspending stops new versions from being created but keeps every existing version, and every version is billed, which is why the lifecycle rule in Step 4 is still needed.

questions.prompt: A museum keeps exhibit-map.svg in a versioned S3 bucket. It has two versions, and the newer one, which is current, is the correct copy. A colleague deletes exhibit-map.svg without naming a version ID, and visitors' apps now get 'not found'. What brings the correct copy back as the current version?
choices: Delete the newer version by naming its version ID.
Set the bucket back to unversioned so the marker is removed.
Suspend versioning on the bucket, which undoes the most recent delete.
Delete the delete marker, so the newer version becomes current again.
questions.why: A plain delete only adds a delete marker as the current version, so removing that marker makes the previous current version current again.

questions.prompt: A law firm uses FSx for Windows File Server, a managed Windows shared drive, and treats its hourly shadow copies as its only backup. The whole file system is accidentally lost. What happens to the shadow copies?
choices: They are kept in a separate S3 bucket and can be restored to a new file system.
They can still be opened through Previous Versions on any Windows computer.
They become MFA Delete protected and can be recovered with a one-time code.
They are lost too, because shadow copies live inside the same file system.
questions.why: Shadow copies are stored in, and use the storage of, the same file system, so they are not a backup and disappear when the file system is lost.

questions.prompt: A monitoring service rewrites heartbeat.txt every minute in a versioned S3 bucket, and the storage bill keeps climbing. Which change addresses the cause of the cost and still keeps versioning on?
choices: Change the bucket back to unversioned for heartbeat.txt only.
Delete heartbeat.txt without naming a version so a delete marker becomes current.
Turn on MFA Delete so versions need a one-time code before they can be removed.
Add a lifecycle rule that expires noncurrent versions after a set number of days.
questions.why: Every stored version is billed, and a lifecycle rule that expires noncurrent versions removes the old copies that build up, which is the usual fix for this cost.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate says, 'We turned on S3 versioning and FSx shadow copies, so we don't need backups.' In your own words, explain what versioning actually protects against, how you would restore a deleted S3 object, and at least one limit or cost tradeoff.
lessons.modelAnswer: Versioning protects against overwrites and accidental deletes inside the same storage. In S3, every upload to a key keeps the earlier copies as noncurrent versions. A plain delete only adds a delete marker, so to bring the object back I delete that marker, or I copy an older version back over the top. FSx for Windows shadow copies let users roll a file back to an earlier scheduled point through Previous Versions. It is not a backup, though. Shadow copies live on the same file system and vanish if it is lost. S3 versions can be permanently removed by a delete that names the version ID, unless we add MFA Delete or similar controls. There is also a cost: every version is billed, so we need a lifecycle rule to expire noncurrent versions. Shadow copies also eat file system space, and the oldest are dropped when that space fills. We still need real backups that are kept separately from the original storage.
rubricPoints: Versioning keeps prior copies so overwrites and accidental deletes can be undone.
A plain S3 delete adds a delete marker, and removing the marker restores the object.
Once enabled, S3 versioning can only be suspended, and existing versions are kept.
FSx for Windows uses scheduled shadow copies stored on the same file system, restored via Previous Versions.
Versioning is not a separate backup, because versions share the fate of the original storage.
Old versions cost storage, so lifecycle rules should expire noncurrent versions.

suggested.rationale: The skill tested is reasoning through recovery situations, such as a deleted object, a bad overwrite or a growing bill, and choosing the right restore step, which exam-style scenarios practise best.

lessons.plain: Disaster recovery (DR) is your plan for getting a service running again somewhere else after the main site is lost, for example when a whole AWS Region (a geographic group of data centres) goes down. There are four common strategies, like four levels of car preparedness. You can carry only a repair kit (backup and restore). You can keep a spare tyre in the boot (pilot light). You can keep a smaller second car idling in the driveway (warm standby). Or you can drive two cars all the time (active/active). More readiness means faster recovery and less lost data, but it costs more every month.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your shop can lose at most 5 minutes of orders and must be back online within 30 minutes. Would a nightly backup copied to another Region be enough? Why or why not?
lessons.teach:
Two numbers drive every DR choice. The recovery time objective (RTO) is the longest the service may be down. The recovery point objective (RPO) is the most data you may lose, measured as time before the failure. You pick the cheapest strategy that meets both.

Backup and restore: you copy backups (point-in-time copies of disks and databases, often called snapshots) to a second Region and build nothing there until disaster strikes. Your RPO equals the gap between backups. Your RTO is often hours, because you must rebuild the network, the servers and the data. It is the cheapest option.

Pilot light: the core data is replicated continuously, for example to a database read replica (a live copy that follows the main database) in the second Region. Servers are switched off or not yet created. RPO is seconds to minutes. RTO is the time needed to launch and scale servers, often tens of minutes.

Warm standby: a complete, working, scaled-down copy of the system runs all the time. In a disaster you scale it up and move traffic with DNS (the system that turns names into addresses), such as Route 53. RTO is minutes.

Active/active, also called multi-site: both Regions serve real users at once. If one fails, the other absorbs the load. RTO and RPO are near zero. It costs the most, and two sites writing the same data can conflict.

Worked example: RTO 30 minutes, RPO 5 minutes. Nightly backups give an RPO of up to 24 hours, so that option fails. Pilot light meets the RPO, but launching and scaling servers plus switching DNS might take 40 minutes, which is risky. Warm standby meets both targets. Active/active also meets both but costs more than needed. The choice is warm standby, unless timed drills prove pilot light finishes under 30 minutes.

Common mistake: judging a plan by its backups instead of a rehearsed restore. Untested plans miss hidden steps such as DNS caching delays, account limits on new servers, or a missing encryption key. In a real outage, those gaps blow the RTO.

questions.prompt: A small accounting firm runs an invoicing app. Its targets are an RTO of 6 hours and an RPO of 1 hour. Step 1: Database and disk snapshots are copied to a second Region every 30 minutes, so at most 30 minutes of data could be lost. That meets the 1-hour RPO. Step 2: In a timed drill, the team rebuilt the network, the servers and the data in the second Region in 3.5 hours. That meets the 6-hour RTO. Step 3: Pilot light, warm standby and active/active would also meet both targets, and each costs more than backup and restore. Step 4: ? Which choice correctly completes step 4?
choices: Choose warm standby, because a shorter RTO than required is always the safer choice.
Choose backup and restore, because it is the cheapest strategy that meets both targets in a tested restore.
Choose active/active, because near-zero RTO and RPO remove the need for timed drills.
Choose pilot light, because any RPO under a few hours requires continuous database replication.
questions.why: The rule is to pick the cheapest strategy that meets both RTO and RPO, and the drill showed backup and restore meets them.

questions.prompt: A clinic's booking system has a recovery point objective (RPO) of 15 minutes. What does that number promise?
choices: After a failure, the service must be running again within 15 minutes.
The team must begin failover no later than 15 minutes after the alarm fires.
If a failure happens, at most the last 15 minutes of data before the failure may be lost.
Backups only need to be kept for 15 minutes before they are deleted.
questions.why: RPO measures how much data you may lose, expressed as time before the failure; the time to get the service back is the RTO.

questions.prompt: A payments company processes card transactions for customers around the clock. Its targets are an RTO under 1 minute and an RPO of almost zero, and leadership has approved the highest DR budget. Which strategy fits these targets?
choices: Backup and restore, with snapshots copied to a second Region every 5 minutes
Pilot light, with a database read replica in a second Region and servers switched off
Warm standby, with a small working copy scaled up and traffic moved by DNS during a disaster
Active/active, with both Regions serving real users at the same time
questions.why: Only active/active, where both Regions already serve users, gives near-zero RTO and RPO; the others need minutes to hours to rebuild, launch or scale.

questions.prompt: A retailer uses pilot light: its database is replicated continuously to a second Region and its servers are not yet created there. The plan was reviewed on paper but never rehearsed. During a real outage, the team tries to launch servers in the second Region and the launch fails because the account is only allowed to run a small number of servers there. What is the main lesson?
choices: The RPO was set too low, because a replicated database cannot meet a strict RPO.
The DNS records should have been updated more often to avoid the launch failure.
The plan was judged by its backups instead of a rehearsed, timed restore, which would have exposed the account limit before a real outage.
Pilot light can never work, so the retailer should switch to backup and restore.
questions.why: Untested plans hide steps such as account limits on new servers, and only a rehearsed restore reveals them before they blow the RTO.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would choose between backup and restore, pilot light, warm standby and active/active for a service. Name the tradeoff that rises as you move up the ladder.
