questions.why: The simulator evaluates the role's policies against that exact action and resource and reports which statement decided it. In this case it shows that nothing allows the call, which justifies the narrow allow added in Step 3.

questions.prompt: A compliance auditor at a travel startup asks who opened a specific customer-records file stored in an S3 bucket last Tuesday. The team has never changed CloudTrail's default settings. They search CloudTrail and find events for the bucket being created and having its policy changed, but no record of anyone reading the file. What is the most likely reason?
choices: CloudTrail only records calls that end in an error such as AccessDenied, so successful reads never appear
CloudTrail events take several weeks to appear, so last Tuesday's reads are not visible yet
Only the IAM policy simulator records object reads, because it replays each request against the bucket
Reading an object is a data event, and data events are only recorded if someone turns them on
questions.why: By default CloudTrail records management events, which are changes to resources. Reads of objects are data events and are only logged if they have been enabled, so no record of the read exists.

questions.prompt: A contractor role at an engineering firm has a policy that allows ec2:StartInstances on the firm's test servers. A second policy attached to the same role denies ec2:StartInstances unless the request comes from the corporate network. The contractor tries to start a test server from home and gets AccessDenied. The policy simulator names the deny statement as the deciding one. What is the right way to understand and fix this?
choices: The allow should win because it is more specific, so the simulator result is wrong and the request should be retried
Attaching administrator access to the role is the fastest safe fix, because administrator access overrides any deny
Adding a second allow for ec2:StartInstances will outweigh the deny, so the request will succeed
The explicit deny wins over the allow, so the contractor should connect from the corporate network rather than have the deny removed or broadened access added
questions.why: In IAM any explicit deny wins regardless of how many allows exist. The condition is doing its intended job, so the fix is to meet the condition instead of opening wider access.

questions.prompt: Months ago, during an outage at a logistics company, someone attached a policy allowing all S3 actions to a reporting role. The team now wants to replace that policy with one that grants only what the role has actually used, based on its recorded activity. Which tool is built to draft that replacement policy?
choices: Administrator access, attached temporarily so that the role's real needs become visible
CloudTrail on its own, because it automatically rewrites attached policies to match the recorded calls
The IAM policy simulator, because it makes real requests for every S3 action and keeps the ones that succeed
IAM Access Analyzer, which can draft a least-privilege policy from the activity CloudTrail recorded for the role
questions.why: IAM Access Analyzer can generate a policy from the role's CloudTrail activity. That draft grants only what the job needs, which is least privilege. The simulator makes no real requests, and CloudTrail only records activity without changing any policy.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would use CloudTrail, IAM Access Analyzer, and the policy simulator to fix an access-denied error without over-granting. Include at least one limit of these tools.
lessons.modelAnswer: First I find the failed call in CloudTrail. The event tells me which identity was denied, which action it tried, and on which resource. If it was an object read in S3, I may see nothing unless data events are turned on. Events can also lag by a few minutes, so an empty search is not proof that nothing happened. Next I put that exact identity, action, and resource into the policy simulator. It tells me whether the denial was explicit, meaning a deny statement, or implicit, meaning no statement allows it. The simulator only judges the policies and context I give it, so a missing condition value can mislead me. Then I add the narrowest allow that fixes it and re-test. Afterwards I use Access Analyzer to check that nothing is now shared externally and that no unused broad permissions are left over.
rubricPoints: CloudTrail identifies who was denied, which action, and which resource.
Data events such as S3 object reads are not logged by default, and events can be delayed.
The policy simulator tests a request without making it and separates explicit deny from implicit deny.
The fix grants only the specific action and resource, not broad or admin access.
Access Analyzer finds external sharing and unused access, and can draft least-privilege policies from activity.

suggested.rationale: An authorization policy evaluator would let the learner trace allow, explicit-deny, and implicit-deny decisions hands-on, which is the core skill the simulator teaches.

lessons.plain: When a company runs many AWS accounts, it needs one place to group them, set limits that every account must obey, and let people sign in once. AWS Organizations groups the accounts into a tree, much like an apartment building. Service control policies are the building rules: no tenant may knock down a load-bearing wall, whatever their own lease says. IAM Identity Center is the front desk. It gives each person one login and hands out keys to the rooms they need. The aim is to give each team freedom inside its own account while keeping hard limits that no single account can switch off.
lessons.guessPrompt: A developer's own permissions say they may do anything in their account. The company has set a rule over all development accounts that blocks one AWS Region. The developer tries to launch a server in that Region. Do you think the launch succeeds or is refused, and why?
lessons.teach:
AWS Organizations is a service that manages many AWS accounts as one unit. The management account creates the organization and pays the bills. Every other account is a member account. Accounts sit under a root and can be grouped into organizational units (OUs). An OU is a folder of accounts, such as Prod or Dev, and OUs can be nested inside other OUs.

A service control policy (SCP) is a guardrail attached to the root, to an OU, or to a single account. An SCP never grants permission. It only sets the maximum an account's users and roles can ever do. An action works only if both of these allow it: the IAM policies on the identity, and every SCP on the path from the root down to the account. An explicit deny anywhere wins. SCPs do not restrict the management account, so keep workloads out of it.

IAM Identity Center is the central sign-in service. A permission set is a reusable template of permissions. When you assign a user or group a permission set on an account, Identity Center creates a matching role in that account, and the user signs in once to use it.

Worked example. Priya has an AdministratorAccess permission set on the account Dev-A. Dev-A sits in the Dev OU. The Dev OU has an SCP that denies all actions outside two approved Regions. Priya tries to launch an instance in a third Region. The first check is her role policy, which allows it. The second check is the SCPs on the path: the root allows it, but the Dev OU explicitly denies it. The request is refused. The fix belongs in the SCP, and only if the business approves that Region. It does not belong in her role.

A common mistake is to replace the default allow-all SCP (FullAWSAccess) with a narrow policy, or to detach it, without giving back the needed allows. In a running system, every role in that OU, including your automation, starts failing at once, even though no IAM policy changed.

questions.prompt: Northwind Labs groups its accounts like this: root, then a Workloads OU, then a Data OU nested inside Workloads, then the account Analytics-2 inside Data. Tomasz has a permission set on Analytics-2 whose policy allows deleting storage buckets. The Workloads OU has an SCP that explicitly denies deleting storage buckets. The Data OU and the root both keep the default allow-all SCP. Tomasz tries to delete a bucket. Step 1: his role policy allows the delete. Step 2: the root SCP allows it. Step 3: ??? Step 4: the request is refused, and any fix belongs in the Workloads OU SCP, and only if the business approves bucket deletion there. Which statement completes Step 3?
choices: The Workloads OU SCP is skipped, because Analytics-2 sits directly in the Data OU, and the Data OU allows the delete.
The Data OU SCP is closest to the account, so its allow replaces the deny inherited from the Workloads OU.
The Workloads OU is on the path from the root down to Analytics-2, so its explicit deny applies, and a deny anywhere wins.
The permission set explicitly allows the delete, so it overrides the Workloads OU deny for Tomasz's role.
questions.why: Every SCP on the path from the root to the account must allow the action, and an explicit deny anywhere on that path wins, so the parent OU's deny blocks the request.

questions.prompt: At Halden Retail, an administrator assigns the group ReportReaders the permission set ReadOnlyReports on three accounts: Sales-1, Sales-2 and Audit-1. What does IAM Identity Center, the central sign-in service, do as a result?
choices: It grants the read access directly, so any SCP on those accounts no longer applies to the group.
It creates a matching role in each of the three accounts, and group members sign in once to use those roles.
It creates a separate IAM user with its own password for every group member in each of the three accounts.
It turns the permission set into an SCP and attaches it to the OU that holds the three accounts.
questions.why: A permission set is a reusable template, and assigning it on an account makes Identity Center create a matching role there that the user reaches through a single sign-in.

questions.prompt: At Brightwave, the account Media-7 sits in the Content OU. The only SCP on the path allows all storage (S3) actions. A developer's role in Media-7 has an IAM policy that grants nothing for storage. The developer tries to read a file from a bucket. What happens, and why?
choices: It is refused, because SCPs only allow actions inside the management account.
It succeeds, because a missing IAM rule counts as neither allow nor deny, so the SCP decides.
It succeeds, because the SCP allows all storage actions for every role in Media-7.
It is refused, because an SCP never grants permission and the role's own IAM policy does not allow the read.
questions.why: An action needs both the identity's IAM policy and every SCP on the path to allow it; an SCP only sets the maximum and grants nothing by itself.

questions.prompt: At Corvid Finance, the management account also runs the company's payment database, because it was the first account created. The security team attaches an SCP at the root that explicitly denies deleting databases. An hour later, an engineer signed in to the management account deletes a test database without any error. What explains this, and what is the sound fix?
choices: SCPs do not restrict the management account, so the fix is to move workloads such as the database out of it into member accounts.
The engineer's IAM policy allowed the delete, and an IAM allow overrides an SCP deny, so the IAM policy must be removed.
SCPs take up to a day to apply, so the deny will start blocking deletions in the management account later.
The root is not on the path for the management account, so the SCP should be attached directly to the management account instead.
questions.why: SCPs never limit the management account, so the safe remedy is to keep workloads out of it and run them in member accounts where guardrails do apply.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how Organizations, SCPs, and IAM Identity Center work together. Then explain why giving someone administrator access in a member account does not mean they can do everything, and name one limit of SCPs.
lessons.modelAnswer: Organizations groups our accounts under a root and into OUs, such as Prod and Dev, with one management account at the top. SCPs attach to the root, an OU, or an account, and act as a ceiling. They never grant anything. An action only works if the identity's IAM policy allows it and every SCP from the root down to the account also allows it. Any explicit deny wins. Identity Center gives people a single login. It assigns permission sets to accounts, and those become roles inside each account. So a user can be an administrator in Dev-A and still be blocked by a Region-deny SCP on the Dev OU. One limit is that SCPs don't apply to the management account, so we keep workloads out of it. Another is a tradeoff: a careless SCP edit, like removing the default allow-all, can break every role in an OU at once.
rubricPoints: Organizations groups accounts under a root and OUs, with one management account.
SCPs set maximum permissions and never grant access themselves.
Effective access requires both the IAM policy and every SCP on the path to allow it, and an explicit deny wins.
IAM Identity Center gives single sign-in and turns permission sets into roles in the assigned accounts.
Names a limit, such as the management account not being restricted or a careless SCP change locking out a whole OU.

suggested.rationale: Tracing a denial through the identity policy and the layered SCPs is a hands-on evaluation skill, and an authorization policy evaluator would let the learner practise it directly.

lessons.plain: AWS Trusted Advisor is a built-in advisor that regularly inspects your AWS account against a list of best-practice checks and tells you where you look risky, wasteful, or fragile. Its security checks look for common unsafe settings, such as a firewall rule open to the whole internet, a storage bucket anyone can read, or the all-powerful root login without a second factor. Think of it as a building inspector walking your property with a checklist: it points at the unlocked back door, but you still have to decide how to lock it without trapping the people who legitimately use it.
lessons.guessPrompt: An advisor tool flags that a server's firewall lets anyone on the internet try to log in on the remote-login port. Before learning anything, what do you think the safest fix is: delete the server, delete the firewall rule, or narrow who the rule allows? Why?
lessons.teach:
AWS Trusted Advisor is a service that runs automated checks across your account and reports each one with a status: green means no problem detected, yellow means investigate, and red means action is recommended. Security checks include security groups (virtual firewalls attached to instances) allowing unrestricted access, meaning source 0.0.0.0/0 or ::/0, to sensitive ports such as 22 for SSH remote login or 3389 for remote desktop; Amazon S3 buckets (object storage containers) whose permissions allow public read or write; no multi-factor authentication (MFA, a second proof such as a code from a device) on the root user, the account's unrestricted original identity; and Amazon EBS or Amazon RDS snapshots (disk or database backups) marked public. Every account gets a core set of these security checks; the full catalogue needs a Business-level or higher support plan.

It works because these settings are visible in your configuration, so a scanner can compare them with known-safe patterns without guessing your intent. That is also its limit: it cannot know who legitimately needs access, so remediation is your judgment.

Worked example. The check for security groups with unrestricted access to specific ports turns red. Step one: open the flagged item and note the group and the rule, port 22 from 0.0.0.0/0. Step two: find which instances use that group. Step three: ask who actually needs SSH; say it is the operations team from one office range, 203.0.113.0/24. Step four: replace the rule with that range, or remove SSH entirely and use AWS Systems Manager Session Manager, a browser or command-line shell that needs no inbound port. Step five: refresh the check and confirm it turns green.

A common mistake is deleting the rule or bucket policy blindly, which cuts off legitimate users and causes an outage, or excluding the item from the report so the warning disappears while the exposure remains. Fix the narrowest thing that closes the risk, then re-run the check.

questions.prompt: A small architecture firm, Lindqvist Design, sees the Trusted Advisor security group check go red. Here, a security group is a virtual firewall attached to instances. The flagged rule opens port 3389 (remote desktop) to ::/0, meaning any IPv6 address on the internet. The engineer works through it. First, they open the flagged item and record the group name and the rule, port 3389 from ::/0. Second, they find that two rendering workstations use that group. Third, they ask who really needs remote desktop. The answer is only the firm's IT contractor, who connects from the fixed range 198.51.100.16/28. Fourth: [MISSING STEP]. Fifth, they refresh the check and confirm it is green. Which action belongs in the missing step?
choices: Replace the ::/0 source on port 3389 with 198.51.100.16/28 so that only the contractor's range can connect.
Change the source from ::/0 to 0.0.0.0/0 so the rule applies to IPv4 traffic instead of IPv6.
Mark the flagged item as excluded in Trusted Advisor so the red status stops appearing.
Delete every inbound rule on the group so nothing can reach the workstations, then deal with any complaints later.
questions.why: Narrowing the source to the one range that legitimately needs remote desktop closes the public exposure without cutting off the contractor, and the re-run check can then turn green.

questions.prompt: A Trusted Advisor security check for a public storage setting shows a red status, and a teammate asks why the service did not simply fix it automatically. Which statement best explains this?
choices: Trusted Advisor compares visible settings with known-safe patterns, but it cannot know who legitimately needs access, so choosing the fix is the engineer's judgment.
Trusted Advisor can only read settings on accounts with a Business-level support plan, so it has no permission to change them.
Red only means the check has not finished running, so there is nothing to fix yet.
Trusted Advisor fixes problems automatically, but only after the status has stayed red for a week.
questions.why: The scanner sees your configuration but not your intent, so it flags risky patterns and leaves the remediation decision to you.

questions.prompt: At Harbour Freight Analytics, Trusted Advisor flags an Amazon S3 bucket (an object storage container) named shipment-uploads because its permissions allow public write. One internal application role legitimately writes files to it, and nobody outside the company should. What is the best remediation?
choices: Exclude the bucket from the Trusted Advisor report, because the application needs to write to it.
Delete the bucket policy entirely without checking what it grants, then re-run the check.
Remove the public write permission, keep write access only for the internal application role, then re-run the check.
Make the bucket public read instead of public write, since reading is less dangerous than writing.
questions.why: This is the narrowest change that closes the public write exposure while keeping the one legitimate writer working, and re-running the check confirms the fix.

questions.prompt: At Cobalt Clinics, an engineer sees a red Trusted Advisor finding: an Amazon EBS snapshot (a disk backup) is marked public. To clear the dashboard quickly, they exclude the item from the report, and the warning disappears. What is the actual result for the running system?
choices: The snapshot is deleted, so the clinic has lost that backup.
Nothing changes, because public snapshots are only a risk on accounts without MFA on the root user.
The snapshot is now private, because excluding an item from the report also changes its permissions.
The snapshot is still public and the exposure remains; only the warning has been hidden.
questions.why: Excluding an item only hides the warning; the snapshot's public setting is unchanged, so the data stays exposed until the setting itself is fixed.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what Trusted Advisor security checks do and how you would safely remediate a red finding, including one thing the tool cannot tell you.
lessons.modelAnswer: Trusted Advisor scans our account against best-practice checks and marks each green, yellow or red. The security ones catch things like security groups open to 0.0.0.0/0 on ports like SSH or RDP, publicly readable S3 buckets, public EBS or RDS snapshots, and a root user without MFA. When something is red, I don't just delete the rule. I find the exact resource, see what depends on it, find out who really needs access, and narrow it, for example limiting SSH to our office range or switching to Session Manager so no inbound port is needed. Then I refresh the check to confirm it went green. The limit is that the tool only reads configuration; it doesn't know business intent, so a bucket meant to be public needs a human decision. Also, the full set of checks requires a higher support plan, and hiding a finding is not fixing it.
rubricPoints: Trusted Advisor runs automated best-practice checks and rates them green, yellow, or red.
Names at least one concrete security check such as open ports to 0.0.0.0/0, public S3 buckets, public snapshots, or root without MFA.
Remediation narrows access to who truly needs it rather than deleting resources or rules blindly.
Re-run or refresh the check to verify the fix.
The tool cannot know intent, so a human judges legitimate exposure; excluding a finding does not fix it.
Notes that the full set of checks depends on the support plan.

suggested.rationale: Remediating a flagged finding is mostly a judgment call about how narrowly to fix it, which an exam-style scenario to reason through practises best since no current mission or planned engine simulates Trusted Advisor.

lessons.plain: Compliance means proving your cloud setup follows a set of rules, such as "all storage must be private" or "customer data stays in Europe". Continuous monitoring means a service checks those rules all the time instead of once a year. Think of a building inspector who lives in the building, notices each change the moment it happens, and writes it down. In AWS you start by choosing where things run (the Region, a geographic area of data centers) and which services you allow. Then AWS Config, a configuration-tracking service, keeps checking your resources. A conformance pack is a bundle of those checks that you deploy and score together.
lessons.guessPrompt: If a monitoring service checks your resources only in the Region where you switched it on, what could go wrong when a teammate launches servers in a different Region?
lessons.teach:
Region and service selection come first. A Region is an independent geographic group of AWS data centers. Data residency rules, meaning laws or contracts that say where data may be stored, decide which Regions are allowed. Not every service is covered by every compliance program, so a team also limits itself to services that the auditor accepts. AWS publishes audit reports showing which services each program covers.

AWS Config is the monitoring layer. A configuration recorder captures a configuration item, which is a snapshot of a resource's settings, every time that resource changes. A Config rule compares those settings to a desired state and marks the resource COMPLIANT or NONCOMPLIANT. AWS supplies managed rules, and you can also write custom rules. A rule can run when a change happens or on a schedule. A remediation action is an automated fix linked to a rule, usually a Systems Manager Automation runbook, which is a scripted sequence of steps. A conformance pack is a template that groups rules and their remediations so they deploy as one unit, across many accounts and Regions if you want, with one combined compliance score.

Here is a worked example. A pack contains the rule "S3 buckets must block public access" with automatic remediation. First, a developer turns off the public access block on a bucket in eu-west-1. Second, the recorder logs a new configuration item. Third, the change triggers the rule, which marks the bucket NONCOMPLIANT, and the pack's score drops. Fourth, the runbook switches the block back on. Fifth, the bucket is re-evaluated and shows COMPLIANT. The history stays on record as audit evidence.

A common mistake is forgetting that Config is Regional. If the recorder runs only in us-east-1, resources in other Regions are never checked, and the dashboard looks clean while it is blind. A second point to remember is that Config detects and corrects problems after they happen. It does not block the change in the first place. Prevention needs separate controls, so in a running system there is always a short window where a resource is out of compliance.

questions.prompt: A clinic network's contract says patient records may be stored only in Canada. Its cloud team works through compliance setup in order. Step 1: they limit all workloads to the ca-central-1 Region, because data residency (a rule about where data may be stored) points there. Step 2: they read AWS's published audit reports and drop one service their auditor's program does not cover. Step 3: they deploy a conformance pack, which is a template grouping Config rules and their fixes, containing a rule that database storage must be encrypted. Step 4: ______. Step 5: when someone creates an unencrypted database in ca-central-1, the rule marks it NONCOMPLIANT and the pack's score drops. Which action belongs in Step 4?
choices: Turn on the AWS Config recorder in us-east-1 only, since one recorder watches every Region
Nothing more is needed, because rules check resources even when no recorder is running
Turn on the AWS Config configuration recorder in ca-central-1 so resource changes there are captured
Rewrite the encryption check as a custom rule, because managed rules cannot run in ca-central-1
questions.why: Config is Regional, so the recorder must run in ca-central-1 to capture configuration items there, and those items are what the rule evaluates.

questions.prompt: A retail company runs 40 AWS accounts. Its security lead wants the same set of Config rules and their automated fixes deployed to every account and Region as one unit, with a single combined compliance score. What does she need?
choices: A Systems Manager Automation runbook
A data residency rule
A conformance pack
A configuration item
questions.why: A conformance pack groups rules and their remediations so they deploy together across accounts and Regions, and it reports one combined score.

questions.prompt: A media firm's AWS Config dashboard has shown 100% COMPLIANT for months. During an audit, an inspector finds several storage buckets in ap-south-1 that break company policy. The recorder has only ever been turned on in eu-central-1. What is the most likely explanation?
choices: The remediation runbooks fixed the buckets, and then the buckets drifted back
Config is Regional, so resources in ap-south-1 were never recorded or evaluated at all
The rules run on a schedule, and the ap-south-1 check simply has not come due yet
Managed rules only check resources created after the conformance pack was deployed
questions.why: With no recorder in ap-south-1, no configuration items exist there, so the dashboard looks clean while it is blind to that Region.

questions.prompt: A logistics company sets up a Config rule requiring that server firewall rules never allow remote login from the whole internet, with automatic remediation turned on. A manager says, "Now nobody can ever create that open rule." What is the accurate response?
choices: Correct: automatic remediation stops the change before it is saved
Not quite: remediation only works for custom rules, so a managed rule will just report the problem
Not quite: Config detects and fixes the change after it happens, so the open rule exists briefly, and blocking it needs a separate preventive control
Correct, but only when the rule runs on a schedule instead of on each change
questions.why: Config works after the fact, so there is always a short window of non-compliance, and prevention requires separate controls.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how a conformance pack keeps an account compliant, and name one limit of relying on it alone.
lessons.modelAnswer:
We pick approved Regions for data residency and approved services that our auditors accept. Then AWS Config records a snapshot of every resource each time it changes. Rules compare those snapshots to what we require and mark each resource compliant or noncompliant. A conformance pack bundles those rules, plus automated fixes such as Systems Manager runbooks, into one template. We can deploy that template to many accounts and Regions and track a single score. The recorded history also gives us audit evidence.

There are two limits. First, Config is Regional, so any Region where the recorder is not enabled goes completely unmonitored. Second, Config is detective, not preventive. A bad change actually happens first, and only then is it flagged and remediated. That leaves a short exposure window, so we still need preventive controls to stop the riskiest changes before they happen.
rubricPoints: Region and service choices are driven by data residency and by which services the compliance program covers.
Config records configuration items and rules evaluate them as compliant or noncompliant, either on change or on a schedule.
A conformance pack is a deployable bundle of rules and remediations with a combined compliance score.
Remediation runs automated runbooks to fix noncompliant resources.
Config is Regional and must be enabled in every Region that is used.
Config detects and corrects after the fact, so it does not prevent the change.

suggested.rationale: No mission or planned engine simulates AWS Config, so reasoning through exam-style audit scenarios, such as a clean dashboard that misses a Region, builds the skill best.

lessons.plain: A data classification scheme is a short, agreed list of sensitivity levels, such as Public, Internal, Confidential and Restricted, plus rules for how each level must be handled. Think of a hospital stamping folders with coloured labels: anyone can read a green leaflet, but a red patient file stays in a locked room and only certain staff may open it. In the cloud, the labels go on storage and servers, and automated checks make sure the handling rules are actually followed rather than just written down. Implementing the scheme means three jobs: finding where sensitive data lives, labelling it, and enforcing the rules that go with each label.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your company labels a storage bucket 'Confidential' but nothing else changes. Who can still read it, and what would you need to add so the label actually protects the data?
lessons.teach:
A data classification scheme is a fixed set of sensitivity levels, each with handling rules such as who may access it, whether it must be encrypted, and whether it may ever be public. On AWS the label is usually a tag, a key-value pair attached to a resource, for example DataClass=Confidential. A label alone does nothing. It only becomes a control when other tools read it.

Implementation has three parts. Discovery: Amazon Macie, a managed service that scans object storage (S3 buckets) for sensitive content such as names, card numbers or credentials, tells you which buckets hold sensitive data so you can label them correctly. Labelling consistency: a tag policy in AWS Organizations (the service that groups many accounts under one management account) defines the allowed tag keys and values, so nobody can type 'confidental' and slip past your rules. Enforcement and detection: attribute-based access control (ABAC) means writing permission policies whose condition keys, extra tests inside a policy, compare tags, for example allowing access only when the caller's DataClearance tag matches the resource's DataClass tag. An AWS Config rule, a continuous check of resource settings, can flag any bucket that is missing the DataClass tag or is Confidential but publicly readable.

Worked example. Macie reports that bucket orders-export contains customer addresses. Step one: tag it DataClass=Confidential. Step two: the tag policy confirms that value is allowed. Step three: an access policy denies reads unless the caller carries DataClearance=Confidential; an analyst without that tag is now denied. Step four: a Config rule marks the bucket non-compliant if the tag is removed or public access is switched on.

Common mistake: treating tags as the whole control. If anyone who can edit the bucket can also change its tags, they can relabel Confidential data as Public and walk around ABAC. Restrict who may change classification tags. In a running system, the consequence of getting this wrong is either quiet exposure of sensitive data or a flood of access denials when legitimate users lack matching tags.

questions.prompt: A payroll firm wants only staff cleared for Internal data to read the bucket payslips-q3. The firm uses attribute-based access control (ABAC), which means permission decisions compare tags. A tag is a key-value label on a resource or identity. The work so far: Step 1: the role used by the payroll clerks is tagged DataClearance=Internal. Step 2: the bucket payslips-q3 is tagged DataClass=Internal. Step 3: a policy statement allows reading objects, but only when a condition is met. Step 4: a contractor role tagged DataClearance=Public tries to read a payslip and is denied, while the clerks can read. What condition belongs in Step 3?
choices: Skip the condition, because the tag policy in AWS Organizations already blocks the contractor
Allow the read whenever the bucket carries any DataClass tag, whatever its value
Allow the read only if the caller also has permission to edit the bucket's tags
Allow the read only when the caller's DataClearance tag equals the bucket's DataClass tag
questions.why: ABAC works by having the policy's condition compare the caller's clearance tag with the resource's classification tag, which is why the clerks are allowed and the Public contractor is denied.

questions.prompt: A retail company tags its loyalty-card bucket DataClass=Confidential. It has no policies, rules or other tools that refer to that tag. What does the tag do on its own to protect the data?
choices: Nothing by itself; it only becomes a control when other tools, such as access policies or Config rules, read it
It denies reads to anyone without a matching clearance tag
It encrypts every object in the bucket
It blocks public access to the bucket automatically
questions.why: A classification label is just a key-value pair. It enforces nothing until something like an ABAC policy or a Config rule acts on it.

questions.prompt: An audit of a travel agency's 40 accounts finds buckets tagged DataClass=Confidental, DataClass=confidential and DataClass=CONF. Because of this, its access rules that look for Confidential miss these buckets. Which control stops these variations from being applied in the first place?
choices: An AWS Config rule that flags public buckets
An ABAC condition comparing the caller's tag to the resource's tag
A tag policy in AWS Organizations that defines the allowed tag keys and values
Amazon Macie, scanning the buckets for sensitive content
questions.why: A tag policy sets the permitted keys and values across the organisation's accounts. This keeps labelling consistent, so misspelled values cannot slip past rules that match on the exact value.

questions.prompt: At an insurer, access to the bucket claims-photos depends on its DataClass=Restricted tag matching the caller's clearance tag. A developer without Restricted clearance has full edit rights on the bucket, including changing its tags. He changes the tag to DataClass=Public and can then read the files. What is the right fix?
choices: Remove the ABAC condition and grant all developers read access
Restrict who may change classification tags, separately from who may edit the bucket
Add more Macie scans of the bucket
Make the tag policy allow the value Public
questions.why: Tags are not the whole control. If anyone who edits a resource can relabel it, they can walk around ABAC, so changing classification tags must be limited to authorised people.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how our data classification scheme is actually enforced on AWS, from finding sensitive data to blocking access, and name one weakness or tradeoff of relying on tags.
lessons.modelAnswer: Our scheme is a list of sensitivity levels, Public through Restricted, each with handling rules. First we find sensitive data: Macie scans our S3 buckets and reports things like personal details or card numbers. Then we label each resource with a DataClass tag, and an Organizations tag policy limits the tag to approved spellings and values. Enforcement comes from ABAC: access policies include conditions that only allow a caller whose clearance tag matches the resource's DataClass. A Config rule continuously flags resources with a missing tag or with Confidential data exposed publicly. The weakness is that everything hangs on the tag being correct. If someone can edit tags, they can downgrade a label and bypass the controls, so tag changes must themselves be tightly permitted. The tradeoff is operational: strict tag matching can cause access denials when users or roles are missing the right tags.
rubricPoints: Defines classification as defined sensitivity levels with handling rules per level.
Names discovery of sensitive data, for example Macie scanning object storage.
Explains tags as the label and tag policies for consistent values.
Explains enforcement through tag-based policy conditions (ABAC) and detection through Config rules.
Names the risk that tags can be changed to bypass controls, or that missing tags cause denials.

suggested.rationale: Classification spans discovery, labelling and enforcement across several services, so reasoning through exam-style scenarios about which piece failed teaches it best.

lessons.plain: Encryption at rest means data sitting on a disk, in a bucket, or in a database is scrambled so that anyone who steals the storage sees only noise. AWS Key Management Service (KMS) is a managed service that holds the master keys and decides who may use them. Picture a hotel: your data is locked in a room, and the room key itself sits in a guarded key cabinet at the front desk. Even a guest who can reach the room door cannot get in unless the front desk agrees to hand over the key. Most encryption problems in operations are really front-desk problems: someone was never allowed to use the key.
lessons.guessPrompt: An application's role has permission to read files from a storage bucket, yet downloading one particular file fails with an access-denied error. That file was encrypted using a KMS key. Before any teaching, guess what extra permission the role might be missing, and who might need to grant it.
lessons.teach:
AWS KMS is a managed service that creates and guards encryption keys and performs cryptographic operations on your behalf. A KMS key is a master key that never leaves KMS in plain form. An AWS managed key is one a service creates for you automatically; a customer managed key is one you create, so you control its policy, rotation (automatic yearly replacement of the underlying key material), and deletion.

It works through envelope encryption: KMS generates a data key, a short-lived key the service uses to encrypt your actual data. The data key is then itself encrypted by the KMS key and stored next to the data. To read, the service asks KMS to decrypt the data key, which only succeeds if the caller is allowed to use the KMS key. So access to encrypted data needs two permissions: one to the data and one to the key.

Permission to use a key comes from the key policy, a resource policy attached to the key itself, combined with IAM policies, which are permissions attached to users and roles. The key policy must allow the account or role; an IAM policy alone cannot grant key use unless the key policy trusts the account.

Worked example: a role reads an object in a bucket encrypted with a customer managed key and gets AccessDenied. Step one, confirm the role has read permission on the bucket: it does. Step two, check the key: the error names kms:Decrypt. Step three, read the key policy: it lists only the admin role. Step four, add a statement allowing this role kms:Decrypt on that key only. The read succeeds.

A common mistake is fixing it with a key policy that allows everyone kms:* , which hands out decryption of all data under that key. Also remember keys are regional, and a disabled key or one scheduled for deletion breaks every read and write that depends on it. After the waiting period, from 7 to 30 days, deletion is permanent and the encrypted data becomes unrecoverable.

questions.prompt: At a regional hospital network, an analytics role suddenly gets errors reading reports from a storage bucket encrypted with a customer managed key (a KMS key the team created and controls). The same reads worked yesterday. The engineer traces it. Step one: confirm the role still has read permission on the bucket. It does. Step two: read the key policy (the resource policy attached to the key). It still allows the analytics role kms:Decrypt on this key. Step three: ______. Step four: re-enable the key, and the reads succeed again without any change to who is allowed to use it. Which action belongs in step three?
choices: Check the key's state and find that someone disabled it
Create a replacement key in a different region and point the bucket at it
Attach an IAM policy to the role granting kms:Decrypt on all keys
Change the key policy so that everyone is allowed kms:* on the key
questions.why: Both permissions were already in place, and step four re-enables the key, so step three must have found that the key was disabled, which breaks every read that depends on it.

questions.prompt: An online bookshop stores customer files in a bucket that uses KMS envelope encryption. In this design, what does the KMS key itself encrypt?
choices: The data key, which is stored next to the encrypted data
Each customer file directly, inside KMS
Only the file names, while the file contents stay in plain form
The bucket's access policy, so attackers cannot read it
questions.why: In envelope encryption a short-lived data key encrypts the actual data, and the KMS key encrypts that data key, which is stored alongside the data.

questions.prompt: At a ticketing startup, a billing role has an IAM policy (a permission attached to the role) that allows kms:Decrypt on a customer managed key. The role still gets AccessDenied on kms:Decrypt. The key's policy names only a security-admin role and does not trust the account. What is the narrowest fix?
choices: Add a statement to the key policy that allows everyone kms:* on the key
Give the billing role full administrator rights in the account
Switch the data to an AWS managed key so that no key policy applies
Add a key policy statement allowing the billing role kms:Decrypt on this key
questions.why: An IAM policy alone cannot grant key use unless the key policy allows the account or role, so the narrow fix is to allow just this role kms:Decrypt in the key policy.

questions.prompt: A logistics company schedules deletion of a customer managed key with a 14-day waiting period. On day 5, the applications that read and write data encrypted under that key start failing. Which statement is accurate?
choices: Data stays readable after deletion because the data key is stored next to the data
The key can be copied to another region after deletion to recover the data
Nothing should fail until day 14, so the errors must come from a bucket permission problem
The failures are expected now, and once the 14 days pass the data under that key becomes unrecoverable
questions.why: A key scheduled for deletion breaks every read and write that depends on it, and after the waiting period the deletion is permanent and the encrypted data is lost.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate, in your own words, why a role that can read a bucket can still get access-denied on an encrypted object, how you would fix it narrowly, and one risk of managing your own KMS keys.
lessons.modelAnswer: KMS uses envelope encryption: each object is encrypted with a data key, and that data key is stored encrypted under a KMS key. To read the object, the service has to ask KMS to decrypt the data key on the caller's behalf, so the caller needs permission to the data and separately permission to use the key, such as kms:Decrypt. Key use is controlled by the key policy on the key plus IAM policies, and the key policy must trust the account or role. If the error mentions kms:Decrypt, I'd add a statement allowing only that role kms:Decrypt on that specific key, not kms:* for everyone. The tradeoff with customer managed keys is that control cuts both ways: disabling the key breaks all access, and once a scheduled deletion finishes its waiting period the data is unrecoverable.
rubricPoints: Describes envelope encryption: data key encrypts data, KMS key encrypts the data key.
States that reading encrypted data needs both data access and key-use permission.
Names the key policy as the resource policy that must allow the role or account.
Fixes with least privilege, granting only the needed action on the specific key.
Notes a risk such as disabled keys breaking access or deletion making data unrecoverable.

suggested.rationale: Doing envelope encryption by hand and seeing a decrypt fail when key permission is missing builds the exact two-permission mental model this objective tests.

lessons.plain: Encryption in transit means scrambling data while it travels across a network, so anyone listening in sees only noise. The usual method is TLS (Transport Layer Security), the protocol behind the padlock in a browser. TLS needs a certificate: a digital ID card proving a server really owns a name like shop.example.com. AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) is a managed certificate service. It issues those ID cards, attaches them to services such as load balancers, and renews them before they expire. Think of it as a passport office that also posts out the replacement passport before the old one runs out.
lessons.guessPrompt: You attach a certificate for www.example.com to your website's load balancer. A customer types example.com, without the www. Do you think their browser will show the padlock or a warning, and why?
lessons.teach:
AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) creates, stores and renews TLS certificates. A certificate binds one or more domain names to a public key. A trusted authority signs it, so browsers believe it. ACM's public certificates are attached to integrated services rather than copied onto your own servers. The main integrated services are Elastic Load Balancing (a managed load balancer), CloudFront (a content delivery network) and API Gateway (a managed API front door). The service handles the TLS handshake for you, which is called TLS termination.

Before issuing a certificate, ACM must confirm you control the domain. DNS validation asks you to add a CNAME record, which is a DNS alias entry. Email validation sends approval mail to the domain's contacts. DNS validation is preferred because ACM renews automatically for as long as the CNAME stays in place and the certificate is in use. Certificates you import from another authority are never renewed by ACM. You must watch their expiry, for example with the DaysToExpiry metric or expiry events.

Worked example: an Application Load Balancer runs in eu-west-1. You request a certificate in eu-west-1 for example.com and *.example.com, choosing DNS validation. ACM shows Pending validation and gives you a CNAME record. You create that record in your DNS zone. Minutes later the status becomes Issued. You add an HTTPS listener on port 443 that uses the certificate. Then you change the port 80 HTTP listener to redirect to HTTPS. Browsers now show the padlock.

Common mistakes: requesting the certificate in the wrong Region, or leaving a name off it. A load balancer can only use a certificate from its own Region, and CloudFront only accepts certificates from us-east-1. A wildcard such as *.example.com covers one label only, so it matches www.example.com but not example.com or a.b.example.com. If you delete the validation CNAME, renewal silently fails. Months later the certificate expires and every visitor sees a security error. Also remember that termination at the load balancer protects only the client-to-balancer hop. Traffic onward to the backends travels unencrypted unless you configure HTTPS to the targets as well.

questions.prompt:
Lumen Books keeps its static shop website in an S3 bucket in ap-southeast-2 (Sydney). Visitors reach it through a CloudFront distribution, which is a content delivery network. The team wants visitors to use https://shop.lumenbooks.net with a valid padlock. Here is how they worked it through.

Step 1: They list the names the certificate must cover. Only shop.lumenbooks.net is needed.

Step 2: (missing)

Step 3: ACM shows the certificate as Pending validation and gives them a CNAME record. They add that record to their DNS zone, and soon the status changes to Issued.

Step 4: They attach the certificate to the distribution for the alternate domain shop.lumenbooks.net. Browsers now show the padlock.

Which action belongs in Step 2?
choices: Request a public certificate for shop.lumenbooks.net in us-east-1 and choose email validation
Request a public certificate for shop.lumenbooks.net in us-east-1 and choose DNS validation
Import a certificate for shop.lumenbooks.net from another authority into ap-southeast-2
Request a public certificate for shop.lumenbooks.net in ap-southeast-2, where the bucket lives, and choose DNS validation
questions.why: CloudFront only accepts certificates from us-east-1, and Step 3's CNAME record shows that DNS validation was chosen, which also lets ACM renew the certificate automatically.

questions.prompt: OrbitPay has an ACM certificate whose only name is *.orbitpay.io. Which hostname does this certificate cover?
choices: orbitpay.com
eu.api.orbitpay.io
orbitpay.io
status.orbitpay.io
questions.why: A wildcard covers exactly one label in place of the asterisk. That means status.orbitpay.io matches, but the bare domain, a name two labels deep, and a different domain do not.

questions.prompt: A retailer's load balancer used an ACM certificate that was issued with DNS validation. It worked for over a year. Then one morning every visitor saw a security error saying the certificate had expired. Months earlier, an engineer had removed DNS records that looked unused. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The HTTP listener on port 80 was not set to redirect to HTTPS
DNS-validated certificates are never renewed by ACM, so someone has to reissue them by hand every year
The validation CNAME record was deleted, so ACM's automatic renewal failed silently and the certificate expired
The load balancer moved the certificate to a different Region, so it could no longer use it
questions.why: ACM keeps renewing a DNS-validated certificate only while the validation CNAME stays in place. Deleting that record makes renewal fail without warning until the certificate expires.

questions.prompt: An audit of a payroll app finds a problem. Browsers connect over HTTPS to an Application Load Balancer, which is a managed load balancer, using an ACM certificate. However, traffic from the load balancer to the backend servers is unencrypted. What fixes this finding without changing anything else?
choices: Configure the load balancer to use HTTPS when it connects to the backend targets
Switch the certificate from DNS validation to email validation
Request the certificate again in us-east-1 and attach the new one
Add a second wildcard name to the load balancer's ACM certificate
questions.why: TLS termination at the load balancer protects only the hop from the client to the balancer. Encrypting the next hop requires configuring HTTPS to the targets as well.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how ACM gets a working HTTPS site onto a load balancer and keeps it working, and name one limit or tradeoff they must watch for.
lessons.modelAnswer: ACM issues a TLS certificate that proves we own our domain names. First we request it in the same Region as the load balancer, listing every name users will type. A wildcard covers only one level, so we add the bare domain too. With DNS validation, ACM gives us a CNAME record to publish. Once it sees that record, the certificate becomes Issued. We attach it to an HTTPS listener on 443 and redirect port 80 to HTTPS. The tradeoff is that the load balancer terminates TLS, so traffic to the backend instances is plain unless we also enable HTTPS to the targets. Renewal is automatic only while the validation CNAME stays in DNS and the certificate is in use. Imported certificates never renew, so we alarm on days-to-expiry. CloudFront is the exception on Region: its certificate must live in us-east-1.
rubricPoints: A certificate binds domain names to a key and lets the service perform TLS for clients.
The certificate must be in the same Region as the load balancer, or in us-east-1 for CloudFront.
DNS validation uses a CNAME record that must stay in place for automatic renewal.
Every hostname users visit must be on the certificate, and a wildcard covers one level only.
Imported certificates are not renewed by ACM, so expiry must be monitored.
Termination at the load balancer leaves the backend hop unencrypted unless re-encryption is configured.

suggested.rationale: No current mission or planned engine exercises certificates, and the exam tests this through scenarios such as wrong Region, missing names or failed renewal, which are best practised by reasoning through situations.

lessons.plain: A secret is any small piece of information that grants access: a database password, an API key, a token. Storing secrets securely means keeping them out of code, config files and server images, and putting them in a locked, managed vault instead. Applications ask the vault for the secret when they run, and the vault checks who is asking before handing it over. Think of a hotel front desk holding room keys: guests don't carry copies home, the desk checks ID each time, and the locks can be changed without reprinting every guidebook. On AWS, the main vaults are Secrets Manager and Systems Manager Parameter Store.
lessons.guessPrompt: If a database password is typed directly into an application's source code, what problems appear when the password must be changed, and who can end up seeing it?
lessons.teach:
A secret store is a managed service that keeps credentials encrypted and releases them only to callers that have permission. AWS offers two. AWS Secrets Manager is a dedicated secret vault that can rotate secrets, meaning it automatically replaces the old value with a new one on a schedule, usually by running a small Lambda function (a short piece of code AWS runs on demand) that updates both the database and the stored value. Systems Manager Parameter Store is a hierarchical configuration store; its SecureString parameter type holds a value encrypted with a key. It is cheaper and simpler but has no built-in rotation. Both encrypt values with AWS KMS, the managed encryption key service.

Why it works: the secret lives in one place, never in code or images, and every read is an authenticated, logged request checked against IAM, the permission system.

Worked example: an app on an EC2 server needs a database password. First, an admin stores it in Secrets Manager with 30-day rotation. Second, the server gets an instance role, an identity attached to the machine, allowed to read only that secret. Third, at startup the app calls the store, receives the value, and connects. Fourth, rotation runs; the next fetch returns the new password, and no one edited code.

If the secret is encrypted with a customer managed KMS key, the role also needs permission to decrypt with that key. Missing that second permission is a common cause of access denied even when the secret permission looks correct.

Common mistake: placing the password in a plain environment variable, launch script or server image. Anyone who can view the instance configuration can read it, and changing it means redeploying. A related mistake is caching the value forever: after rotation, the app keeps using the old password and database logins start failing, so apps should refresh the cached value periodically or retry with a fresh fetch on authentication errors.

questions.prompt: A regional bakery chain runs an order-processing Lambda function (a short piece of code AWS runs on demand). It needs an API token for its payment provider. The team works through it like this. Step 1: an admin stores the token in AWS Secrets Manager, the managed secret vault, and encrypts it with a customer managed key in AWS KMS (the managed encryption key service), rather than the default key. Step 2: the function's role, the identity it runs as, gets permission to read only that one secret. Step 3: [missing]. Step 4: on each invocation, the function asks Secrets Manager for the token, receives it, and calls the payment provider without an access denied error. Which action belongs in Step 3?
choices: Turn on 7-day rotation for the secret so that the function always receives a freshly issued token
Change the role's permission so that it can read every secret in the account, not just the one
Give the same role permission to decrypt with the customer managed KMS key that protects the secret
Also copy the token into an environment variable on the function as a fallback if the read fails
questions.why: When a secret is encrypted with a customer managed KMS key, the caller needs permission to decrypt with that key as well as permission to read the secret, and granting only that key is the narrowest fix.

questions.prompt: A logistics company keeps a warehouse database password that must be replaced automatically every 45 days. The team does not want to build its own scheduler to do this. Which store fits that requirement as described?
choices: A plain-text parameter in Parameter Store, with a reminder in the team calendar
AWS Secrets Manager, with rotation configured on a 45-day schedule
A KMS customer managed key, saving the password directly inside the key
Systems Manager Parameter Store, saving the value as a SecureString parameter
questions.why: Secrets Manager has built-in rotation that replaces the value on a schedule. Parameter Store SecureString encrypts the value but has no built-in rotation, and a KMS key protects data rather than storing it.

questions.prompt: A ticketing company's reporting service reads its database password from Secrets Manager once at startup. It keeps that value in memory for weeks. The secret rotates every 20 days. Right after a rotation, the reporting service alone starts failing database logins, while freshly started services connect fine. What is the most likely cause and fix?
choices: The service's role lost permission to read the secret, so the role should be granted access to all secrets
Rotation broke the secret, so rotation should be turned off and the password hardcoded in the service
The KMS key was deleted during rotation, so the key must be restored before the service can read again
The service cached the old password indefinitely, so it should refresh the value periodically or re-fetch it when a login fails
questions.why: After rotation, the store returns the new password, but an app that cached the old value forever keeps sending it, so it needs to refresh periodically or re-fetch when authentication fails.

questions.prompt: An audit at a veterinary clinic network finds an email server password written in plain text in the launch script of its EC2 servers. Anyone who can view the instance configuration can read it. Which remediation closes the finding without granting more access than needed?
choices: Move the password out of the launch script and bake it into the server image so it is no longer visible
Store the password as a SecureString in Parameter Store, and let the servers' instance role read only that parameter
Store the password in Parameter Store, and let the instance role read every parameter in the account
Keep the password in the launch script, but restrict which administrators can view the instance configuration
questions.why: Putting the secret in an encrypted store and letting the machine's role read only that one item keeps it out of the configuration and limits access. Moving it into the image still exposes it, and broad read access opens the door wider than needed.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would store a database password for an app on AWS, when you would choose Secrets Manager versus Parameter Store, and one limit or tradeoff to watch for.
lessons.modelAnswer: I'd keep the password out of code, environment files and server images and put it in a managed secret store. The app runs with a role that may read only that one secret, and it fetches the value at runtime. I'd pick Secrets Manager when I want automatic rotation, because it can replace the password on a schedule using a Lambda function. For simple configuration values or secrets I rotate by hand, Parameter Store SecureString is cheaper and simpler, but it has no built-in rotation. Both encrypt with KMS, so if we use our own KMS key, the role needs decrypt permission on that key too, or reads fail with access denied. The tradeoff with rotation is caching: if the app holds the old value forever, it breaks after rotation, so it must refresh periodically or re-fetch when authentication fails.
rubricPoints: Secrets are kept out of code, config files and images and fetched at runtime from a managed store.
Access is granted through a narrowly scoped IAM role, and reads are authenticated and logged.
Secrets Manager offers automatic rotation; Parameter Store SecureString is simpler and cheaper without built-in rotation.
Values are encrypted with KMS, and a customer managed key requires decrypt permission as well.
Caching a secret forever breaks the app after rotation, so it must refresh or re-fetch.

suggested.rationale: That mission has the learner fix a deployment that cannot authenticate by wiring a secret correctly without exposing it, which is the core practical skill here.

lessons.plain: These five services are the security alarm system of an AWS account. Each one watches a different thing. GuardDuty looks for signs of an attacker in activity logs. Inspector looks for known software weaknesses on servers, container images and functions. Config records how resources are set up and flags settings that break your rules. Security Agent is an AI-assisted reviewer that checks application designs and code and can run penetration tests. Security Hub gathers everyone's findings in one place. Think of a building: motion sensors, a lock inspector, a floor-plan checker, and one front desk that watches every screen and decides who responds.
lessons.guessPrompt: If a monitoring service reports that one of your servers is talking to a known cryptocurrency-mining address, would you delete the server immediately, or do something else first? Why?
lessons.teach:
A finding is a record that one service has spotted a possible security problem. Each finding names the resource, the problem type and a severity. Each service produces its own kind of finding. Amazon GuardDuty is a managed threat detector: it reads API activity logs, network flow logs and DNS queries, and it reports behaviour that looks hostile. Amazon Inspector is a vulnerability scanner: it checks EC2 instances, container images and Lambda functions for software with known flaws, called CVEs, and for network exposure. AWS Config is a configuration recorder: Config rules judge each resource as compliant or noncompliant. AWS Security Agent is an AI-assisted application security service that reviews designs and code against your requirements and runs penetration tests on demand. AWS Security Hub is the aggregator. It collects all these findings in one common format and runs security standards, which are sets of automated checks, many of them built on Config. It can also gather findings from many accounts and Regions into one delegated administrator account.

For reporting, you can use Security Hub insights, which are saved, grouped views of findings, or you can export findings to storage. Remediation can also be automated. Amazon EventBridge is an event router: a rule matches a finding and starts a fix, such as a Lambda function or a Systems Manager Automation runbook.

Worked example. First, a Config rule marks an S3 bucket noncompliant because it allows public reads. Second, Security Hub shows the failed control. Third, an automatic remediation attached to the rule runs a runbook that turns on Block Public Access, using an IAM role scoped to only that action. Fourth, Config re-evaluates the bucket, finds it compliant, and the finding's workflow status moves to RESOLVED.

One common mistake is to suppress or archive findings just to turn the dashboard green. A second mistake is to terminate a compromised instance right away. A safer response to a GuardDuty threat is to isolate the instance with a restrictive security group and snapshot its disks first. That keeps the forensic evidence and stops the damage without destroying the record.

questions.prompt: A veterinary clinic chain runs its booking system on AWS. A security standard in Security Hub (a set of automated checks) includes a check that no security group allows SSH (port 22) from 0.0.0.0/0, meaning from any address on the internet. The team wants such failures fixed automatically, with no human clicking. Step 1: A developer adds an inbound rule allowing port 22 from 0.0.0.0/0 to a security group named web-tier. Step 2: The check fails, and Security Hub records a finding that names the web-tier group, the problem type and a severity. Step 3: ??? Step 4: The function removes only that one inbound rule. The check is evaluated again, passes, and the finding's workflow status moves to RESOLVED. Which choice correctly fills Step 3?
choices: An administrator archives the finding so the Security Hub dashboard shows no failed checks for web-tier.
An Amazon EventBridge rule matches this finding and starts a Lambda function whose IAM role may revoke security group inbound rules and nothing else.
A Lambda function with full administrator permissions deletes the whole web-tier security group so it cannot be misused.
Amazon Inspector scans the web-tier security group for CVEs and patches the instances that use it.
questions.why: EventBridge is the event router that matches a finding and starts an automated fix, and giving the fix a narrowly scoped role repairs the problem without opening the door wider than needed.

questions.prompt: A logistics company runs a fleet of container images in a registry and a few Lambda functions. The security lead asks which service will tell them that one of those images contains a library with a known, published software flaw (a CVE). Which service produces that kind of finding?
choices: Amazon Inspector, because it scans instances, container images and Lambda functions for known flaws
AWS Config, because its rules mark each resource as compliant or noncompliant
AWS Security Hub, because it collects findings from other services in one format
Amazon GuardDuty, because it reads API activity logs, network flow logs and DNS queries
questions.why: Inspector is the vulnerability scanner that checks EC2 instances, container images and Lambda functions for software with known CVEs; Security Hub only aggregates such findings.

questions.prompt: At 02:10, GuardDuty raises a high-severity finding: an EC2 instance in a payments team's account is sending traffic to a server known for controlling hacked machines. The on-call engineer must act now. Which first response best limits damage while keeping evidence?
choices: Reboot the instance and change the root password, then keep it serving traffic
Apply a restrictive security group to isolate the instance, then snapshot its disks
Terminate the instance immediately so the attacker loses access to it
Suppress the finding until the payments team is awake to review it
questions.why: Isolating with a restrictive security group stops the hostile traffic, and snapshotting the disks first preserves forensic evidence that termination would destroy.

questions.prompt: A university IT department runs 25 AWS accounts across 3 Regions. The auditors want one place where they can see every security finding, grouped by severity and by resource, without logging in to 75 account-and-Region combinations. What should the CloudOps engineer configure?
choices: Amazon GuardDuty in each account, with the auditors given read access to all 25 accounts
Security Hub in a delegated administrator account that gathers findings from all accounts and Regions, with insights saved as grouped views
Amazon EventBridge rules in each account that terminate any instance named in a finding
An AWS Config rule in each Region that archives low-severity findings so fewer remain to review
questions.why: Security Hub can aggregate findings from many accounts and Regions into one delegated administrator account, and insights are saved, grouped views of those findings for reporting.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how Security Hub, GuardDuty, Inspector, Config and Security Agent fit together, and how you would automatically fix a finding. Name one tradeoff of automatic remediation.
lessons.modelAnswer: Each service watches a different thing. GuardDuty spots threatening behaviour in activity, network and DNS logs. Inspector finds known vulnerabilities in instances, container images and functions. Config checks resource settings against rules. Security Agent reviews application designs and code and can run penetration tests. Security Hub pulls all their findings into one format, runs security standards built largely on Config, and can aggregate across accounts and Regions, so I triage in one place. To fix a finding automatically, I write an EventBridge rule that matches the finding type and starts a Lambda function or an SSM Automation runbook. The runbook runs under a role that can do only that one fix. Afterwards I confirm the finding resolves on re-evaluation. The tradeoff is that automation is fast but blunt. A wrong match can break a legitimate resource or destroy evidence. So I automate low-risk fixes like blocking public access, and for threats I isolate and snapshot rather than delete.
rubricPoints: Names what each detection service watches: threats, vulnerabilities, configuration, and application design and code.
Explains that Security Hub aggregates findings and runs standards across accounts and Regions.
Describes automated remediation through EventBridge triggering Lambda or Systems Manager Automation.
Mentions least-privilege permissions for the remediation role.
Names a tradeoff, such as automation breaking legitimate resources or destroying forensic evidence.
Warns against suppressing findings just to clear the dashboard.

suggested.rationale: No current mission or planned engine simulates these AWS findings services, so the best practice is reasoning through exam-style scenarios: matching a finding to the service that raised it and choosing a fix that is no wider than needed.

lessons.plain: A VPC (virtual private cloud) is your own private, walled-off network inside AWS. You divide it into subnets, smaller address ranges that each sit in one data center zone. Picture an office building. The VPC is the building and subnets are floors. Route tables are the signs telling traffic which exit to take. The internet gateway is the front door to the street. Two kinds of guards check traffic. One stands at each floor's stairwell and checks a list in both directions; that is the network ACL. The other stands at each office door and remembers who left, so it lets them back in; that is the security group. A NAT gateway is a mailroom that lets private floors send letters out without letting visitors in.
lessons.guessPrompt: A server sits in a private subnet with no public address, yet it needs to download software updates from the internet. Nobody on the internet should be able to start a connection to it. What kind of middleman would you put between that server and the internet?
lessons.teach:
A VPC is an isolated virtual network with an address range written in CIDR notation, for example 10.0.0.0/16. The /16 means the first 16 bits are fixed, which leaves about 65,000 addresses. A subnet is a slice of that range, such as 10.0.1.0/24, placed in one Availability Zone (an isolated group of data centers).

A route table is a list of rules. Each rule maps a destination range to a target. Every subnet uses exactly one route table, and every table includes a local route so all subnets in the VPC can reach each other.

An internet gateway (IGW) is the VPC's two-way door to the internet. A subnet counts as public only because its route table sends 0.0.0.0/0 (all other IPv4 traffic) to the IGW. Its instances also need public IP addresses.

A NAT gateway (network address translation) sits in a public subnet. It lets private instances open outbound IPv4 connections but refuses connections that start from outside. An egress-only internet gateway does the same outbound-only job for IPv6. IPv6 addresses are globally unique, so no address translation is needed.

A security group is a stateful firewall attached to a network interface. It holds allow rules only, and replies to allowed traffic return automatically. A network ACL (access control list) is a stateless firewall on a subnet. Its numbered allow and deny rules are checked lowest number first, and return traffic needs its own rule.

Worked example: a private server at 10.0.2.15 fetches a patch over port 443. First, its security group allows outbound 443. Second, the subnet's network ACL allows outbound 443. Third, the route table sends 0.0.0.0/0 to the NAT gateway. Fourth, the NAT gateway replaces the source address with its own fixed public address and forwards the traffic through the public subnet's route to the IGW. Fifth, the reply comes back. The security group passes it automatically, but the network ACL must allow inbound traffic on ephemeral ports 1024-65535 (the temporary ports clients use for replies).

Common mistake: people assume the network ACL is stateful like the security group and skip that return rule. In a running system, the connection then times out silently even though every outbound rule looks correct.

questions.prompt: A bike-rental company runs a web server at 10.20.1.40 in a public subnet of the VPC 10.20.0.0/16. A customer on the internet opens the site over HTTPS (port 443). Trace the path. Step 1: the subnet's route table sends 0.0.0.0/0 to the internet gateway, and the server has a public IP address. Step 2: the subnet's network ACL allows inbound TCP 443. Step 3: the server's security group allows inbound TCP 443. Step 4: the server sends its reply, and the security group lets the reply out automatically because it is stateful. Step 5: ______. Step 6: the reply reaches the customer through the internet gateway and the page loads. Which statement correctly fills step 5?
choices: The network ACL must allow outbound traffic to ephemeral ports 1024-65535, the temporary port the customer's browser is waiting on.
The route table must send the reply to a NAT gateway, because only a NAT gateway can return traffic to the internet.
The network ACL must allow inbound traffic on ephemeral ports 1024-65535 so the reply can leave the subnet.
Nothing more is needed. Because the security group passed the reply, the network ACL also treats it as part of the allowed connection.
questions.why: A network ACL is stateless, so the reply leaving the subnet needs its own outbound rule to the client's ephemeral ports 1024-65535, even though the security group passes the reply automatically.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm has a subnet 10.8.3.0/24 in its VPC. A new engineer asks what actually makes that subnet a public subnet. Which answer is correct?
choices: A NAT gateway has been placed inside it.
Its route table sends 0.0.0.0/0 to the internet gateway, and its instances also need public IP addresses to be reachable.
The security groups of its instances allow inbound traffic from 0.0.0.0/0.
Its address range sits outside the VPC's local route.
questions.why: A subnet is public only because its route table points all other IPv4 traffic (0.0.0.0/0) at the internet gateway; its instances also need public IP addresses to be reached.

questions.prompt: A research lab runs servers in a private subnet that use only IPv6 addresses. The servers must download dataset updates from the internet, but nothing on the internet may start a connection to them. What should the route table point the IPv6 internet route at?
choices: The internet gateway directly, because IPv6 addresses are globally unique
An egress-only internet gateway
A NAT gateway, because it translates the servers' addresses to a public address
The local route, because it already covers all traffic inside the VPC
questions.why: An egress-only internet gateway gives IPv6 traffic outbound-only access with no address translation, which is what a NAT gateway does for IPv4.

questions.prompt: A media agency's subnet network ACL has these inbound rules: rule 90 denies TCP port 22 from 203.0.113.0/24, and rule 100 allows all traffic from 0.0.0.0/0. The instance's security group allows inbound port 22 from anywhere. An admin at 203.0.113.25 cannot connect over SSH (port 22). Why?
choices: Network ACL rules are checked lowest number first, so rule 90 matches and denies the traffic before rule 100 is reached.
Rule 100 wins because a broader allow rule always overrides a narrower deny rule.
The instance's security group must also allow outbound port 22 for the inbound connection to start.
The security group's allow rule is ignored because security groups can hold deny rules that override it.
questions.why: A network ACL evaluates its numbered rules from the lowest number, and the first match (rule 90, a deny) decides, so the traffic is blocked at the subnet before the security group matters.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how a server in a private subnet reaches the internet for updates. Walk through every piece the traffic touches, and name one tradeoff or limit, such as stateful versus stateless filtering or the difference between IPv4 and IPv6 outbound access.
lessons.modelAnswer: The server's outbound request first passes its security group, a stateful firewall on its network interface, so we allow outbound 443. Next it crosses the subnet's network ACL, which is stateless, so we allow outbound 443 there too. The private subnet's route table sends 0.0.0.0/0 to a NAT gateway.
